en: Homage to the Supreme God, whose self is unconquered by the three qualities (guṇas),
who is everywhere the form of yoga, and who is the cause of the cessation of saṃsāra.
Salutation to the wise Mahādeva, the twenty-sixth principle, the Pradhāna, who spreads within as the cause of maintenance, destruction, and creation.
In the great field of Prajāpati, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Kālindī,
at Prayāga, the supreme and most meritorious path to the world of Brahmā.
Sages of disciplined soul, whose impurities had been destroyed by austerity,
having performed their daily rites on the full-moon day, set out for the purpose of bathing at the sacred fords.
Not seeing the Sūta, who was devoted to truth and a knower of the Purāṇas,
they bathed in that great sacred ford and approached him for the purpose of paying their respects.
Seeing the charioteer approaching, the sages, with joyful minds,
prepared for him a seat and a place to rest as was appropriate.
Having bowed down to all those bulls among sages, the Sūta,
endowed with all virtues, took the seat that was offered to him.
In ancient times, O virtuous one, the sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest, who had been strengthened by their austerities, questioned him as he sat at the Brahma-sacrifice.
"The narrative of the Mahābhārata and the supreme Purāṇa have been told by you;
therefore, you appear to us as the son of Satyavatī himself."
He knows the supreme meaning of all scriptures, is devoted to truth and righteousness, and is constantly intent on honoring the twice-born; therefore, you ought to question him.
We ask you indeed about the birth of the wise Kārttikeya— that which is distinguished among the Purāṇas and is like the Bhārata narrative.
For all these sages are devoted solely to your worship,
their minds filled with eager longing to serve Skanda’s birth.
Thus addressed by those perfected, eminent sages, Sūta then spoke these words, which expressed the true state of affairs, to all the munis.
Listen, all you sages, to the birth of Kārttikeya,
his devotion to Brahman, his majesty, and his valor which surpasses that of the thirty gods.
When the great-souled Śuka had departed for the supreme abode out of a desire for liberation,
Vyāsa, tormented by grief for his son, beheld Tryambaka.
Upon seeing Maheśāna, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, became free from all suffering; at that time, the sage wandered through the worlds.
Then, on the peak of Mount Meru, he beheld the first-born son of Brahmā,
Sanatkumāra, the granter of boons, endowed with the sovereign power of yoga.
He stood in a celestial chariot resembling the sun, possessing a radiance like fire,
surrounded by high-souled sages who were perfected in yoga and devoted to asceticism.
It was surrounded by those who knew the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, who were endowed with the knowledge of all dharmas and scriptures,
and who had acquired every branch of learning, as if by the four faces of Brahmā himself.
Having seen that great-souled sage Vyāsa standing there,
he paid homage with supreme devotion, as if to the Grandfather himself.
Then the son of Brahmā, having embraced the highly effulgent Vyāsa who had arrived, spoke these auspicious words with supreme affection.
"By good fortune, O knower of dharma, through the grace of the Supreme Lord, you have attained freedom from sorrow; ask whatever you wish, and I shall explain it to you."
O Brahmins, having heard the words of his son, that bull among sages spoke these words to Brahmā, which had long resided in his heart.
How was the birth of the wise Kumāra Kārttikeya? For what reason and from whence did it come? Indeed, I wish to know this.
How was he the son of Rudra, and how was he the son of Agni and Gaṅgā? Furthermore, how was he the son of Umā, and again, how was he the son of Svāhā,
of Suparṇī, of the Mothers, and of the Kṛttikās?
Who was he that arose in the past, what were his austerities, and what was his valor?
For this [account] is indeed a delusion for all beings; tell it to me exactly as it happened.
Sūta said:
Thus questioned, that radiant and most excellent son of Brahmā,
the omniscient one, related everything to Vyāsa, who performs his deeds without effort.
Listen to that, O sinless ones, as it is being recounted by me according to its true nature.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. Sanatkumāra said:
I take refuge in the god Īśāna, the omniscient and unconquered,
the Great God, the Great-Souled One, the Lord of the entire universe.
His power is unimpeded and his sovereignty is universal;
they declare that his lordship and pervasiveness are the fruits of his own deeds.
Having bowed down to that divine Soma, being self-restrained and pure,
I shall relate the auspicious account of the origin of Skanda for one who desires to know the ancient narratives.
The descent of the body of the god Rudra, the Supreme Self;
his consecration by Prajāpati; and likewise the severing of his head.
The vision of those belonging to the six families, the dismissal of the wheel, the origin of Naimiṣa, and the conclusion of the sacrificial session.
In that place, there is the arrival of Brahmā, as well as the practice of asceticism,
the vision of Śarva, and the manifestation of the Goddess.
The truth regarding the dispute, as well as the curse of Dakṣa,
the birth of Menā, and how the Goddess’s svayaṃvara took place.
The granting of boons by the gods, the account of the wise Vasiṣṭha,
and the births of Parāśara and the high-souled Vyāsa.
The occurrence of the conflict between Vasiṣṭha and Kauśika, the desolation of Vārāṇasī, and the description of the greatness of the sacred field (kṣetra). SkP 2.9.
And here is the presence of Rudra, as well as the grace of Nandin,
the vision of the Gaṇas, and their narration in its entirety.
The utterance of Kālī, as well as the performance of ascetic penance,
the narrative concerning Somanandin, and likewise the granting of the boon.
The state of being Gaurī, the obtaining of a son, the very origin of the Goddess,
Kauśikī’s status as the mother of the Bhūtas, and likewise the lions who are her chariot-warriors.
The abode of Gaurī on the Vindhya mountains, the meeting of the Vindhya range with the sun,
the majesty of Agastya, and the slaying of Sunda and Nisunda.
The departure of Nisumbha and Sumbha, the slaying of Mahiṣa,
the consecration by the Kauśikī river, and likewise the granting of boons.
The birth of Andhaka, the binding of the Earth,
and likewise the slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakaśipu.
The binding of Bali, the agreement with the Goddess, the departure of the gods, and Agni’s role as a messenger; SkP_2.16 //
The granting of boons by the gods and the dismissal of Śukra;
likewise, the birth of a son and the sight of Andhaka by the Goddess.
The crushing of the Daityas beginning with Śailādi, the hundredfold forms of the Goddess,
the granting of boons by Āryā, and the hymn of praise (stava) to Śailādi.
The arrival of the god, as well as the narration of what had occurred,
the account of the devoted wife, and the service rendered to the preceptor.
The narrative of Pañcacūḍā and the invincibility of her splendor,
the arrival of the messenger, their conversation, and then his dismissal.
The dialogue with the Asura Andhaka, the arrival at Mount Mandara,
the arrival of the Gaṇas, and likewise the hearing of their enumeration.
Then there was the subduing of Andhaka through a great battle,
as well as the granting of half his body and the taking in of Aśoka’s son.
The origin of Bhasmasoma, as well as his dwelling in the cremation ground;
the blue-throated nature of Rudra, and likewise the description of his sacred abodes.
The birth of Kubera, the wise king of the yakṣas;
the subduing of the lords of serpents; and the felling of Śikhara.
And indeed, the subjugation of the three worlds together with Śakra,
the granting of the army of the gods, and the consecration as commander-in-chief.
The arrival of Nārada, who had been sent by Tāraka,
the fierce slaughter of Tāraka, and the expedition to Bhadravaṭa.
The slaying of Mahiṣa, the destruction of Krauñca,
the extraction of the Śakti, and the auspicious killing of Tāraka.
The origin of fear among the gods and asuras, the battle of the three cities (Tripura), the conflict with Prahlāda, and the narrative of the ungrateful— these,
along with the great majesty of the Brahmins, are proclaimed in detail.
Having understood this correctly, one should become an attendant of Kumāra;
being strong and endowed with intelligence, he obtains a highly esteemed son.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. Sanatkumāra said:
Listen to this divine narrative, which destroys all sins, as it is being told by me—wondrous, rich in meaning, and equal to the Vedas;
having heard which, even one who has committed sinful deeds shall attain the supreme goal. (SkP 3.1)
One should never relate this discourse to an atheist, one who lacks faith, a rogue, nor to a man who is envious.
O Great Brahmā, this should be told to a son, a disciple who is righteous and free from malice, or to one devoted to the gods,
as well as to one devoted to Kumāra and possessed of faith.
In ancient times, Brahmā, the overseer of creatures, was born within this cosmic egg;
yet, enveloped by darkness, that Brahmā did not know his father due to ignorance.
Realizing "I am alone," he surveyed all the worlds;
yet, endowed with the power of austerity and yoga, he saw no other there.
When he was addressed as "Son, son" by the wise Śarva, Brahmā,
bowing down with palms joined in reverence, sought refuge in him alone.
Having bestowed upon Brahmā the power of creation accompanied by knowledge,
as well as sovereignty over the worlds, Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, vanished.
Therefore, O Vyāsa, this eternal Upaniṣad has been proclaimed by me,
hearing which yogins attain Maheśvara through meditation.
To him who in the beginning created Brahmā as his son and who bestowed knowledge upon him—
to those wise ones who perceive Him abiding within themselves belongs eternal peace, and not to others.
Seeing his father endowed with supreme radiance, Vyāsa,
desiring a son for the sake of progeny, performed intense austerity.
The father was indeed fully satisfied within a very short time by that great-souled one, who was endowed with great yogic austerity.
He beheld him, and [the deity] said, "I am the Giver of Boons. Bowing down and placing his joined palms upon his head, he offered praise.
Salutation to the Supreme God, the creator even of the gods;
salutation indeed to the Ordainer of the world, the Lord of Brahmā.
To the one who is endowed with power and free from incapacity,
who is infinite and immeasurable, and who is beyond the reach of the senses.
To the all-pervading one, who was previously pervaded by [the Supreme], the sustainer, the impeller,
the one who has performed the act of conscious awareness, and the one who effects the arrangement of the principles (tattvas).
He is for the sake of granting peace to those possessing qualities who have urged him as their primary leader,
for the sake of bestowing vision upon all, and indeed for his own manifestation.
To the one who perceives objects, to the one who effects restraint,
and likewise to the mind, the sense organs, and the very act of restraint therein— [to him I bow].
To the creator of the qualities of beings, likewise the giver of power,
the maker of the cosmic egg and of me, the inconceivable, the first-born,
the immeasurable Father— being eternally pleased with us, grant us the Śakvarī hymn.
O Vyāsa, while he was thus praising him, the Great Lord Maheśvara, the God of gods,
being pleased, spoke himself to his son Brahmā, who was likewise prostrate before him.
"Because this subtle [reality] has been known by you, O child of great splendor,
therefore you shall attain renown in the worlds by the name 'Brahman'."
And because I have been called "Father" by you, O best among the wise,
therefore your status as "Grandfather" (Pitāmaha) shall become renowned in the world.
Because you have performed fierce and extremely difficult austerities for the sake of progeny, I grant you the status of Prajāpati, O self-restrained one.
Having spoken thus, that Lord of Gods created women in embodied form—
those eight primary elements (prakṛtis) along with the specific objects (viśeṣas) together with the sense organs;
and all those states of being (bhāvas), assuming their own forms, waited upon the God.
Then the Lord, joined with his own splendor, said to them:
"Complete this consecration today; do not delay."
Having each taken up their own inconceivable divine disposition,
Prajāpati, of exceeding splendor, became consecrated by them.

In that regard, having thus seen the subtle with the divine eye, the yogins who know the reality of yoga sing this ancient [hymn] endowed with the three qualities: SkP_3.26: "In that very place, having thus seen the subtle with the divine eye, those who know the reality of yoga sing the ancient [hymn] which is associated with the three qualities."
For Rudra is the creator of all beings and of you as well, O Lord;
together with us, you are the one who sets the world in motion.
That god, fully gratified and possessing supreme sovereign power,
consecrated his first-born son Brahmā in the office of Prajāpati.

He who, having performed various paths joined with yoga, out of reverence established this world called "Reality," and [established] for the gods the supreme, infinite union with yoga, while by means of his powers of illusion he rendered the three worlds blind and devoid of grace.

Ever abiding in the minds of all, knowing both the auspicious and the inauspicious, the Lord of Beings— to that God, the Master of the Pramathas, who is most subtle of the subtle, I bow with devotion and eternally go for refuge.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having obtained the status of Prajāpati, he set about creating progeny;
however, those beings being created did not increase in number for him.
While performing such creation, the Grandfather, being devoid of power,
then began once more to practice austerities for the sake of creation.
Knowing his asceticism to be for the sake of creation, the Lord of the Three Worlds,
the Creator and Master of the Universe, entered the world with his splendor and approached him; he revealed the entire universe within his own body.
Having come in person, Hara, the Lord of Gods and Master of the Great Elements,
as if pervading the entire universe with his supreme own splendor,
Śambhu said to the Grandfather: "O child, ask for a boon."
Brahmā, for the purpose of creating the world, mentally declared, "You are my son.
Having understood that intention of Brahmā, the Supreme Lord,
the bestower of boons, reflected, "This one is deluded," and spoke himself.
"Since you desire a son from your father who has arrived here, therefore,
by my command, your son shall be an embodiment of myself."
And that leader of my gaṇas, Rudra, having become your son and assumed a physical form, O fool, will humble you.
He possesses sovereignty over all branches of knowledge and over all forms of yoga;
he holds lordship over the forces and is a master in the employment of missiles.
All these things given by me shall immediately attend upon her in every respect:
the bow Pināka, the trident, the sword, and even the battle-axe.
A water-pot, a staff, the Pāśupata weapon,
the thunderbolt of universal destruction, and the wheel of reabsorption—
thus endowed with all supernatural powers, that son of yours shall come to be.
When that great-souled one had spoken thus and vanished,
Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, desiring sons, then performed a sacrifice.
While offering oblations, joined with the *śramasa* cup and possessed of restraint,
he wiped his forehead with his hand holding the fuel-sticks.
A drop of sweat born from his forehead, produced by the friction of the fuel-sticks,
fell into that fire and was doubled in size by its brilliance.
For that splendor of Maheśvara, which had been gathered and poured into the Veda,
was impelled by the God of gods and fell into the consumer of oblations.
At that very moment, having remembered that supreme boon, Maheśa dispatched the leader of the Gaṇas, Rudra; and he then became Sadyojāta instantly.
And that fire born of moisture, having first been joined with a flame and become red,
then suddenly turned blue once again.
Because he cried out, "Blue-and-red! (nīlalohita), the Lord thus became so;
three-eyed, ten-armed, and glorious, he stood as if overshadowing Brahmā.
Having praised that omnipresent god, the imperishable Nīlalohita, with names beginning with Śarva and with forms such as water and the rest, Brahmā [proceeded].
Having first known the creator of all, who is established in the great elements,
that Lord then created other various kinds of beings in the world.
He too, having established himself in yoga and endowed with sovereign power,
entered all the worlds and sustained them at all times.
Then, from that [Brahmā], the auspicious sons Dakṣa, Dharma,
and the others created all beings, teeming with gods and humans.
Then, after a great length of time had passed through successive kalpas,
as he sustained the creatures through his yoga, this present kalpa arrived.
When the means of livelihood were established, when the release of rain had begun,
and when the subjects had increased, he was indeed performing a sacrifice at Prayāga.
Those sages of firm vows belonging to the six families of Brahmā were the Marīcis, the Atris, the Vasiṣṭhas, and likewise the Kratus.
The Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases, their sins consumed by austerity,
approached Brahmā together during an interval between rites and spoke.
"O Blessed One, we are enveloped by a great darkness; exhausted and disputing, we do not perceive what lies beyond. (SkP 4.26)
O God, this doubt of ours has long resided within our hearts;
for you alone know the ultimate cause according to its true nature.
What is the supreme among all beings, and what is the strongest in every respect? By whom is the universe presided over? Who is eternal, and who is everlasting?
Who is the creator of all beings and the impeller of primordial nature?
Who is that high-minded one who employs us in all our tasks?
To whom are all beings subject? Who is the director of all?
How may we behold him? Tell us this in its entirety.
Thus addressed, Brahmā then spoke in the presence of all—
the gods, the sages, the gandharvas, the serpents, and the rākṣasas.
Those among the yakṣas and asuras who were leaders anywhere,
along with the birds, the piśācas, and others who were near him,
rose up with palms joined in reverence and uttered the word "Rudra" three times with a protracted tone.
He can be seen through austerity alone, and by no other means;
he is the creator of all beings, powerful, and this world is composed of him.
All beings are subject to his will, and by him this world is sustained.
Then all those lords of the worlds paid homage to that Great-Souled One.
The sages said:
"O God, what is that great penance by which that Lord may be seen?
Tell us that, O Lord of Gods, and grant us a boon."
The Grandfather said:
"Perform a great sacrificial session (sattra), free from the defects of speech and mind;
and I shall tell you the region in which you shall carry it out."
Then, having created that mind-made wheel, he said to them:
"This wheel has been hurled by me; follow it without delay!"
"Wherever its rim should break, that place shall be auspicious for asceticism.
Then he released that discus, and they followed after it.
As he was traveling swiftly, the place where his wheel-rim shattered became known by the name Naimiṣa; it is meritorious and honored everywhere.
It was worshipped by gods, humans, and siddhas; by fierce rākṣasas and divine serpents;
by yakṣas along with hosts of gandharvas and piśācas; by all the apsarases and by the sons of Diti.

It was praised by self-controlled Brahmins engaged in the yoga of tranquility, by all the holy places and the lords of the earth, as well as by Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Cāraṇas, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and the Pitṛs.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: [Chapter 5 of the Skanda Purāṇa]
Having reached that Naimiṣa forest, sages of blazing splendor performed a great divine sacrificial session lasting for a thousand years.
All of them were single-minded, free from the sense of "mine," and devoid of egoism;
they constantly meditated upon the Lord of Lords, together with their wives, sons, and sacred fires.
All of them were devoted to him, intent on him, united with him, and taking refuge in him;
performing all their actions, they had gone to him alone in their minds.
Perceiving their state of mind, the illustrious and auspicious Mātariśvan, the great ascetic who moves within all living beings and impels all creatures,
appeared in embodied form before those performers of the sacrificial session.
Having seen and honored that imperishable Mātariśvan as he sat upon a holy seat, the sages of firm vows questioned him regarding the entire origin of the world as well as its dissolution.
And the entire duration [of the world], the lineages, the ages (yugas), and the intermediate periods (manvantaras);
the complete history of the dynasties, as well as the divine measure of time.
The origin and dissolution of the eight classes of divine beings,
as well as the entire creation of the ancestors and the measurement of Brahmā himself.
The entire course of the moon and the sun, as well as the movement of the stars and planets; the station of all sovereign lords, and the laws of the continents in their entirety;
the establishment of the castes and stages of life, and the performance of sacrifices.
The Lord related all of this in its entirety,
as well as how they remained engaged in that pursuit for a thousand divine years.
Then she appeared with a divine form, having the Sāman as her speech, the quarters of space as her gaze,
the Yajus as her sense of smell, the Atharvaśiras as her head, and the Śabda-veda as her auspicious tongue.
She whose ears are logic, who moves through the words, verses, lines, and syllables of etymology;
she whose arms are time, who causes the rains, and who bears the fingers that are the days.
With her joints as the *kalās* and other divisions, her months as her fingernails,
she was divine, equal to a *kalpa*, and possessed high breasts through her mastery of the sciences.
With the science of prosody as her waist and Mīmāṃsā as her navel,
she has the Purāṇas for her broad hips and the treatises on Dharma as her longings.
Her thighs were the stages of life (āśrama), her knees were the social classes (varṇa), her ankles were the sacrifices (yajña), and her toes were the fruits [of action].
Her body was the worlds and the Vedas, covered with the auspicious hairs of the Vedic meters (chāndasa).
Clad in the garments of faith and virtuous conduct, proclaiming the teachings of yoga,
she emerged from the center of the altar and flowed forth with supreme waters.
At its conclusion, having plunged into the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), they were joined by Vāyu;
they asked him, "Who indeed is this? to the god Vāyu of great intelligence.
That one of great splendor spoke to the sages who were imbued with dharma:
"You are all pure through your asceticism, and great dharma has been performed by you."
Since this meritorious river has come here from the world of Brahmā,
she is named Sarasvatī, the ornament of the world of Brahmā.
"First, she has come to this mortal world for the sake of your success;
there exists no one more meritorious than she in the three worlds."
The sages said:
How did this highly meritorious [river], which leads to the world of Brahmā, come into being?
And what was the cause therein? We wish to know this.
Vāyu said:
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history,
the conversation between Brahmā and the Sacrifice (Yajña) in former times.
In ancient times, having performed sacrifices with blazing splendor, the god Brahmā created all beings, both stationary and moving.
Having seen this, the radiant god, endowed with supreme splendor,
gazed upon his own worlds with his four lotus-like faces.
Having repeatedly beheld the gods and others, as well as humans and others, the high-minded one thought: "In this world, there is no one equal to me, nor anyone superior."
I am he who devours and emits all these creatures established in the seven worlds, among gods, humans, and animals.
For I am indeed the creator of all beings; no other whatsoever exists.
There is no one equal to me anywhere as a ruler or as a maker of the world.
While he was thinking thus, the high-minded Sacrifice arrived;
and that radiant being said to him, "O high-minded one, do not think so!
For this delusion of yours will lead to your destruction. (SkP 5.27)

Such a thing is not fitting for you today, who are established in goodness and born of your own self; for you alone are the creator and there is no other, yet even so, this is not conducive to your glory.
"For I am indeed the creator of beings and likewise of the world;
yet I do not fall into delusion, as you boast, O God."
Then Brahmā said to him: "O Lord, you are not the sustainer;
for I alone am the supporter and the nourisher of all beings.
All beings were created by me; it is you who are utterly deluded in this matter."
Then the Veda, supremely radiant, arrived there in great agitation;
and the Lord Veda said to the two of them, "It is not so."
"I am the best, O highly fortunate ones; I never speak an untruth.
Listen to who is the creator of all beings, and indeed of you two."
The Supreme Lord Mahādeva, Rudra, the omnipresent Master,
is he by whom I was given to you and by whom you were made the Lord of Creatures.
This sacrifice, its origin, and the cosmic egg wherein it is established—all these have indeed proceeded from him;
there is no other creator for us anywhere.
To him who spoke thus, the divine Brahmā addressed this Vedic revelation:
"I am the leader and likewise the creator of all the Śrutis."
"By my grace, you are indeed the Veda and this sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.
You two have been deluded, or else unrighteousness has been committed by you. Perform an expiation, and then you shall be released from that sin."
When he had spoken thus, a great sound arose; and a circle, having the form of the solar disc, was seen in the sky above, accompanied by that immense sound.
And he, having fallen from that state and reached the surface of the earth,
arrived at a thicket of the Himalayas resounded by various birds;
after remaining in the sky for a long time, he indeed became one who dwells upon the ground.
Then Brahmā, the Grandfather, having gazed toward all the directions with his four lotus-like faces, did not see him stationed in the sky.
He created a fifth blazing face situated upon his head;
with that [face], he beheld him stationed in the sky, possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns,
having the form of the solar disc, and appearing terrible with a roaring sound.
Seeing that fifth head of his, which was born of wrath,
immense and resembling the fire of universal destruction, [the serpent] grew in order to swallow it.
Then that [fire], increasing like the mouth of the submarine mare,
blazing and accompanied by sound, was that god whose orb was radiant.
With the nail of the thumb of his left hand,
he indeed swiftly and with utter disdain severed that great and terrible fifth head of Brahmā.
Then, his head severed by the blazing [weapon], afflicted by intense suffering and with a bewildered mind, he indeed fell, deprived of the practice of yoga.
Then, as if having regained consciousness after waking from sleep,
that great ascetic praised Mahādeva, who was stationed within the mandala, with a plaintive voice.
Brahmā said: Salutations to the thousand-eyed one, and indeed salutations to the hundred-eyed one;
salutations to the one with the wide-open mouth, and indeed salutations to the hundred-faced one.
Homage to the thousand-faced one, indeed homage to the one who possesses all faces;
homage to the thousand-footed one, indeed homage to the one who possesses all feet.
Salutation to the thousand-handed one, and salutation to him whose hands are everywhere;
salutation to the creator of all, and salutation to you, the seer of all.
Homage to the one who has the color of the sun, and homage to the one who effects the severing of the head;
likewise, homage to the creator of emanation and dissolution, and to the creator of maintenance.
Salutation to the one with a thousand lingas and a thousand feet;
salutation indeed to the one whose linga is the act of dissolution and whose linga is water.
To Him who moves within, who is all-pervading, who impels primordial nature (prakṛti),
who is omnipresent, and who impels all living beings as the Puruṣa.
To the one who brings about excellence in the senses and their objects,
to the ordainer, to Śarva, who exists in the past and the future, and who is eternally devoted to the welfare of living beings.
O All-pervading Lord, you alone are the creator of the worlds, their thinker, and likewise their giver;
it behoves you to show favor to one who has come for refuge and is self-controlled.
As he was thus praising with perfect and supreme devotion,
that Lord of the Gods of gods then granted him divine vision.
Then, with that eye, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds,
beheld a mass of splendor within a celestial chariot as radiant as the sun.

Then, from the midst of that [sound], they heard a great voice—profound, sweet, appropriate, and endowed with auspicious characteristics—which was first uttered by the god, saying, "O son! O son! in a clear manner.
"O son born from perspiration, because you are blue-and-red (nīlalohita),
and because I previously spoke thus when searching for a son," SkP_5.57.
"O fool, that leader of my attendants who is like an image of me shall attain supreme knowledge and discipline you."
This accomplishment of its fruit—the severing of your head—has been brought about by me alone; therefore, be at peace now.
O Great-minded One, he alone shall cut off the head of that sacrifice which has strayed onto a wrong path for some other reason;
for I am pleased by this hymn— what may I give to you, O sinless one?
Vāyu said:
Then that blessed one, delighted, bowed with auspicious words and,
with palms joined in reverence, spoke to that Lord who was both visible and invisible.
“O Blessed One, the sight of you does not cause me any pain;
rather, I desire that this head of yours be held by you forever, so that I might remember this severing of the head, O Lord. (SkP 5.62)
Furthermore, I desire that you yourself restrain me from unrighteous deeds;
and thus, with this task in mind, may I behold you at your ease.
Having heard the request of Brahmā, the Lord of the World said:
"He who is known as your son is none other than Nīlalohita, my own form;
he shall cut off the head of the sacrifice and he shall carry away your head."

Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods vanished right there. When that Great God had departed, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, together with the sacrifice and the Vedas, returned to his own world.
Vāyu said:
That mortal who should hear this secret, which is equal in meaning to the Vedas, shall,
upon the dissolution of the body, attain union with Brahman.
Whoever constantly recites this in the presence of Brāhmaṇas,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Rudra.
This divine narrative is not to be told to those who are not sons, disciples, or yogis;
nor should it be told to one who lacks understanding, nor to the deceitful, nor to the arrogant.
One should always recite this great, divine ordinance of Dharma in an assembly of Brahmins and physicians;
such a man gains an opportunity here, and upon the dissolution of the body, he shall enter the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. Sanatkumāra said:
Then that blessed god, Kapardin Nīlalohita,
by the command of the Supreme Lord, seized the head of Brahmā.
Having seized that blazing head and assumed a deformed appearance,
he set out for alms, employing the play of yoga.
O twice-born ones, he then went to the abode of the gods for the sake of alms;
yet no one gave that lord a fitting alms-offering.
He went by way of the bridge to the house of the high-souled Viṣṇu;
he stood at his door, uttering the auspicious word for alms.
Having beheld that vulva with his eye of yoga, Viṣṇu split open the head from the forehead and caused a stream of blood to fall;
and it fell, spreading out to a width of fifty yojanas at that time.
O best of Brahmins, although she flowed for many years as a stream from that skull of the Grandfather, not even half of it was filled.

Daughters are given in marriage but once; the sacred fire is kindled but once;

"I am pleased with this appropriate gift of yours, O bestower of honor!
Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—for I am indeed the granter of boons to you today."
Viṣṇu said:
"This alone is a praiseworthy boon,
that I behold the god Śaṅkara, the lord of the deities— the fierce Śarva with matted hair."
Then, seeing the shadow in the liquid contained within the skull,
the god created a radiant man, powerful and resembling Viṣṇu.
He said to him: "You are indeed imperishable and truly ageless and immortal;
you are without rival in battles and the unsurpassed friend of Viṣṇu.
O glorious one, perform the work of the gods and move about together with him."
Since your birth was from the *nārāḥ* (waters) and from the body of Viṣṇu,
you shall therefore be known by the name Nara, and you will be dear to him.
Vāyu said:
Having then comforted him and entrusted that man to Viṣṇu himself,
the Lord went to the abode of Brahmā, and those two entered the house.
Whoever, having obtained this human birth here, should hear or recite this,
shall be endowed with supreme fame and honored in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. Vāyu said: [Chapter 7 of the Skanda Purāṇa] Vāyu said:
Having reached the world of Brahmā, the Blessed One, the protector of all worlds,
stood at the gate, saying, "Alms, alms."
Having seen him thus transformed, adorned with a skull in his hand, Brahmā understood through great yogic power and praised the Lord of the World.
Then the God, pleased with him, spoke: "I am the giver of boons;
choose, without anxiety, whatever boon resides in your heart."
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, I desire that this mark be made by you,
by which mark this world may be marked, O Lord of the universe."
Having heard those words of his, the Blessed One, the best among speakers,
uttered "Om," which is Brahman consisting of all the Vedas.
By the mere utterance of Śambhu,
this goddess of divine form emerged from his mouth and stood there, bowing low.
Then the God spoke to her with a voice that seemed to restore her to life:
"Since you have emerged from my speech as an imperishable being,
O Goddess, you shall therefore become the presiding deity of all knowledge."
"Since this Sarasvatī has taken refuge in my mouth,
therefore you shall attain fame in the world by the name 'Sarasvatī'."
Having purified this world with excellent waters, O Suprabhā, you shall again deliver all the worlds; of this there is no doubt.
And those gods, together with the Grandfathers, will grant you a share of the sacrifice;
you shall become the most meritorious of all rivers—of this there is no doubt.
Then, having been granted permission by Śaṅkara,
that radiant goddess created the meritorious Brahmasaras, which is exceedingly purifying in the world of Brahmā.
It was completely filled with the nectar of water, adorned with golden lotuses,
crowded with flocks of various birds, and its waters agitated by fish;
emerging from there once more, it purified this world.
Taking that skull of immeasurable power, Mahādeva reached this world and established himself in an excellent region.
There, the Lord of the Devas, the Master, placed that great, divine skull— blazing with radiant flames— in front of his attendants.
Then, seeing that which had been established by the Great-Souled One, all the Gaṇas let out a tremendous roar,
making the ten directions resound;
it was like the agitated ocean or a thunderbolt, by which the sky was rent asunder.
At that terrible sound, the Asura known as Hālāhala, a thorn to the gods,
approached that region.
Unable to endure this, the evil-souled one, blinded by rage and a destroyer of sacrifices,
was invulnerable to all living beings due to the boon granted by Brahmā;
Mahiṣa was surrounded by hundreds of Asuras who had assumed concealed forms.
Beholding that buffalo, the thorn in the side of the gods, charging forward in a rage, the leader of the Gaṇas addressed all the attendants of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
"O leaders of the Gaṇas, this wicked Daitya is a thorn to the gods of the three worlds;
he approaches in haste, therefore you must slay him."
Then all those leaders of the Gaṇas, filled with rage, pierced the approaching enemy of the gods with their tridents and deprived him of his life.
When he was slain, the god then gazed upon all the quarters;
from them emerged Piśācas with gaping mouths and mighty Piśācīs,
who approached the Lord of Gods and reported this to him.
Having been fully provided for and assigned duties by them,
they returned once more to that very abode ordained by the gods.
Because those Mothers of the Skulls (Kapālamātaraḥ) ate the buffalo by repeatedly dividing it up, they were thus designated as such by the wise God.
Because the skull was placed in that place by the wielder of the Pināka bow,
it is therefore called Mahākapāla throughout the three worlds.
When the skull had been established, it then became as described;
that place became renowned as Śivataḍāga, which liberates one from all sins.
Then Brahmā, having arrived there surrounded by hosts of deities,
addressed Kapardin and took possession of that place.
This field will extend for half a yojana on all sides;
it will undoubtedly become a field of accomplishment for the Great-Souled One.
For the wise know that *śma* denotes evil and *śāna* denotes destruction; because it is purified through meditation and religious observances, it is designated as *śmaśāna*.
It is the secret, supreme, and most beloved place of the God beyond gods, unsurpassed in excellence.
In this way, a person shall abandon all evil there;
having fasted for three nights and worshipped the bull-bannered god,
he will obtain that fruit which belongs to the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
And that man who shall there renounce his dear life-breaths will attain equality with the gods of the Guhyaka hosts.
Vāyu said:
Then, having established there two auspicious images of the God—
the great-bodied Śūleśvara and the beautiful sanctuary of Rudra— [he departed].
By merely approaching that place, one brings about the destruction of sin and attains the world of Rudra; thus spoke the Grandfather (Brahmā).
And where the Lord of the World cut off his head,
that place became the most meritorious region forever known by the name Kaśmīra.
Then the Lord, having assumed a transformed form along with his attendants,
vanished from the sight of all the gods.
And when the Lord of the Gods had departed, he then endowed the imperishable station of Kapāla with the fruit of bathing at all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Even today, O best of Brahmins, that great divine lake is seen there;
it is known as Mahākapāla, and the worlds attained there are imperishable.

This auspicious, divine Mahākapāla is the destroyer of unrighteousness, yielding great fruit, and is worshipped by Indra, the gods, and the asuras; it reveals the primordial nature and is beneficial for penetrating the worlds of the Lord of the Gods and beyond.

The man who always recites or listens to this, which is praised by those whose wealth is austerity and by hosts of Siddhas, and in which the circle of the twice-born kings is equal to those dwelling in heaven, goes to the third heaven, being greeted with joy.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. Vāyu said: [Chapter Eight of the Skanda Purāṇa] Vāyu said:
Thus this Blessed Goddess, following the path of the world of Brahmā,
emerged from the center of the altar for the sake of your success in the Dharma.
Sanatkumāra said:
When their thousand-year sacrificial session had thus concluded and the Sarasvatī had begun to flow, the Grandfather (Brahmā) went there.
Brahmā said:
"Perform sacrifice once more to the Lord, the God, with another sacrificial session;
when an obstacle arises for you, then your austerity will become free from blemish."
Having overcome that very obstacle and performed radiant austerity,
and having attained the great yoga with which you are now joined, you shall then behold Śaṅkara.
Having said "So be it," when he had departed,
those devoted to great vows then performed many sacrificial sessions of various forms with diligent application.
O twice-born ones, having rendered this entire earth devoid of Soma,
they then desired to consecrate King Soma himself.
Then, even though he had been offered hospitality, the Soma was seized by the evil-minded Svarbhānu, who remained invisible; consequently, they became distressed.
Having gone there, all those sages dwelling in the village of Kalāpa brought King Purūravas and consecrated him.
And those highly fortunate ones said to him: "O Lord, our Soma has indeed been stolen by someone;
therefore, may you bring it back here quickly, without delay."
Having been addressed thus, the Lord, while searching, found Nata;
then, bowing down and tormented by fear, he spoke to the brahmins.
"Exerting the utmost effort, I have searched for Soma, O Lord; yet I do not know by whom he was taken, nor where he has been led."
To him who spoke thus, all the sages of rigid vows, enraged and highly agitated, said to the high-minded son of Ilā: SkP_8.12 //
"O King, why have you been made our protector by us, who are tormented by fear?
And you are not capable of destroying that fear of ours even in an instant."
"With your soul excessively attached to sense-objects, you do not perceive that through yoga;
therefore, by persisting in this hostility, you shall meet your death at the hands of the twice-born."
"O Indra among kings, behold our supreme power; by means of our own ascetic heat (tapas), we ourselves shall bring back the king Durvida. SkP 8.15.
Then all those sages, whose sins had been burnt away by their asceticism,
praised Gāyatrī, the source of the Vedas, with pleasing words.
Then, while they were offering praise, Gāyatrī, the source of the Vedas,
appeared in bodily form before them and spoke these words to those twice-born ones.
"I am pleased, my children; what shall I do for you today? I am a granter of boons to you.
Speak, and that shall be accomplished here without a doubt."
The sages said:
"O Goddess, our Soma has been carried away by some very wicked soul.
Bring him back; salutations to you! This is our supreme boon."
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus, she made her decision and, seeing with her divine eye,
quickly transformed into a hawk and flew toward the asura Svarbhānu.
While the Asuras were distracted, she took the Soma and returned;
having arrived, she said to those Ṛṣis, "Let this Soma be pressed."
Having approached him and obtained the great fruit of their sacrifice, those twice-born sages thought, "Our austerity has become stainless. (SkP 8.22)
Then Brahmā himself, having arrived there along with the gods, serpents, and others, spoke to those sages: "Perform your ascetic penance; do not delay."
Having gone together with Brahmā to Maināka, the best of mountains,
they performed austerities with all the hosts of gods, their minds fully concentrated.
After a long time, for those whose selves had been purified by asceticism, the practice of yoga arose;
consequently, they became engaged in subtle [meditation].
Those sages, together with the gods, joined with Brahmā;
fixing their minds upon Maheśvara, they remained as motionless as stones.
Then Mahādeva, the wielder of the Pināka bow, blue-and-red in hue,
approached that place by means of a celestial chariot possessing the brilliance of the sun.
Having recognized their state of being permeated by that very essence through his supreme,
true nature, he, whose roar was like a thundercloud and whose voice resounded like a hundred kettledrums, spoke to me.
"O gods, including Brahmā, along with Viṣṇu, the ṛṣis, and the cāraṇas:
I grant you divine vision; behold me as you desire!"
Sanatkumāra said: Then they all beheld a celestial chariot, possessing the splendor of ten thousand suns, resembling Mount Meru, and adorned with various jewels.
In its center stood a massive, blazing mountain-peak of fire,
encircled by garlands of flames and adorned with radiant rays.
His face was terrifying with its fangs, his eyes were like blazing fire,
his matted locks were tawny like the three sacrificial fires, and he wore a girdle made of serpents.
He has polished earrings, and his great hand is fixed upon a trident;
he carries the Pināka bow, holds a staff in his hand, and has a mallet and a thunderbolt in his grasp.
He held a thousand sword-blades and a discus, with his phallus erect;
he held a rosary and was difficult to behold by those of unrefined self,
yet he was adorned with garlands and ornaments fashioned from the moon, sun, and planets.
All those gods beheld him with their divine vision— him,
upon seeing whom death would never again occur even for a mortal.

Through their ascetic power, the sages— yogis engaged in disciplined application, endowed with the vision granted by Īśvara in the sky, and filled with joy along with the gods— bowed down to Bhava, who is as stainless as the moon.
Having observed that the Great Lord of Asuras was like Death himself, and having reflected in their minds upon his unbearable nature,
they— having abandoned all thought of self-preservation— bow down together with the gods, praising the Source of the World.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. Sanatkumāra said:
Having beheld the Lord of the gods of gods, all the deities, including Brahmā,
bowed down to him who has the bull as his vehicle and praised him with pleasing words.
The Grandfather said:
Homage to Śiva, who is accompanied by Umā, the remover of fear for his devotees;
homage to him who holds a trident-tip in his hand and carries a water-pot.
To the one who wields the staff, to the blue-throated one, to the one with formidable teeth,
to the one whose eyes blaze like the three sacrificial fires, to the three-eyed one, and to Hara.
Salutations indeed to the wielder of the Pināka bow;
let there be salutations to the bearer of the thunderbolt, to him who has a serpent as his sacred thread and who is adorned with earrings.
Salutations to the wielder of the discus and to the wearer of the tiger skin;
likewise to him who has a black antelope skin as his upper garment and a serpent for his girdle.
And to Rudra, the giver of boons, likewise to the one created by Sarasvatī,
who wears garlands of the moon, sun, and stars, and who holds a rosary in his hand.
Salutations indeed to the one with thousands of garlands of flames, to the upward-pointing Liṅga;
salutations to the dweller of the mountains and to the one who formerly took away my head.
Homage to the destroyer of Hālāhala, who wears the excellent skull-bowl,
whose vehicle is the best of celestial chariots, who is my very progenitor,
the giver of boons, the most eminent one, and the lover of the cremation ground.
Homage to the maker of man and homage always to the sustainer; homage to the creator of origins and dissolutions, and to the all-enduring one.
O Lord of the ṛṣis and gods, sovereign of all beings, O Śiva, gentle one, Lord of the deities, be gracious to us, you who are affectionate toward your devotees!
Sanatkumāra said: While Brahmā was thus offering praise, that god of gods, the protector of the worlds,
being pleased, spoke to those gods and sages who were strengthened by their asceticism.
"O seers and deities, I am well-pleased with this penance of yours. Choose a boon; I shall grant it. Let that which has been well-considered be spoken. (SkP 9.12)
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O best of Brahmins, having beheld them all— satisfied and strengthened by their asceticism— Brahmā spoke these words merely by the sight of him.
Brahmā said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to us,
then be auspicious, gentle, and visible to us."
He is always easy to deal with and likewise ever-contented in mind;
in all undertakings he is always beneficial, wholesome, and auspicious.
"O God, who grants thousands of boons, let him be given to us— along with his queen, his son, and even with the hosts of gods."
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by Brahmā, that Blessed One,
the best of gods and a knower of all yoga, emitted his own great and divine splendor.
From half of his own splendor, the Lord, who assumes all forms, emitted a meteor from his mouth; he said to it, "Become a woman. (SkP 9.18)
Having pervaded the sky, the earth, and the atmosphere with her majesty,
she stood there, shining like a flash of lightning, and approached the Lord of the Gods.
The God laughed and said to that lotus-eyed Goddess:
"O Goddess of pure smiles, propitiate Brahmā, the bestower of boons."
Having promised "So be it," she began to perform austerities.
And Rudra said to those sages, "Listen, O best of the fruitful ones, O you whose wealth is penance, to what I say regarding the fruit of pleasing me."
"Immortal, free from old age, healthy, and devoid of rebirth—
my devotees, endowed with ascetic power, shall dwell right here."
And this very hermitage, the golden-peaked best of mountains,
will undoubtedly become a meritorious and sacred place.
Since I became gold on Maināka, the most excellent of mountains,
and since I created the goddess Svarṇākṣī, that place is therefore remembered as Svarṇākṣa.

"O Ṛṣis of the six clans, you whose wealth is asceticism, you shall dwell here at Svarṇākṣa by my command; indeed, that sacred field extending for a yojana all around Svarṇākṣa is undoubtedly pure. (SkP 9.25)
It was frequented by gods and gandharvas and served by throngs of apsaras; it was filled with lions, elephants, and śarabhas, and teeming with tigers, bears, and deer;
it was crowded with many birds and thick with creepers, trees, and shrubs.
A celibate student, observant of the rules, having conquered anger and mastered his senses,
who fasts for three nights, prepares an oblation of cooked rice (caru), and offers it—
wherever he may die, he shall dwell in the world of Brahmā.
Even one who, being likewise devoted to sensual desires, should behold the bull-bannered god there,
shall obtain the fruit of a thousand cows through my grace;
and having died here according to the prescribed rule, he shall dwell with me.
"As long as the worlds endure, and as long as this mountain Maināka remains,
so long shall you, O gods, move about together with me through my grace."
Having thus spoken to those sages and looked upon them with a gentle eye,
he vanished right there while everyone was looking on.
Sanatkumāra said:
That mortal who should hear this, or cause the twice-born to hear it,
shall also attain that fruit and move about free from death.
Victorious is the bearer of the clouds, the time of destruction for all beings, the remover of afflictions for ascetics restrained by tranquility and self-control;
he is the remover of birth and death for those who strive in righteousness, possessed of various instruments, moving through the sky and treading upon the earth.

The destroyer of the city of Madana, who plucks out eyes and teeth, free from fear and despondency, the wise one among all beings, constantly proclaiming himself as Cekitāna, adorned with hands and feet, the all-seeing God of gods.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. Sanatkumāra said:
That goddess, addressed by Tryambaka, performed penance for a very long time;
at times she was without food, then again subsisting on a single leaf,
then again subsisting on air, and once more subsisting only on water.
Knowing that she was engaged in the practice of asceticism and was exceedingly radiant, Brahmā said to her:
"Speak, O Goddess; I am pleased; what may I do for you?"
She said to the three-eyed god, her husband of moon-like luster: "O God, salutations to you; having obtained you as my husband, may I wander happily through all the worlds."
Brahmā said: "Indeed,
it is not by that very body with which supreme austerity is performed that the Supreme Lord, the Master Śambhu, is attained."
Therefore, through this yoga, you shall become the daughter of Dakṣa, the Prajāpati in this world; having been born as his daughter, you will obtain Rudra as your husband.
Then, having heard those words, that high-minded goddess,
the daughter of Dakṣa and a supreme yoginī, was born through her yogic power under the name Satī.
Dakṣa gave that blameless woman as a wife to Tryambaka at the word of Brahmā, in whom he begot his mind-born sons.
Many thousands of Rudras of immeasurable splendor, equal to himself in strength, radiant, and free from old age and death.
Seeing them being created, Brahmā forbade him, saying:
"O Lord of the gods, do not create subjects who are exempt from death."
"Create other offspring endowed with death; may you have prosperity.
Because he replied, "I am standing firm," he was therefore known as Sthāṇu.
The God said:
"O Brahmā, I shall by no means create subjects joined with death.
I stand today by your word; I am not to be addressed by you again."
But these high-souled and mighty beings who have been created from my mind—
all of them shall indeed wander with me as performers of sacrifice.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O Vyāsa, after some time had passed, Dakṣa, on account of the curse,
summoned his other sons-in-law along with their wives and honored them in his home.
Filled with rage, he did not invite Satī to be with Tryambaka;
but Satī, having understood all that had occurred, went and spoke to her father.
"I am the eldest and the most excellent, O observer of noble vows; it does not behove you to honor these women along with their husbands while excluding me."
Then, overcome by anger and his senses impaired by wrath,
Dakṣa looked at him and spoke as if burning him with his gaze.
"O virtuous lady, these women with their husbands worship me with affection;
you, however, O lady of great vows, do not worship me in that manner along with your husband."
"Ascetics rich in austerity enter my house accompanied by their wives;
therefore, I always consider them to be most excellent, and for that reason I worship them."
Therefore, whatever I do today, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious,
accept that as an offering, my daughter, or go wherever you please.
Sanatkumāra said:

Then, her face blazing with anger and being exceedingly provoked, that auspicious lady did not accept the unwelcome and inferior worship, and she spoke this to him: SkP_10.20: "Then, her face blazing with anger and being exceedingly provoked, that auspicious lady did not accept the unwelcome and inferior worship, and she spoke this to him."
"O Father, since you perform this unwelcome worship toward me—
which is praiseworthy, faultless, and supreme— you revile me."
Therefore, I shall abandon this body of mine; here is your daughter.
What is the use to me now of this inauspicious life, since she has been treated with such disrespect?
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having mentally offered salutation to Tryambaka,
she who is the source of speech spoke these words with great agitation.
"Wherever I may be reborn in a body again by my own will,
may I there likewise be born unconfused, virtuous,
and faithful, and become the lawful wife of the wise Tryambaka himself."
Then, having suddenly performed the fire-element concentration (dhāraṇā),
that virtuous woman indeed consumed her own body with the fire arising from within herself.
Having learned that the goddess had become thus, the highly illustrious Tryambaka,
skilled in speech, approached Dakṣa and spoke these words.

"Since I have been censured by you and the others, your sons-in-law along with their wives, have been praised separately, therefore, O Vaivasvata, these very sons-in-law of yours shall be born again at your sacrifice during the Vaivasvata interval."
"And you too, O King, shall become a Kṣatriya by my curse;
you shall be the son of the Pracetasas through the daughter of the Śākhis.
And there, I shall create an obstacle to the dharma for you, who are of cruel deeds."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Dakṣa, with a truly grieving heart, spoke to him:
"If my own daughter was indeed spoken of by me, or even if she was abandoned; [then what can be done?]"
"What have you done here, O God? I am always her master."
"Since you have cursed me, therefore, O Śaṅkara,
you too shall dwell eternally in the world of mortals (bhūrloka) and never in the heavenly world (svarloka)."
And having given you a share in their sacrifices, O Mahādeva of great luster, all the twice-born shall touch water everywhere.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that three-eyed god, laughing, said to him:
"The world of the earth (bhūrloka) is said to be the root of all the worlds."
Desiring the welfare of the worlds, I alone sustain him;
for when the earthly realm (bhūrloka) is supported, all the worlds remain eternal.
Therefore, I stay here perpetually, and not merely by your command.

Having given portions to others, those twice-born ones, desiring to give to me, touch water for the sake of purification; then they offer a portion to me. Having given, they touch water again for the very increase of dharma.

For just as pure people carry away the withered garlands of the gods, and those desiring to touch what is impure cast them off and then touch water; ||| SkP_10.35 ||| so too [should one act regarding the body].
When the bulls among brahmins, desiring to give portions of water to the gods and others in this manner,
touch the waters, what cause for lamentation is there?
But you, scorched by my curse, a perverted and lowest of men,
being deluded in mind, shall procreate a son upon your own daughter.
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus cursed Dakṣa, the blessed Lord, the master of the universe,
possessed of great splendor, ceased speaking and departed as he had come.

We bow perpetually here to Him whose eyes are like the moon, the sun, and fire; whose face resembles the moon and whose eyes are like lotus petals; who is borne by a bull, who possesses an immeasurable flood of virtues, and who carries the moon.
He who, being restrained in his vows, should hear this account of Dakṣa’s curse and the bodiless state of the Goddess, or should cause the Brahmins to hear it,
shall be liberated from all sins and attain the world of Rudra.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. Sanatkumāra said:
Once, when Kaśyapa, the best of bipeds, had arrived at his own home,
Himavat asked him a question concerning what brings renown in the world.
O Sage, tell me that by which the worlds may become inexhaustible, supreme renown may be attained, and likewise, one may become worthy of worship among the virtuous.
Kaśyapa said: "O mighty-armed one, all this is obtained through offspring;
it is by means of offspring that my fame, as well as that of Brahmā and the sages, has been established."
"Do you not see, O Lord of Mountains, that you ask me this? I shall relate to you, O Mountain, that which was seen by me in the past."
While traveling toward Vārāṇasī, I beheld stationed in the sky a divine celestial chariot, resonant, incomparable, and irreproachable.
Beneath that, in the place of a pit, I heard a cry of distress;
having recognized them through my ascetic power, I remained right there, hidden from view.
Then, O Lord of Mountains, a brahmin arrived there— one who was observant of vows, pure,
whose soul was purified by ablutions in sacred fords, and established in supreme austerity.
Then, O Mountain, as that twice-born man was proceeding along, pursued by a tiger,
he entered that region where the pit was located.
Then, seeing those sages hanging from a clump of vīraṇa grass in a pit, the distressed brahmin, himself afflicted by grief, questioned them.
"Who are you, O sinless ones, hanging head-downwards from this clump of vīraṇa grass? Why are you suffering, and by what means will your liberation come to pass?"
The ancestors said:
"We— your father, grandfather, and great-grandfather— are suffering because of your evil deeds, you who have performed no meritorious acts."
"O illustrious one, this hell is situated in the form of a pit;
you are a clump of *vīraṇa* grass, and we are hanging from you. (SkP 11.12)
"O Brahmin, for as long as you live, we shall remain;
but when you die, we, being of sinful mind, will go to hell."
If you, having entered into marriage, procreate a son of superior qualities,
by that means we shall each be released one by one.
"Not by any other austerity, my son, nor by the fruit of sacred fords;
therefore do that, O one of great intelligence, and deliver your ancestors from fear."
Having promised "So be it" and having propitiated the bull-bannered god,
he rescued his ancestors from the pit and made them leaders of the Gaṇas.
And he himself, beloved of Rudra and known by the name Sukeśa,
became an esteemed and powerful leader of Rudra’s attendants.
Therefore, O Lord of Mountains, having performed severe austerity, procreate a most virtuous offspring; through that, you shall attain fame.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been thus addressed by the seer, the lord of mountains remained steadfast in his observance and performed extensive penance, by which Brahmā was indeed gratified.
Then Brahmā, having approached him, said, "I am the giver of boons;
speak, O mountain of good vows, for I am pleased with this austerity of yours."
Himavat said:
"O Blessed One, I desire a son adorned with all virtues;
if you are pleased with us, O Lord, grant me this boon."
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of Mountains, a daughter of excellent complexion shall be born to you,
by whose power you will obtain abundant fame everywhere."
Worshipped by all the gods and surrounded by ten million sacred fords,
it shall be purifying and meritorious even for the gods in every respect;
O auspicious one, she shall be your elder sister, and the others shall follow after her.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus, Brahmā then vanished on that very spot;
and in due time, he [the Lord] was born from Menā, the queen of the lord of mountains.
Aparṇā, Ekaparṇā, and likewise Ekapāṭalā.
Nyagrodha had one leaf, and Pāṭala had one *pāṭala* flower;
these two resorted to Aparṇā, who was without a home,
and performed austerities difficult for gods and dānavas to practice for a hundred thousand years.
Saiikaparnā subsisted on a single leaf for her food,
while Ekapāṭalā likewise provided for herself with a single pāṭala flower.
Every thousand [steps] being completed, the two of them took food;
but Aparṇā remained without food, and her mother, distressed by maternal affection, addressed her while trying to dissuade her, saying, "Do not do this."
Thus addressed by her mother at that time, the goddess who had performed difficult deeds became renowned in the worlds by that very name, honored by the gods.
This entire world, both stationary and moving, belongs to these three maidens;
it was obtained by their ascetic power for as long as the earth shall endure.
All three of them had austerity for their bodies, were endowed with the power of yoga,
were all highly fortunate, and all possessed perpetual youth.
They are indeed the mothers of the world and practitioners of celibacy;
they always sustain the worlds through their own ascetic power.
Umā was the most excellent and the best among them, a woman of supreme complexion;
endowed with the power of great yoga, she attended upon Mahādeva.
Dattaka and Uśanas were her sons, that descendant of Bhṛgu;
and Asita’s wife, Ekaparṇā, gave birth to a son, Devala.
Among those maidens, the third was indeed Ekapāṭalā;
she attended upon Jaigīṣavya, the son of Śataśalāka. Of him as well, Śaṅkha and Likhita are remembered as two sons not born from a womb.
But as for Umā, that woman of excellent complexion whom I have described to you—
then, perceiving the entire three worlds to be filled with smoke due to her application of ascetic penance, Brahmā spoke these words:
Brahmā said:
"O Goddess, O most beautiful one, why do you torment the worlds with penance?
This universe was created by you; do not destroy it once it has been made."
For you indeed sustain all these worlds by your own splendor;
speak, O Mother of the World, what do you desire? Be gracious to us.
The Goddess said:
"O Grandfather, you already know the truth regarding the purpose for which I am performing this penance; why then do you ask me again?"
Brahmā said:
"O Goddess, source of the world's being, he for whose sake you weary yourself with ascetic penance will himself come here and choose you as his bride."
He is the supreme lord of all the gods, the sovereign of the lords of all the worlds;
we, together with the gods, are subject to his will and speak as his servants.
That God of gods, the Lord of the Supreme Lord, the protector of the world, will himself come into your presence;
he possesses a sublime form, appearing both transformed and beautiful, for his form is not like that of anyone else.
Maheśvara, who dwells in the world of the mountains, the lord of the moving and the unmoving, the first and immeasurable one—
though his face is like the moon, he stands here in a foremost form that is terrifying in the absence of the moon.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. Sanatkumāra said:
Then the Blessed Lord Brahmā spoke to her in a melodious voice:
"O Goddess, he by whom you were created in his mind and who was chosen by you—he, the Lord of Gods, shall be your husband; do not perform further penance."
Then, having circumambulated the daughter of the mountain, Brahmā vanished from her sight, and she too ceased [speaking].
Having said, "So be it," that goddess stationed herself, taking refuge at the foot of an aśoka tree growing at the entrance of her own hermitage.
Then Hara, the moon-crested one who removes the suffering of the thirty gods, arrived,
having assumed a deformed appearance— short in stature and possessing only arms.
Having become one with a crooked nose, hunchbacked, with tawny hair and a deformed face, he said, "O Goddess, I choose you as my bride."
Then Umā, perfected in yoga and purified in her inner being, knowing that Śaṅkara had arrived, desired to perform ritual acts.
Having brought the guest-offering (arghya) and the honey-mixture (madhuparka),
the one dear to Brahmins honored that Brahmin and, once he was comfortably seated, spoke to him.
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, I am not independent; I have a father and likewise a mother. They alone have the power over my giving, for I am a maiden, O bull among the twice-born."
"Go and beg my father, the imperishable Lord of Mountains;
O Brahmin, if he gives me to you, that shall be pleasing to me."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that Blessed Lord, the powerful deity who had likewise assumed that transformed form, spoke to that king of mountains: "O king of mountains, give Umā to me."
Recognizing him as the imperishable Rudra by his transformed appearance, he became afraid of the curse and, with a troubled mind, spoke these words: SkP_12.11 //
O Blessed One, I do not disregard the brahmins, who are the deities of the earth;
however, O one of great asceticism, hear that which was previously desired by me.
"A svayaṃvara for my daughter shall take place, honored by the brahmins;
whoever she herself chooses there, he shall become her husband."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard those words of the mountain, the high-minded Lord whose banner bears the bull approached the Goddess and spoke this.
"O Goddess, it has been heard that your father has commanded a svayaṃvara;
O sinless one, whomever you choose there, he shall indeed become your husband."
Therefore, I take my leave; I shall depart, O fair-faced one, for you are difficult to find.
Having rejected one so handsome, how could you choose someone like me?
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having been addressed by him there, she contemplated what he had uttered,
as well as the disposition placed within her by Rudra and the grace of his mind.
Having approached the Lord of Gods, he said: "May your mind not be otherwise;
I shall choose you as my husband, and never any other being whatsoever."
Or if you have some doubt regarding me in any way, O Brahmin,
then here and now, O illustrious one, I grant you the fulfillment of your heart's desire.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having taken a cluster of flowers situated there with both her hands and placed it upon the shoulder of Śambhu, the Goddess said, "You are chosen by me."
Then that Blessed Lord, accompanied by the Goddess as before,
spoke to Aśoka, as if reviving him with his voice.
"Since I have been honored by you with this cluster of beautiful flowers,
therefore, abandoned by old age, you shall become immortal."
He can assume any form at will, he is the flower of desire, he goes wherever he wishes, and he is dear to me;
he is enriched with all kinds of ornaments and flowers, and he possesses the fruits of every tree.
"You shall be the consumer of all food and the flow of nectar itself;
you shall be the essence of all fragrances and will become a steadfast favorite of the Goddess.
Free from fear in all worlds, you shall wander in perfect peace."
And whoever, seeking merit, shall visit this hermitage widely renowned as Citrakūṭa, he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
and wherever he may die, he shall go to the world of Brahmā.
And whoever here, endowed with religious observances, should completely renounce his life-breaths,
he, joined with the austerity of the Goddess, shall become a great Gaṇapati.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus and then taking leave of the daughter of Himavat,
the Lord, the creator of the world and protector of all beings, vanished from sight.
When that Blessed One of immeasurable soul had departed,
the goddess too remained there with her face turned upward and sat down upon the rock.
When that great archer, the progenitor Prajāpati, had departed, she,
looking up at him, then appeared dejected like a night devoid of the moon.
Then Śailajā heard the sound of a distressed child near the hermitage, by a lake filled with water.
Then Śiva himself, the God of gods, having assumed the form of a child for the sake of sport, became seized by a crocodile in the middle of the lake.
Then, resorting to his yogic power (yogamāyā), which is the cause of the emergence of the phenomenal world,
he assumed that form in the middle of the lake and spoke these words:
"May someone come here to save me, whose mind has been seized by a crocodile!"
"Alas, what misery! Though still but a child, with my desires for wealth unfulfilled, I shall meet my death in the mouth of this wicked crocodile."
Though seized by a crocodile and suffering, I do not grieve for my own body as much as I grieve for my father and my poor mother.
Hearing that I have met my death in the jaws of the crocodile,
those two who have but one son and are longing for their beloved child will surely give up their lives.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard that cry of the distressed Brahmin, the beautiful goddess rose up and ran quickly to where that twice-born man was standing.
That moon-faced woman saw the boy of beautiful form,
trembling as he stood there being swallowed by a crocodile.
That illustrious and excellent crocodile, seeing that the goddess had approached,
seized her and quickly went into the very middle of the lake.
As he was being dragged away, the radiant one then let out a cry of distress.
Then the Goddess of great vows, afflicted by grief upon seeing the boy, spoke.
O King of Grāhas, O Great Being, O one with great fangs, O you of terrifying prowess, release this child, who is indeed your only son; do so quickly!
The crocodile said:
"O Goddess, he who first comes to me on the sixth day has been ordained as my food from of old by the creators of the world."
"O highly fortunate daughter of the king of mountains, this very thing was surely ordained for me by Brahmā on the sixth day; I shall not escape it by any means."
The Goddess said:
"O King of Grāhas, by virtue of the supreme austerity I performed on the peak of Himavat, release this child; homage be to you!"
The crocodile said:
"O Goddess, daughter of the lord of mountains, do not let your ascetic merit go to waste;
even the King of the Gods himself is not able to release him."
From Śarva, the fierce wielder of the trident, my lord being pleased with me,
[I obtained] immortality, invincibility, and indeed inexhaustible strength.
Furthermore, the liberation from self-seizure and imperishable knowledge were granted;
therefore, I tell you that he shall not attain liberation.
Or rather, O Goddess of auspicious countenance, you have great compassion for this child;
I tell you what you must do, and by that he will attain liberation.
The goddess said:
"O Lord of the Grāhas, speak quickly that which is not censured by the virtuous;
it has been done, there is no doubt here, for Brāhmaṇas are firmly honored by me."
The crocodile said:
"Whatever penance you have performed, even if it be very slight, give all of that to me; then you shall obtain liberation."
The Goddess said:
"O great crocodile, whatever merit has been earned by me since birth—all that I give to you; release the child before me."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the crocodile blazed forth, strengthened by that ascetic power;
like the sun at midday, he then became difficult to look upon.
With a satisfied soul, he spoke thus to the Goddess, the sustainer of the world:
"O Goddess, O lady of great vows, why have you done this without due deliberation?
For the acquisition of ascetic merit is difficult, and its abandonment is not praised."
"Accept this austerity and this boy as well, O lady of pure smiles;
I am pleased with your devotion to the brahmins, and therefore I grant you a boon."
Thus addressed by the crocodile, she of great vows replied:
"O great crocodile, having reflected well, the liberation of the boy has been accomplished;
there is no austerity superior to that toward Brahmins, for I consider Brahmins to be supreme."
"O Lord of Grāhas, it is known to you that once I have given something, I do not take it back;
for no man, O Grāha, would ever reclaim what has been given."
"This has been given by me to you; I shall certainly not take it back.
Let this remain with you alone, and let this boy be released."
Having been addressed thus, he then praised her, released the child, and paid homage to the goddess who shone with the brilliance of the sun; then and there he vanished.
Then the boy, having been released by the crocodile on the shore of the lake,
vanished right there, like a mass of wealth obtained in a dream.
Then, perceiving the depletion of her ascetic merit, the goddess, daughter of the Lord of the Snowy Mountains,
began once again to perform penance, applying herself with great effort.
O Vyāsa, Śaṅkara himself, perceiving that she desired to perform even greater asceticism, spoke these words: "Do not perform penance."
“O Goddess of great vows, this ascetic power was given to me by you;
because of that, it shall become yours in an inexhaustible thousandfold way.”
Having thus obtained the supreme and inexhaustible boon from her asceticism, the goddess remained there,
filled with joy and looking forward to the *svayaṃvara*.
Indeed, that man who always recites this account of Śambhu’s conduct while in the state of a child shall,
upon the dissolution of the body, become purified and a Gaṇa equal to Kumāra.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. Sanatkumāra said:
On the vast expanse of the Himalayas, crowded with hundreds of celestial chariots,
the svayaṃvara of the Mountain’s Daughter took place in due course of time.
Then that Himavat, the king of mountains, skilled in meditation,
learned that his daughter had been consecrated by the God of Gods.
Although he already knew [the answer], the Great Mountain, desiring to perform the proper rites of social custom,
then proclaimed the self-choice marriage (*svayaṃvara*) of the Goddess throughout all the worlds.
"May he choose the Supreme Lord in my presence, so that my daughter may [be united with him] by all those who dwell in every world— the gods, the dānavas, and the siddhas."
"Only that is well-done, praiseworthy, and conducive to my prosperity,"—
having reflected thus, the lord of mountains placed Maheśvara in his heart.
In the worlds up to the realm of Brahmā, that best of mountain lords,
having made the region filled with jewels for the Goddess, caused the svayaṃvara to be held.
Then, O Vyāsa, as soon as the svayaṃvara of the daughter of Mahīdhra had been thus proclaimed,
the gods and all other inhabitants of the world arrived, having assumed celestial attire.
Seated upon a full-blown lotus throne and surrounded by immeasurable perfected yogis,
the Grandfather (Brahmā) arrived there at the request of that king of mountains.
Bearing a thousand eyes and possessing a noble form adorned with divine ornaments and garlands, that king of the gods, the sovereign of all immortals,
mounted Airāvata— the foremost of all lordly elephants, from whose temples flowed streams of trickling rut—
and holding his thunderbolt, he came forward at the head of the deities.
Possessing a divine form exceeding in brilliance and majesty, illuminating all directions like the sun,
he ascended a golden celestial chariot with fluttering banners and arrived swiftly with great speed.

Wearing earrings blazing with the brilliance of jewels, Kaśyapa’s son, the Brahmin, arrived in a celestial chariot resembling the splendor of fire and the sun; he was Āditya, who bears the name Bhaga.
With a stout body and well-fashioned ornaments upon his limbs, possessing a majesty equal to his splendor, strength,
and authority, Kṛtānta arrived with speed, mounted upon a formidable buffalo and wielding his staff.
With limbs as massive as the height of the great mountains, wearing a beautiful garment adorned with gold and other jewels,
the Wind-god, the sustainer of the entire world, arrived having mounted his celestial chariot.
Scorching all the lords of the gods and asuras, and having entered into a splendor superior to their own splendor,
Agni approached the midst of the lords of the gods and stood forth blazing, wearing a magnificent garb.
With his slender body blazing with various jewels,
that lord of all masters of wealth, the king of kings, mounted an excellent celestial chariot that traverses the world and approached in haste.
Gladdening all the lords of the gods and asuras with his beauty and attire,
the moon, possessing a lovely form, arrived having ascended a celestial chariot that shone with the variegated splendor of great jewels.
With a dark-limbed frame, dressed in most wonderful attire, and wearing fragrant garlands bound with every kind of flower,
that wielder of the mace arrived swiftly, mounted upon Tārkṣya, who resembled a mountain.
Likewise, the two Aśvins, the preeminent physicians of the gods, having swiftly ascended a single celestial chariot,
arrived at the assembly of the gods— those two heroes, captivating and dressed in brilliant, beautiful attire.
The noble-souled Śeṣa, possessing the brilliance of a blazing sun, bore a thousand hoods flashing with the color of fire;
