accompanied by other great serpents, he ascended a celestial chariot and approached.

Having assumed a form suitable for his boon, he approached before the host of gods as a group of great Asuras, the sons of Diti, whose splendor was equal to that of fire, the sun, Indra, and the wind.
And that Gandharva king, of beautiful form, moving through the divine air and traveling in a celestial chariot,
arrived there at the command of Śakra, accompanied by hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
And other gods, lords of the three heavens, having each separately assumed beautiful attire,
arrived, as did the gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and kiṃnaras, having mounted the backs of celestial chariots.
There, in the midst of the lords of the gods, the husband of Śacī— his form distinguished by the excessive marks of royal authority,
and deluded by the power of his commands and sovereignty— exerted himself with futile excess.
She is the cause of the three worlds and the mother of the universe, including the gods and asuras;
she is the wife of Śambhu, the abode of the Supreme Person, and is celebrated in the Purāṇas as the primordial nature (prakṛti) for the sake of the highest purpose.
Out of Dakṣa’s wrath, she, the consort of the Supreme Lord, went to the home of Himavat for the sake of her task.
Thus, because the lords of the gods did not know her, delusion entered them from that supreme being;
therefore they came seeking boons, utterly bewildered, since they had been rendered so by the Lord.

Then, with apsarases dancing and throngs of gandharvas with the sounds of beautiful singing, and with hosts of gods, asuras, and other denizens of the triple heaven standing there in various forms and attire; ||| SkP_13.26 |||
Seated upon the back of a celestial chariot variegated with jewels and gold, her body fanned by waving chowries,
the goddess set forth with haste, holding a most fragrant garland of flowers from every season.
Sanatkumāra said:
When the Goddess stood holding the garland in the assembly of the gods,
Śakra and the other deities had arrived, having come to the *svayaṃvara*.
Out of a desire to test the Goddess, the omnipresent Lord Śambhu suddenly became a five-crested infant and lay down, fast asleep, upon the surface of her lap.
Then, suddenly, the goddess, perceiving through her yogic concentration that the five-crested infant was standing there, rejoiced, filled with affection.
Then she, whose resolve was pure and who had obtained the excellent fruit of her desire,
remained as if liberated, having fixed him alone within her heart.
Then, seeing the infant resting in the lap of the goddess, the gods consulted among themselves, "Who is this? and, being greatly afflicted, they became enraged.
Lifting up his arm, the slayer of Vṛtra fashioned it into a vajra;
that arm of his remained raised in that very position.
Paralyzed by Śambhu, the God of gods, who had assumed the form of a child,
he was unable to hurl his thunderbolt nor even to move his arm.
Then the powerful god Āditya, the son of Kaśyapa, named Bhaga,
being deluded, raised up a flaming club and desired to hurl it;
the Blessed One likewise paralyzed his arm at that very moment.
Shaking his head, Viṣṇu looked at him with anger;
the Lord then brought about baldness upon that head as well.
Pūṣan, his teeth grinding against each other, looked at Śarva in bewilderment;
yet as soon as he was seen by Śambhu, his own teeth fell out.
The Lord paralyzed Yama’s staff, the brilliance of Agni, the radiance of the Moon,
the strength of Vāyu, and likewise the power, splendor, and yogic mastery of all the other inhabitants of heaven within him.
Then, while those gods remained thus filled with resentment,
Brahmā, deeply agitated, respectfully engaged in meditation and perceived the Lord of the Gods of gods seated upon the lap of Umā.
Having recognized the Supreme Lord, the Grandfather (Brahmā) rose quickly and with reverence prostrated at the feet of Śambhu,
praising him with ancient Sāman chants and holy, secret names.
O God, you are the unborn, the immortal, the creator, the destroyer, the all-pervading, and the supreme;
you are Pradhāna, Puruṣa, the Tattva, and that imperishable Brahman which is to be meditated upon.
He is the nectar, the supreme self, the Lord, the great cause,
the creator of Brahmā, the fashioner of primordial nature (prakṛti), the creator of all, and the Supreme Lord.
And this Goddess Prakṛti is always the cause of your creation;
having assumed the form of a wife, she has come as the cause of the world.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the World, and constant salutations to the Goddess as well;
by your grace and by your command, O Lord of Gods, [I have created] the subjects.
"These gods and others who were created are now deluded, bewildered by your yoga;
show them favor so that they may become as they were before."
Then, having thus petitioned the Supreme Lord, the immensely radiant Brahmā spoke these words to all those gods who had been paralyzed.
"You are all deluded, O deities; you do not recognize this Śaṅkara, the God of gods who has arrived here, the very cause of my own birth."
This is Rudra, Mahādeva, Śarva, Bhīma, and the one with matted hair;
he is Ugra, Īśāna, the Self, the Unborn, and indeed Śaṅkara.
The god of gods, the supreme abode, the Lord, Paśupati, the Master;
the creator of the world, the sustainer of the world, and the cause of the world's maintenance.
"Go quickly for refuge in this very manner, O lords of the immortals,
together with me alone, to the Lord of Gods, the Supreme Self, the Imperishable."
Then all those inhabitants of the third heaven were likewise paralyzed;
with minds purified by their inner disposition, they bowed mentally to Śarva.
Then Maheśvara, the God of gods, became pleased with them;
he then swiftly restored the bodies of the deities as they were before.
Then, while all the gods were thus engaged in their efforts to ward him off, the Lord of Gods assumed a supreme and most wonderful three-eyed form,
before whose splendor those gods sought refuge with the All-pervading Lord.
To them, the supreme Lord of Gods granted his own supreme eye, endowed with the power of vision for his own body; then they beheld the Lord.
Having seen the Supreme Lord bearing the third eye,
all those lords of the gods, beginning with Brahmā, quickly bowed down.
Then the goddess, delighted, placed a garland of flowers at the feet of that one of immeasurable luster, in the presence of the inhabitants of heaven.
Having cried out "Excellent! Excellent!", those deities again paid homage to the Lord together with the Goddess, bowing their heads until they touched the surface of the earth.
Then, O Vyāsa, in the meantime, the Grandfather of the worlds, Brahmā,
of great splendor, spoke thus to Himavat, the great mountain:
"Indeed, because you have this great alliance with Śarva, you are today praiseworthy, worthy of worship, and venerable to us all.
Let the marriage be performed quickly; for what purpose do you remain further?"
Then Himavat, having bowed to that god, replied:
"O God, you alone are the cause by which this Śarva has come to me."
This sudden grace has arisen, and you alone are indeed its cause;
therefore, O Grandfather, ordain the marriage in whatever manner and according to whatever form it shall be.

Then, having heard these words from the king of mountains, the Grandfather said to the god, "O Lord, let the marriage be performed. To him, Śaṅkara, the protector of the world, replied to the god, "As you wish."
And at that very moment, O Vyāsa, a city fashioned by Brahmā for the wedding of Maheśvara appeared,
adorned with various jewels.
Jewels, various gems, gold, and pearls,
having approached in embodied form, adorned that most excellent city.
The ground was variegated with emeralds, adorned with pillars of gold,
with walls of radiant crystal from which pearl necklaces hung down.
In that beautiful city of Śiva, which had been constructed for the purpose of the wedding,
the great-souled Maheśvara, the God of gods, shone resplendently.
There, the moon and sun shone equally like two great jewels;
and having inhaled the delightful fragrance of the bull, the wind blew with a pleasant touch,
propitiating the devotion of the Lord.
There are the four oceans there, as well as Śakra and the other foremost gods,
the celestial rivers, the great rivers, and the perfected ones and sages.
All the Gandharvas and Apsarases, the Nāgas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas,
the Guhyakas, other sky-dwellers, the Kinnaras, and the celestial Cāraṇas.
Tumburu, Nārada, Hāhā, and Hūhū— the singers of the Sāman hymns—
then arrived at that city, bringing jewels and musical instruments.
There, the sages whose wealth was their asceticism, with joyful minds, chanted in their entirety the sacred marriage mantras sung in the Vedas.
All the mothers of the world and all the daughters of the gods,
in their entirety, sang with joy at the wedding of the Supreme Lord.
There, the six seasons were present in person, bringing equal and diverse fragrant pleasures; they had arrived as the wedding procession of Śaṅkara.
It was filled everywhere with peacocks dancing and uttering their cries, delighted by the thundering of clouds as dark as masses of blue rain-clouds.
It was illuminated by flickering streaks of clear, tawny lightning,
and adorned with cranes as white and yellow as water-lilies.
Fresh *śilīndhra* mushrooms and *kandala* sprouts have just appeared; creepers and trees have put forth lovely new shoots;
and the ground resounds with throngs of frogs, languid with passion, awakened by the affectionate embrace of auspicious rain showers.
For passionate women whose minds are uplifted by pride toward their beloveds, even when they are firmly resolved,
their sense of self-importance is shattered in an instant by the charming cries of peacocks.

Likewise, she was resplendent with the great bow of Indra, which was beautiful with its form shining in three colors, curved like the crescent of the moon, and situated near a mass of clouds on all sides.
With breezes that were cool due to contact with dense clouds, fragrant from the touch of various flowers,
and enchanting as they caused the beautiful rows of tresses belonging to the celestial damsels to tremble.
With the orb of the moon veiled by thundering clouds, and with beautiful dūrvā grass sprouting from the sprinkling of fresh rainwater,
the earth was gazed upon with longing and respect by the wives of travelers, who sighed like smoke.
Rich with the sound of swans and anklets, with uplifted breasts,
her girdle like a flickering streak of lightning, and her eyes clearly like lotuses.
With flocks of swans unafraid of the dark clouds, with the tips of its lotuses bent by the falling streams of pure water,
and with the beauty of all its limbs fashioned from the pollen of fragrant flowers, the rainy season arrived for the prosperity of the mountain-daughter’s wedding.
Freed from her garment of clouds, with breasts emerging from the sheaths of lotuses,
resounding with the anklets of swans, she filled all the quarters of space with her loveliness.
Her broad hips are like a wide sandy bank, her girdle is the warbling of cranes,
and she is enchanting with eyes that have the full expanse of blooming blue lotuses.
Her lower lip was like a ripe bimba fruit, she smiled with teeth like kunda flowers,
and she was adorned with a line of body hair as dark as a fresh śyāmā creeper.
With her excellent necklace of moonbeams gliding across her lofty chest,
she delighted the hearts of all the inhabitants of heaven.
She speaks with a sweet voice sung by the assembly of *samādāli* birds,
and she is adorned with beautiful earrings that resemble clusters of swaying white water-lilies.
She held as fingers the tender sprouts arising from the tips of the branches of the red Aśoka tree,
and she was beautifully adorned with garments made from a collection of its flowers.
Her feet were like the tips of red lotuses, her rows of nails like jasmine flowers,
her beautiful thighs like the trunks of plantain trees, and her face was like the moon.
Touching the gods with her hands— the tips of her fingers being the winds mingled with the filaments of lotuses—
the delightful autumn arrived like a beloved woman out of love.

At the wedding of the Goddess, autumn arrived there— her garment of dark clouds cast off, her face like the orb of the full moon, her lotus-eyes like the buds of blue water-lilies, her beautiful breasts emerging like blossoms, delighting the minds with breezes fragrant with the pollen of various flowers, and sounding with the tinkling of swans as if they were her anklets.
Flooding the mountain rocks with exceedingly cool waters,
the two seasons of Śiśira and Hemanta, of surpassing splendor, arrived.
With those two seasons having arrived, that Himavat, the best of mountains,
quickly shone like silver, raining down a powder of frost.
Then, with that dense and unfathomable rain of frost, the Himālaya shone like the ocean Kṣīroda.
In the snowy regions, Himavat suddenly destroyed the trees that were hospitable to virtuous beings, like a wicked man who has achieved his purpose.
With its peaks covered by layers of frost,
that mountain shone like a lord of the earth with large, white parasols.
White, vast, glorious, and auspicious,
the lofty mountain peaks shone like palatial mansions.
In the caves of that king of mountains, which were teeming with flocks of most variegated deer,
streams of frost— white as the rays of the moon— fell down like streams of cow’s milk.
Breezes, their bodies laden with heaps of many flower-pollen and rendered cool by contact with droplets of frost,
blew gently, causing the exceedingly fine garments of the lords of the hosts of immortals to flutter slowly.
The spring season, having shaken off the defects of harsh winds and cold, and with sprouting mango shoots as its ear-ornaments,
quickly came to the Himalayas for the sake of serving the Daughter of the Mountain.
When that truthful one had approached the mountain to attend upon the wedding of the Daughter of the Mountain,
the trees, shrubs, and thickets all around burst forth into flower-decorated crests.

Fragrant, auspicious, and very cool breezes blew repeatedly, their bodies laden with heaps of pollen from the tips of various flowers; they intensified the passion of the gods and the celestial nymphs.
And likewise, lotus ponds filled with clear water and endowed with buds of red and blue lotuses became most beautiful,
like women whose breasts have just begun to emerge.
Due to the nature of the season and the arising of passion, as the branches blossomed,
the male cuckoos, their wings settled upon them, warbled with exceeding sweetness— a sound that delights the hearts of the celestial maidens.

The foremost among the divine elephants, filled with joy, drank the waters of the lakes— which were neither too hot nor too cold and turned tawny by the pollen of lotus filaments— while they were made resonant by the calls of pairs of ruddy geese.
The *priyaṅgu* trees and the mango trees, and the mango trees and the *priyaṅgu* trees as well,
shone as if threatening one another with their flower clusters.
Upon the peaks white as snow, clusters of flowers shone like elders who had gathered together for some purpose.
There, flowering *aśoka* creepers clinging to the *śāla* trees shone like beloved women with their bodies entwined around the necks of their lovers.
With clusters of flowers on their creepers being sung over by flocks of bees,
the mālatī vines shone as if they were conversing with one another.
The waters were made blue by blue lotuses, white by white ones with their stalks and stems,
and intensely red by red ones whose petals had been half-bitten by intoxicated bees.
In some lakes with vast waters, golden lotus groves grew everywhere; in others, they were made entirely of emeralds; and in yet other lakes, there arose lotus forests with stalks of lapis lazuli.
There were beautiful ponds there, adorned with lotuses and water-lilies,
resounding with the cries of various birds, and featuring rows of golden steps.
O Sage, the peaks of that mountain, densely covered with well-flowered *karṇikāra* trees, shone as if they were made of gold.
All the directions became pale-red with *pāṭala* trees, their forms trembling in the wind, covered with slightly blossomed flowers.
The blue *aśoka* trees, resembling the peaks of mountains of black collyrium,
grew in full bloom upon the mountain as if in mutual competition with one another.
And forests of *kiṃśuka* trees, resounding with the cries of *cīruvāka* birds,
appeared on all the ridges of the mountain.
At that time, the splendor of the Himalaya was like that of Tamāla thickets,
appearing as if masses of dark clouds were nestled within its crevices.
Then the Himalaya mountain shone exceedingly with its lofty campaka trees, which had abundant flowers and very broad branches, and with the warbling of intoxicated male cuckoos.
Hearing from all sides the sound of cuckoos warbling with the passion of spring, the peacocks, their wings fluttering, cried out with most sweet notes;
by those sounds, the bodiless god of love—whose strength was augmented, who held the flower-bow and arrows in his hand—became ready to pierce the limbs of the celestial women.
With its sharp sunlight and generally warm reservoirs of water,
the summer season arrived at the Himālaya for the purpose of serving the wedding of the Goddess.
And he, too, adorned the peaks of the snowy mountain on all sides with many trees and clusters of blossoms.
And during that season, delightful winds blew there,
bearing the fragrance of trumpet-flowers, *kadamba*, and *arjuna* trees.
The ponds, filled with clusters of blossoming lotuses whose forms were reddened by filaments,
resounded upon their banks with flocks of kalahamsa geese.
Likewise, the kuravaka trees as well, their forms white with blossoms and frequented by swarms of bees, grew upon all the peaks.
And on the broad slopes of the mountains, bakula trees released beautiful flowers in every direction.

Thus, O hero among sages, the six seasons— whose trees were variegated with blossoms and whose regions were delightful with the songs of various birds— approached for the prosperity of the wedding of the daughter of the Snowy Mountain.
Then, when the assembly of all beings had thus gathered and was filled with hundreds of various musical instruments, my father Brahmā himself appeared.
Having adorned the Daughter of the Mountain with a wealth of suitable ornaments,
the Sustainer of the World himself took her and led her into the city.
Then Brahmā once again addressed the omnipresent Lord:
"Standing in the position of preceptor, I shall offer oblations into the fire;
if you grant me permission, this ritual procedure must be performed."
To him, the god Śaṅkara, the God of gods and Lord of the universe, said:
"O Lord of the gods, do whatever you desire, exactly as you wish;
O Brahmā, O all-pervading Lord of the world, I shall carry out every word of yours."
Then, with a joyful heart, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, bowed down and joined the hands of the God and the Goddess in the yogic gesture.
And having himself prepared the fire, he stood with palms joined in reverence,
while the great mantras, personified and standing before him, were chanted by the Vedas.
Having offered oblations according to the prescribed rule with clarified butter and that very nectar,
he should cause him to circumambulate that blazing god three times.
Having released his joined palms and accompanied by all the deities and all his mind-born sons, with a heart full of joy at the conclusion of the wedding ceremony,
he bowed down to the bull-bannered god.
O Vyāsa, through yoga alone that supreme marriage of Umā and the Supreme Lord took place,
which the gods do not know anywhere.
Thus has all this been narrated to you— the auspicious self-choice marriage (svayaṃvara) and the most wonderful wedding of the God, as you were listening.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, named [the thirteenth], in the Skanda Purāṇa. Sanatkumāra said:
Then, when the marriage of Bhava, who possesses immeasurable splendor,
had been performed, the gods together with the Grandfather (Brahmā), having attained incomparable joy,
praised Maheśvara with pleasing words while bowing down.
Salutation to the mountain-liṅga, salutation indeed to the Lord of the Mountain;
salutation to him who has the speed of the wind, to the multiform one, and to the unconquered.
Homage to the destroyer of afflictions and the bestower of auspicious perfections;
homage to Nīlaśikhaṇḍin, the husband of Ambikā.
Homage to him who has the form of the wind, and indeed homage to him who possesses a hundred forms;
homage to him who has the form of Bhairava and to him whose eyes are deformed.
Salutations to the thousand-eyed one and to the thousand-footed;
salutations again and again to the secret of the Vedas and to the limb of the Vedas.
Salutations again and again to the one who paralyzed the arm of Śakra, to the sprout of the Vedas,
to the lord of the moving and the unmoving, and to the pacifier.
Salutations to the one whose linga rests upon the waters, whose linga is as vast as the end of an eon;
salutations to the one who wears a garland of skulls, salutations to the one who possesses a wreath of skulls.
Homage to the one who holds a skull in his hand, to the fanged one, to the wielder of the mace;
homage to the vehicle of the three worlds and to the chariot of the seven worlds.
Homage to the one who holds a skull-topped staff in his hand and who removes the afflictions of the Pramathas;
homage to the one who severed the head of the sacrifice and who took away the black hair [of Aruṇa].
Salutations to the one who struck out Bhaga’s eyes and tore away Pūṣan’s teeth;
salutations to the bearer of the Pināka bow, the trident, the sword, the scimitar, and the mallet.
Homage be to the Death of Death, and to the one with the third eye;
homage indeed to the end-maker of the End-maker, and to the dweller in the mountains.
Salutation to Suvarṇaretas, who wears serpent-earrings; to Vāḍvali, the destroyer of yoga, and the teacher of yogins.
Salutations to the one whose eyes are the moon and the sun, and to the one who has an eye on his forehead;
salutations to the one who delights in cremation grounds and to the one who grants boons from the cremation grounds.
Homage to the Lord of the gods, to Tryambaka, homage again and again;
to him who laughs like a hundred thunderbolts, who is devoted to the Brahmins, and who is unconquered.
Salutations always to the one who is virtuous as a householder, to the one with matted hair, and to the celibate student;
salutations to the shaven-headed and the half-shaven-headed, and salutations to the Lord of Creatures.
Salutations to the one who is being heated within the waters, who bestows the sovereign power of yoga, who is peaceful and self-controlled, and who causes both dissolution and creation.
Homage to the one who bestows grace and homage again and again to the one who maintains the world;
homage to Rudra, to Vasu, to Āditya, and homage to the two Aśvins.
Salutations to the Father, and then to Sādhya, and indeed salutations to Viśvedeva;
salutations to Śarva, to Sarva, to Ugra, and to the Bestower of Boons.
Homage to Bhīma, the leader of the army; homage to the Lord of Creatures;
homage to the Pure One, who licks repeatedly, and indeed to the one newly born.
Salutations to Mahādeva, the wondrous one, and to Citraratha;
to the primordial matter, the object of knowledge, the effect, and the instrument.
Salutation be to you, O Puruṣa, and to the one who brings about the desires of Puruṣa;
salutation to the one who effects the qualities of Pradhāna through its union with Puruṣa.
To the impeller of primordial nature (prakṛti) and of the person (puruṣa) in every respect;
to the witness of what has been done and what has not been done, and to the one who bestows the connection with the fruit.
Salutations everywhere to the Knower of Time, to the Ordainer of Restraints;
salutations to the Creator of Imbalance and to the Bestower of the activity of the qualities.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods; salutations to you, the creator of all beings.
O Lord, be auspicious, gentle, and pleasant to behold; indeed, be like the moon to us.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus praised by all the gods, that Blessed Lord, the Master of the World and Lord of Umā, spoke these words to the immortals.
"O gods, O blameless ones, I am pleasant to behold and gentle even to the gods;
choose whatever boon you desire, for I shall grant it—speak, O sinless ones!"
Then all those gods, including Brahmā, bowed down and said:
"O Blessed One, let this boon remain in your very hand;
when the time for action comes, you shall grant us our desired boon."
Having said "So be it" to them and dismissed the gods,
Hara then entered his abode together with the Pramathas and the worlds.
But he who sings of this wonderful festival of Hara in the presence of deities and Brahmins, shall,
upon the dissolution of the body, become equal to the peerless Gaṇeśa and be happy.
Sanatkumāra said: O son of Parāśara, whoever should hear or recite this hymn of praise,
he shall go to the heavenly world and be honored by the gods like the king of the immortals.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. Sanatkumāra said:
When the god had entered the palace and was well-seated upon an excellent throne,
that cruel Manmatha remained outside, intent on piercing the god with his arrows.
He was joined with improper conduct, evil-minded, the lowest of his lineage,
tormenting all the worlds, and devoid of compassion for anyone.
He came with Rati, in the form of Cakrāhvaya, to create obstacles for the sages who were engaged in their observances and vows.
Then, O Vyāsa, he looked with his third eye at the Lord of the Gods, who was an assailant desiring to pierce him, with a look full of contempt.
Then, the fire born from his eyes, possessing thousands of garlands of flames,
enveloped the Lord of Rati and consumed him along with his retinue.
Burning with pain, distressed and crying out in a discordant voice,
he fell to the surface of the earth while seeking to propitiate that god.
Swiftly, with his limbs enveloped by fire, that Manmatha, the scorcher of the worlds,
fell down and in an instant was reduced to ashes.
But his wife, deeply distressed, lamented piteously;
afflicted by grief and moved by compassion, she entreated both the god and the goddess.
And having heard her lamentation, those two gods, whose very nature is compassion,
looked upon the suffering woman, comforted her, and spoke to her.
"O blessed lady, he has certainly been consumed; his rebirth here is not expected.
Even though he is bodiless, he will perform all your tasks in due time."
But when Viṣṇu becomes the son of Vasudeva, O auspicious one,
then he shall become your husband, and this [son] shall be his son.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having obtained that boon, she— the beautiful-faced wife of Kāma—
departed for her desired destination, filled with joy and free from fatigue.
Sanatkumāra said: Having thus burned Kāma, whose mind was deluded, Śaṅkara spoke to the daughter of Himavat with devotion toward the best of sages.
The lord of brahmins named Vasiṣṭha, holding me in his heart, is performing austerities;
O lady of great vows, I shall go there to grant him a boon.
Having spoken thus to the goddess with devotion and affection,
the omnipresent Lord then went into the presence of the ascetic sage Vasiṣṭha.
Then [he saw] Vasiṣṭha, the best among the excellent sages, the most eminent, the foremost of those who practice austerities, that tiger among ṛṣis, performing supreme penance.
When a full thousand years had passed, the Blessed One approached him—who was like a blazing fire—and said: "Tell me, what shall I give you?
O twice-born one, I grant you divine vision; behold me along with my retinue."
Having seen that Lord Īśāna, he bowed his head to the Master,
placed his joined palms upon his head, and praised him with a joyful countenance.
Vasiṣṭha said: Salutations to the golden liṅga; salutations indeed to the Vedic liṅga.
Salutations to the thousand-fold liṅga; salutations indeed to the fiery liṅga.
Salutations to the ancient Liṅga; salutations indeed to the Liṅga of the Vedas.
Salutations to the Liṅga of the wind; salutations indeed to the Liṅga of Brahman.
Salutations to the Liṅga of the three worlds; salutations indeed to the Liṅga of burning. Salutations to the Liṅga of the mountain; salutations indeed to the Liṅga of stability.
Homage to the secret liṅga, whose liṅga rises above the seven continents;
homage to the liṅga of all purposes, whose limbs are the liṅgas of all worlds.
Homage be to the one whose mark is the unmanifest; indeed, homage to the one whose mark is the intellect.
Homage to the one whose mark is the ego-sense; indeed, homage to the one whose mark is the elements.
Salutations to the one whose mark is the senses; salutations to the one whose mark is the subtle elements;
salutations to the one whose mark is the Puruṣa; and indeed salutations to the one whose mark is existence.
Homage to the one whose mark is all objects, and indeed homage to the one whose mark is darkness;
homage to the one whose mark is passion and the upper [quality], and indeed homage to the one whose mark is goodness.
Homage to the sky-linga, and indeed homage to the fire-linga;
homage to the wind-upward-linga, and indeed homage to the sound-linga.

Homage to you who possess the characteristics of the Ṛgveda hymns; indeed, homage to you who possess the characteristics of the Yajurveda. Homage to you who possess the characteristics of the Atharvaveda; indeed, homage to you who possess the characteristics of the Sāmaveda.
Homage to the one whose mark is the constituent parts of sacrifice; indeed, homage to the one whose mark is sacrifice itself.
Homage to you, the one of infinite marks, whose marks are followed by the gods.
Grant us supreme yoga, as well as offspring equal to yourself;
O God, grant us imperishable Brahman and supreme tranquility, O All-pervading Lord;
grant the indestructibility of our lineage and an inexhaustible mind devoted to dharma.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, being thus praised by Vasiṣṭha of immeasurable soul, the Blessed One was pleased; and being pleased, he spoke this to him.
The Blessed One said:
"I am pleased with you; I shall grant you all this that is in your heart, as well as the supreme, subtle, imperishable yoga that fulfills all desires."
"And I shall grant you a divine grandson, equal to yourself and endowed with the power of asceticism and yoga, O best of sages; he will indeed manifest before you."
Self-restraint, tranquility, as well as fame, contentment, and freedom from anger shall be yours eternally, along with immortality in every respect.

"O Brahmin, [grant me] invincibility, invulnerability, and eternal imperishability; as well as the non-interruption of my lineage and undecaying devotion to dharma. Speak of other boons too; I shall grant them, O best of sages."
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Blessed One, O best of gods, all that is to be in the future is already known to you.
For it shall not be otherwise than what you, O Lord, intend, O God."
The god said:
"It is my firm conviction that the future cannot be made otherwise;
since I am the creator of the future, how could I make it otherwise?"
Thus there is no doubt in this matter regarding that which has been ordained by me;
therefore, your imperishable son shall again bestow grace upon you.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus, O brahmin-sage, the god Kapardin Nīlalohita then vanished in an instant while that seer was looking on.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. Vyāsa said: [Chapter Sixteen of the Skanda Purāṇa] Vyāsa said:
Having obtained boons, our grandfather, the venerable Vasiṣṭha,
begot which son who was equal to himself in splendor?
Sanatkumāra said:
By virtue of that boon from the trident-bearing God of gods,
he begot [a son] upon Arundhatī who was endowed with the power of austerity and yoga.
He had a son named Śakti, the eldest of a hundred sons, who was most devoted to Brahman.
From his very childhood, that high-souled son of Vasiṣṭha possessed supreme devotion for the one who has the bull as his banner, with a most focused mind.
Once, for the sake of obtaining offspring, he propitiated the Lord of Umā;
Mahādeva, being pleased with him, spoke: "I am the giver of a boon."
Then, having seen that Lord, he spoke these words with a bowed face:
"By what means, O God, shall I praise you, who are the Lord of the entire world?
O All-pervading One, you sustain all the worlds by yourself through the power of your own law."
You alone are the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment, the agent and likewise the action; you are the producer, that which is produced, and the very act of production in every respect.
"O Lord, O Master of the Gods, I desire that you grant me a son named Ātman, equal to me in virtues; let this boon be granted to me."
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa,
the God, the best among speakers, laughing at him who spoke thus,
addressed him with words that made all the quarters resound.
"O Śakti, I have been requested by you, and he shall be born from you;
O bull among sages, he will be equal to you and a knower of all the Vedas."
And likewise, that which has arisen from the nature of a seed becomes itself the nature of a sprout;
having undergone a transformation, it no longer exists as the nature of a seed.
Thus, that self of yours, having come into being as what is designated as "offspring," will no longer exist as its own self once it has undergone a change of state through transformation.
Sanatkumāra said: Having spoken thus to him, the god, laughing and looking upon him,
that yogi of exceeding splendor suddenly departed and became invisible.
When Mahādeva had departed, your grandfather Śakti reflected upon those words and thought, "It is exactly so."
Then, after a very long time had passed, O Śubhavratā,
the one of great wisdom, though purified by great austerity, conceived a supreme embryo while possessing a radiance equal to fire within Adṛśyantī.
While she was pregnant, King Kalmāṣapāda,
his mind carried away by a Rākṣasa, became enraged and devoured the Ṛṣi.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. Vyāsa said: [Chapter 17 of the Skanda Purāṇa] Vyāsa said:
Why did that king devour the seer endowed with ascetic power?
And for what reason was the king’s mind carried away by a *rākṣasa*?
Sanatkumāra said:
There was a powerful king named Mitrasaha, the sacrificer of Vasiṣṭha;
he was the son of Sudāsa and possessed a splendor equal to that of Indra and the Moon.
Having approached him, Śakti said: "O King of kings, having been initiated, I shall practice a vow;
therein, at night, I must always consume flesh."
"Grant to me, who have come here, that which is pure, endowed with all virtues,
free from any remedy [against decay], and bestowed in solitude at a single time."
Having been told by him, "So be it," that high-minded one departed; then, O best of sages, the Rākṣasa vanished from the king's sight, and he no longer commanded the cook for his sake.
Then, when the day had passed, O dear one, that self-restrained lord of men, remembering [his promise],
summoned the cook and spoke to him like one in distress.
Saudāsa said: "O Amṛtāvasu, I have promised the wise son of my preceptor that his flesh, prepared as food, shall be eaten by me this evening."
Therefore, act accordingly with haste, so that our time does not pass us by.
Thus addressed, the cook Amṛtavasu then replied:
"O King, O bull among men, you did not tell us beforehand;
at present, there is not even a small amount of meat that we desire."
Because the flesh itself was so small, because there were so many who ate it,
and because of the giving away of what was immeasurable, nothing at all remained.
The king said:
"I know your complete devotion, and I know your integrity;
I know that the flesh is small in quantity, and this task is likewise of such a nature."
"Seek flesh quickly; you shall obtain it wherever you deem fit."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus, Amṛtāvasu applied himself with great effort;
yet, though he searched thoroughly for flesh, he did not find any at all.

When he did not obtain any meat, he went at night to the great king, the lord of men, and spoke these meaningful words: SkP_17.12: "When he did not obtain any meat, he went at night to the great king, the lord of men, and spoke these meaningful words."
"O King, there is no meat at all that is ever pure in this city;
I am exhausted from searching, so command what I should do for you."
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus by the cook at that time, O lord of men,
the king said nothing to that cook and remained silent.
Immediately thereafter, a Rākṣasa named Rudhira, impelled by Viśvāmitra, entered the body of the king.
Then, possessed by that evil-minded Rākṣasa and drenched in blood, the one of great splendor spoke softly into the ear of the cook: SkP_17.16 //
"Go, and having brought whatever meat you can find— even human flesh at the very least, or that of a donkey or a camel— you should prepare it all."
Will he recognize you again at night?
Furthermore, quickly prepare a refined meal that is both flavorful and fragrant.
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus by him, O Vyāsa, the king then took human flesh from a certain man who had died and been cast away, having done harm to the king.
Then, at the time of midnight, he beheld that best of sages, possessing a radiance like the form of the sun and a brilliance equal to a hundred fires.
Having honored him according to the prescribed rites with water for the feet, water for the guest-offering, and an excellent, foremost seat, he served him food.
Having touched that food which had been brought, the great ascetic became enraged;
and being angry, he spoke to the king as if burning him up.
Śakti said:
"O lowest of kings, the feeding of Brahmins is not fit for Rākṣasas;
it is not given by one who knows the ritual rules, yet you treat me with contempt."
"Since you desire to give this Rākṣasa as food to me, therefore,
by that very act, you shall become a man-eater."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus, the radiant king then reflected upon those words;
with his eyes red with anger and his mind possessed by the Rākṣasa, he spoke.
"Since you have said to me, 'Become a man-eater,' therefore,
O twice-born one, I shall devour you along with your brothers."
Having eaten [the flesh] for the sake of purification, I shall thereafter be released from the curse; then, having restrained the collection of my senses, I will practice pure austerity and,
permitted by your father, dwell in heaven as I desire.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: [Chapter 18 of the Skanda Purāṇa]
Then that king, having abandoned his own kingdom, entered the forest with his wife; there he became a man-eater of great strength.
There, in the very presence of the great sage, he first devoured Śakti,
and then the hundred brothers of Vasiṣṭha, even as he looked on.
Then, having witnessed the terrible slaughter of his sons, the lord Vasiṣṭha, son of Brahmā, did not direct his wrath toward Kauśika; rather,
he was utterly overwhelmed by the great grief for his sons.
Having tied a great stone around his neck, that powerful son of Brahmā threw himself into the river; out of fear, it split into a hundred channels.
Therefore, the sages of strict vows call it the Śatadru.
Having bound him again with firm nooses, the self-controlled one released him into another; in her he became Vipāśa, and from that she became the Vipāśā.
Then, having reached the forest, fasting and with his senses subdued,
he remained there subsisting on air alone, causing his own body to wither away.
Then he suddenly heard the melodious sound of the Vedas being recited by someone there, and he immediately entered into a state of meditative absorption.
Then his wife, whose every limb was beautiful, with full and elevated breasts,
and with a dejected face and downcast eyes, stood before Śakti.
He said to her, "From where do you come, and whose sound is this that is heard?
Then, weeping, she spoke with a piteous voice to her father-in-law.
Adṛśyantī said: "O Guru, from the very moment you departed from the hermitage due to grief for your son,
I have remained invisible, devoted to the Blessed One ever since."
O Lord, this is the sound of your son studying while he still dwells within your womb; do not set your mind on sorrow.
Sanatkumāra said:
"Now, my child, I have hope for life," he said;
then, having established himself in patience and fortitude, the sage departed for his hermitage.
While going toward that hermitage, he saw on the path King Saudāsa,
his limbs smeared with fat and blood, and his eyes red with rage.
As he rushed forward with speed, the sage paralyzed him with mantras;
then, from his body, there emerged an exceedingly dreadful *rakṣas*.
And he said to him: "O evil-souled one, I would burn you along with your kinsmen!
But what use is it to me that you are burned? Go, you are released, O wicked-minded one! (SkP 18.15)
Then that wretched-souled Rākṣasa, a doer of cruel deeds, being released,
bowed his head in fear and went into the presence of Kuśika.
When the night-stalker had departed, the king, bowing his head to the sage, sought his favor; and he then spoke these meaningful words.
O Indra among kings, there is indeed no fault on your part for being possessed by a Rākṣasa;
your sons were slain by Kṛtānta (Death), and the Rākṣasa was merely the instrument in that matter.
"Rule the kingdom, O Indra among kings, inherited from your father and grandfather, O Lord!
Tell me, O bull among men, what pleasing thing may I do for you today?"
The king said:
"O Blessed One, O Acyuta, I desire a son begotten by you upon this queen;
O Great Being, do that which is pleasing to me."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having then said "So be it" to that wife, he of great vows,
being at peace, begot a son named Śoṇaka.
Then, having consecrated his own son Śoṇaka upon the throne,
he quickly departed for the forest with his wife, intent on ascetic practice.
In the course of time, a powerful son named Parāśara was born to Vasiṣṭha’s son Śakti by Adṛśyantī.
Then the wise one regarded Vasiṣṭha as his very father;
he repeatedly addressed the teacher of his father, saying, "Father! Father! (SkP 18.24).
Then, at one time, having learned that his father Śuci had been devoured by a *rākṣasa*, he performed a sacrifice to the *rākṣasas* through asceticism and mantras.
There, that one of great splendor offered fifty crores of Rākṣasas of cruel deeds into the fire, and then Brahmā quickly approached him.
Having approached and paid homage to him, the Lord, together with Vasiṣṭha, the sages, and the deities, spoke these words to Parāśara: SkP_18.27.
Brahmā said:
"Those deities fall even while performing sacrifices preceded by mantras;
for this eighth station is indeed the foremost of such stations for the gods."
Parāśara said:
Together with the gods, I shall consume all the worlds with fires;
having burnt the others, I will propagate the worlds there—of this there is no doubt.
Sanatkumāra said: Having heard those words so full of pride, the god Pitāmaha spoke these words to him,
consoling him with gentle speech.
The Grandfather said:
"O high-minded one, what you have done is exactly as you say; there is no doubt about it.
All of this must be forgiven by me out of a desire to do what is pleasing to you."
"O highly fortunate one, those by whom my father was devoured along with his brothers—
those very ones must be offered as oblations into the fire while Viśvāmitra looks on.
May there be well-being for all others everywhere, including the gods together with the Rākṣasas."
Tormented by his resolve, he spoke of the root of his wrath:
"O illustrious one, my son, you must restrain Vasiṣṭha."
All the gods, with palms joined in reverence, bowed down to that great sage;
and all those seers likewise praised him then with words of hymn.

Whosoever among these— whether a Brahmin or even a Kṣatriya— who is evil-minded,
shall resort to the side of the Rākṣasas and attempt to take retaliatory action.
Even him, enraged here, endowed with the power of austerity and yoga,
I shall strike down through the application of my asceticism and consume in the blazing fire.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the gods, together with the gandharvas, led by the Grandfather (Brahmā),
having recognized that power of his, worshipped Parāśara.
And when those evil-minded Rākṣasas had been sacrificed,
he then withdrew the sacrificial session with the permission of Brahmā.
Sanatkumāra said:
"He who, having become pure, causes this to be heard by the twice-born at the time of a śrāddha or during a rite for the gods, the rākṣasas do not harm him."
Having heard this account of Parāśara— which arose from undaunted origins, was produced by the performance of pure speech and action,
and resulted in the spiritual perfection of his lineage— a brahmin does not enter again into the womb of a Rākṣasa.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
In this manner, O Vyāsa, your father performed a sacrifice against the Rākṣasas;
having completed it, he again practiced radiant asceticism.
Having approached him, who was radiant as the sun due to his ascetic power, the imperishable Vasiṣṭha spoke these meaningful words to him who was filled with joy.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Desiring sons, the Pitṛs indeed performed extremely difficult austerities and produced a son endowed with ascetic power and knowledge.
"Those who know the Vedas understand that this man, possessed of knowledge and endowed with ascetic power, will ensure our lineage and provide for our ultimate destiny."
O Lord, though you are endowed with asceticism, possessed of knowledge, and filled with glory,
you are the best among those who have sons, yet you are deprived of offspring.
Therefore, O best of those who observe vows, go to freedom from debt toward your ancestors;
procreate a son quickly, whether one who excels you or one who is your equal.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus by Vasiṣṭha of immeasurable soul,
that radiant one reached Mount Maināka and performed a most difficult penance.
After a long time, to him who had been purified by ascetic penance,
the Lord of Umā granted a boon, and he chose a virtuous son.
Having obtained the boon, he returned and requested, for the sake of a son,
a perfectly pure field where his son might be born.
Then, in his agitation, he beheld Kālī, the daughter of the King of Daśārṇa, who had attained the state of being his own daughter, possessing a divine form.
Born from the womb of a fish, she was formerly a consumer of the seed of Vasu;
she was Adrikā, the most excellent of Apsarases, auspicious and composed of the splendor of Brahman.
Having granted her a boon, that great ascetic begot upon her you,
the source of all austerities and the promoter of the Śrauta and Smārta traditions.
Your son was Śuka, the best among those who know yoga;
he had four sons and one daughter of slender waist.
Vyāsa said: How did the enmity between Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha arise, and how was it subsequently removed? I wish to know this.
Sanatkumāra said:
When Parāśara was still in the womb and the son of Gādhi had attained the status of a brahmin,
there were the two hermitages of those two at Sarasvatī in Kurukṣetra.
There, recollecting his enmity, the wise Viśvāmitra,
while Vasiṣṭha looked on, slew a hundred of his sons in a fit of rage.
Thereupon, the powerful sage Viśvāmitra also spoke to Sarasvatī in private: "O great river, having swept Vasiṣṭha away with your mighty current while he was bathing here, bring him back to me."
Thus addressed, she went to Vasiṣṭha and spoke to him in her distress;
and he, for his part, spoke to the great river regarding what Gādheya had said.
"Do so, O illustrious lady; take me wherever you desire, lest that cruel son of Gādhi cast upon you a curse most difficult to endure."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, as Gādheya was offering oblations into the fire at midday, that auspicious river, having reached its full force, swiftly carried Vasiṣṭha away by her current.
Seeing that best of sages carried away by the current, Vyāsa said: "Since you have carried him away with such speed through deceit, therefore,
by this very act, you shall become a river of bloody water."
Cursed by Viśvāmitra, that river which bestows happiness upon the world flowed with blood,
as well as flesh and fat.
Then, on the occasion of visiting the sacred fords, the sages who had gathered there bestowed their grace upon her, by which she became possessed of clear water.
Then, through the power of his great asceticism and after a long time,
that bull among sages recognized Vasiṣṭha’s forbearance.
The immensely radiant Viśvāmitra abandoned his enmity toward Vasiṣṭha;
thus those two best of sages relinquished their mutual hostility.
Sanatkumāra said:
He who would constantly hear this, or cause the Brāhmaṇas to hear it,
crosses over difficult and impassable obstacles with unwearied manliness.

Endowed with the qualities of modesty, manliness, and magnanimity, and possessing a radiant and beautiful appearance, he shall become equal to all the kings of the immortals; and if he so desires, he may sport at will in the triple heaven.
Thus, O Vyāsa, that enmity between Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha came to an end, for the sake of the welfare of the worlds once again.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said: [Chapter Twenty of the Skanda Purāṇa] Vyāsa said:
O great sage, tell me in its entirety and without omission everything that the two lords of the gods, Umā and Hara, did when they were united.
Sanatkumāra said: Then Umā and Hara, both irreproachable, having come together,
united a brahmin of the Śālaṅka lineage with a boon.
And that son, who was not born from a womb, having propitiated the Supreme Lord and attained equality with Rudra, shone forth as Mahāgaṇapati.
Vyāsa said: How was Nandin born, and how, having propitiated Śaṅkara,
did he attain equality with Śambhu as well as the office of doorkeeper?
Sanatkumāra said: There was a virtuous and powerful sage named Śilāda;
his livelihood consisted of stones (śilaka), and for that reason he became known as Śilāda.
That twice-born man saw his ancestors hanging in a pit,
their lineages severed, having indeed fallen into a terrible hell.
Addressed by them, who were desirous of offspring, he said: "O best of the twice-born, propitiate the imperishable Lord of the World, Mahādeva, for the sake of a son."
As he was performing austerities for a thousand years, Śarva, the bearer of the trident, surrounded by his hosts, spoke to him: "I am the granter of boons."
Having seen that Soma, the Lord of Lords, he bowed at the feet of the All-pervading One and praised the Sovereign of the Gods with a voice faltering with joy.
Homage to the supreme deity, the Great Lord, the Great Soul;
homage to the creator of all lords of the gods, the Lord of Brahmā.
Homage to the destroyer of the body of Kāma, the cause of the arising of yoga;
homage to the mountain-dweller, the creator who is attainable through meditation.
Salutation always to the Lord of the sages, salutation to the Lord of the gods;
salutation indeed to the Lord of the Vedas and to the Lord of the yogins.
Constant salutation to Pradhāna, to the reality known as Amara;
salutation to the bestower of boons upon devotees, and to the one who is omnipresent.
Salutations to the creator and lord, the all-powerful one, together with the qualities of the transformations of the subtle elements, the senses, and the gross elements.
Salutations always to the Lord of the world and to the Creator of the world; eternal salutations to the Lord of primordial nature (prakṛti) and to Him who transcends the Puruṣa.
Homage ever to the Lord, who is accessible through yoga,
who is impetuous speed, who is the cause of the arising and destruction of saṃsāra, and the bestower of all desires.
Homage always to the one worthy of refuge; homage to the one whose limbs are smeared with ashes;
homage to you who hold the moon in your hand; homage to the lord of splendors.
Salutations always and eternally to the Creator of the three worlds, who abides as the sun, wind, fire, water, moon, ether, and earth.
O God, how can there be rest for you who are to be praised,
since you alone are the cause of this world’s maintenance and destruction?
O Lord of Gods, for me who am without refuge and who seeks refuge in you,
grant your supreme grace and become a bestower of boons, O Creator of the Universe!
Sanatkumāra said:
That twice-born man who, being pure and observant of his vows, recites this entire hymn in the morning before the twice-born—
him neither Brahma-rākṣasas, night-stalkers, spirits, nor Yakṣas harm, nor do bipeds, serpents, or Pūtanās.
Then that Blessed Lord, being praised along with Umā, said:
"I am a granter of boons; tell me what is in your heart."

"O Blessed One, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me,
I desire a son equal to myself, free from death and not born from a womb."
Having been addressed thus, the three-eyed God, being well-pleased, said to him,
"So be it," and vanished right there.
When that great archer had departed, the highly honored sage returned to his own hermitage and then spoke to the sages.
O best of sages, having been thus praised by them, he then, desiring to perform a sacrifice, ploughed his own sacrificial ground with a plough after some time had passed.
As that furrow was being plowed,
a youth appeared, arisen from it, resembling the fire of universal destruction at the end of an aeon.
Seeing the prince thus arisen and blazing with splendor,
he realized, "This is a Rākṣasa," and out of fear did not approach him.
The prince, having likewise arisen, approached his father of blazing splendor with a dejected soul and cried out, "Father! Father!"
When, even though addressed as "Father," he did not respond to him,
Vāyu then spoke in a melodious voice to Śilāda from the sky.
Vāyu said:
O Śālaṅkāyana, this son of yours who was formerly granted by the god Śambhu, not born from a womb— rejoice in him!
"Since this son of yours, O best of the twice-born, shall always bring you joy, therefore he shall be known by the name Nandin."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, at the word of Vāyu, he embraced Nandin and,
taking him along with his own hermitage, led him away, increasing his own satisfaction.
He performed for him the rites of tonsure, initiation, and so forth.
And having composed them, he taught the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs in their entirety,
as well as Ayurveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharvaveda, and the science of grammar (Śabdalakṣaṇa).
The behavior of elephants, the characteristics of men and women,
all the arts and crafts, and the knowledge of omens as well.

O Vyāsa, he mastered in just five years everything concerning the treatment of the hosts of spirits, the conduct of the Mothers, all that pertains to serpents, and whatever else there is of their activity.
He was skillful, pure, undepressed in spirit, pleasant of speech, and free from envy;
he was always beloved by all the world and a delight to the mind and the eye.
Then, in the seventh year from that time, two divine rishis, rich in ascetic merit and possessed of great luster, arrived at the hermitage of Śilāda.
Having honored them according to the prescribed rule, Śilāda, who was a great ascetic,
observed that they were seated comfortably on highly venerated seats.
The two named Mitra and Varuṇa, endowed with the power of asceticism and yoga,
were masters of all beings throughout the three worlds, including both the moving and the unmoving.
Permitted by those two, he sat down upon an excellent seat;
having sat there, being pleased, he praised them with pleasing words.
And questioned by them, he said: "Is your son auspicious and a giver of satisfaction?
Is he devoted to the study of the Vedas? And is there a continuity of dharma?"
I hope that the fool does not show contempt for the elderly or for his teachers; I hope he observes his religious observances and bestows satisfaction upon the virtuous.
Thus addressed, the radiant Śilāda, who was devoted to his son,
virtuous, and the enhancer of his family lineage, replied properly.
Having summoned his son Nandin, who was steadfast and dear to him,
he fell with his head at the feet of those two out of joy.
Those two gods bestowed upon her a blessing consisting of constancy in dharma,
a disposition toward service of their preceptor, and likewise imperishable worlds.
Sanatkumāra said: Then Śilāda, observing that blessing from the two gods,
dismissed Nandin and, being afraid, questioned those two best of sages.
Śilāda said:
"O venerable sages, you who are truthful and know the destiny of all embodied beings, for what reason have both of you granted long life to my son?"
The two best of sages correctly applied themselves, yet they did not receive any blessing.
Mitra and Varuṇa said:
"O dear one, this son of yours is short-lived, though esteemed by all;
he shall indeed sustain his life for only one more year."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, tormented by grief and distressed, he fell to the ground;
having dismissed those two tigers among sages, he lamented all alone.
Hearing the sound of him lamenting out of grief, his auspicious son Nandi came and then beheld his father, who was exceedingly distressed.
Nandi said:
"O father, by what sorrow are you tormented that you weep?
From where has this suffering arisen? O father, I wish to know."
Śilāda said:
"O son, you will surely lose your life within a year.
When the two sages spoke thus, distress then took hold of me.
Nandin said:
"It is true, O dear one, that the divine sages did not speak a falsehood;
nevertheless, death shall have no power over me, so do not grieve."
Śilāda said: What is your austerity, what is your higher knowledge, what is your yoga, and what is your exertion, by which you will elude Death who is intent upon you? Tell me.
Nandin said:
"O father, I shall not evade death through asceticism nor through knowledge;
by the grace of Mahādeva alone shall I conquer death, and not otherwise."
"I shall behold the god Śaṅkara; then death shall not be mine.
When death has perished, I shall dwell for a long time with you, free from sorrow."
Śilāda said:
"In the past, after performing extremely difficult austerities for a thousand years,
Mahādeva was beheld by me, since you were obtained as my son."
But you, having practiced asceticism for only a single year and not yet being highly refined by it, how will you behold Mahādeva? This is what I wish to know.
Nandin said:
"O Father, the Lord is not seen through austerity, nor is he seen through knowledge;
the Supreme Lord is seen through a pure mind and through devotion."
"O Father, once released by you and having gone, I shall behold the Three-eyed One before long; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, release me quickly."
"Yama approached me while I was standing there, and even as you were looking on, he did not harm me; therefore, my dear son, I am departing from here."
Whether standing, lying down, running, or fallen—
realizing that death indeed does not wait, attain tranquility.
Having descended into the divine water and established myself in a state of pure being,
I shall practice the Raudra-adhyāya and thereafter behold Śaṅkara.
And for me, who am engaged in recitation, disciplined, and surrendered to the state of Rudra,
many deaths and times of end will not cause me distress.
Sanatkumāra said:
Perceiving him speaking thus with pure speech,
the great ascetic of undepressed soul released his son from his distress with difficulty.
Having saluted his father’s feet with his head, that highly illustrious one circumambulated him to the right and departed with firm resolve.
Having saluted all the sages, that sage of noble intellect, desiring to behold him,
went to Lord Hara, the remover of the distress of those who bow before him.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then Nandi departed from there and went to the best of rivers,
renowned as Bhuvana, which brings happiness to all the worlds.
Having entered it, the wise one then remained at the lake with one-pointed concentration;
terrified of death, he then recited the Rudra-hymns with a composed mind.
As he was reciting there with single-minded devotion, by that very blessing,
when one crore had been recited, the God was indeed pleased.
Having approached him, the blessed Śarva, the fierce one with matted hair, said:
"Nandin, I am pleased; may it be well with you. Choose a boon as you desire."
Bowing down, he spoke to Hara, the remover of the distress of those who bow before him:
"O Lord, O All-pervading One, I wish to recite a second ten million [verses] of the Blessed Ones.
Having said, "So be it," the God also departed as he had come.
Sanatkumāra said: Having descended from there once more, with his self thus restrained,
he likewise recited another ten million [mantras], meditating solely upon Rudra.
Then, when the second ten-million-year period was completed, the bull-bannered Lord approached him and said, "I am here as a granter of boons."
He said, "O Blessed One, O Lord of Gods, O All-pervading One, by your grace I wish to recite even a third crore [of mantras], O Time."
"So be it," the Blessed One replied once more;
having spoken, the one of great splendor went to his own abode together with the Goddess.
Then he muttered another third crore of Rudra-mantras;
thereupon, O twice-born one, he became like the sun at the end of a Yuga.
O Vyāsa, when three crores of those [years] had passed for him who possessed the brilliance of fire,
the god Soma, together with his attendants, approached that place.
Having grasped him with his trunk and lifted him out of the water,
Kālahasta spoke to Nandin while rubbing him with the tip of his hand.
The God said:
"O Śailāda, I am the granter of boons to you, gratified by this penance.
Well recited, O wise one! Speak what is in your heart."
Śailādi said: "By your power, O Lord, I shall again chant another ten million [times].
O All-pervading One, if you are pleased with me, O God, I choose this boon."
The Blessed One said:
"What is the use of your further recitation? I am entirely satisfied with you;
whatever desire you choose, I shall grant it all to you."
"Shall it be the state of Brahmā, or the state of Viṣṇu, or the state of Indra, or the state of Vāyu? Become the Āditya, or Rudra? Speak, or what shall I give to you?"
Sanatkumāra said: Having been thus addressed by the God, he bowed his head at the Lord’s feet and praised Him, the destroyer of the mountain-like sacrifice of Pura, Kāma, and Aṅga.
Nandin said: "Homage to the God beyond gods, to Mahādeva;
homage indeed to the destroyer of the body of Kāma, to Nīlakaṇṭha."
Homage to the destroyer of Tuṣita and to the burner of the three worlds;
homage to Kāla, the wielder of the fierce staff, and indeed homage to the one of terrible punishment.
Homage to Nīlaśikhaṇḍa; homage to the thousand-headed one, and indeed to the thousand-handed and the thousand-footed one.
To Him whose hands and feet are everywhere, whose eyes and faces are everywhere,
and who possesses hearing everywhere, who stands encompassing all.
Salutations to you who are gold-colored and likewise beyond the senses;
salutations to the golden emblem, and indeed salutations to the universal emblem.
Salutations to the one whose color is like the moon and the sun, the Lord of Yoga, the unconquered;
salutations to him who holds the Pināka bow in his hand, and who holds the trident and the mallet in his hands.
Salutations indeed to the one armed with a mace and a sword, to the bearer of the battle-axe,
to the chariot-warrior, to the one clad in armor, and to the great archer.
Salutation to the one who holds a trident in his hand and who wields a fierce staff;
salutation to the Lord of the Gaṇas, and salutation to the Lord of the Rudras.
Salutations to the thousand-eyed one, and indeed salutations to the hundred-eyed one;
salutations to the Lord of the Ādityas and to the Lord of the Vasus.
Homage to the Lord of the Earth, homage to the Lord of Space;
homage to the Lord of the heavenly world, homage to the Lord of Umā.
Homage to the Lord of Yoga, the bestower of all yoga;
to the meditator, the one being meditated upon, and the one praised by those who practice meditation.
To Death, to the Staff of Time, to the Great-Souled Yama,
to the Lord of the Gods, and to him of divine constitution.
To Savitṛ, the giver of wealth for sacrifice, the progenitor of heaven,
the dharma of all the gods, who possesses manifold forms.
To the one who is the supreme nectar, the most excellent, praised by all the gods,
and the seizer of the head of Brahmā and of the great-souled Sacrifice.
To the destroyer of Tripura, to the fierce one, to the remover of all that is inauspicious,
to him whose form consists of half the body of Umā, and to him who has an eye upon his forehead.
To the destroyer of Mahiṣa and Andhaka, to the creator, indeed to the Supreme Lord,
to the teacher of Brahmā and to the progenitor of Brahmā.
And salutation indeed to the teacher of the youth, to the bestower of boons upon the youth, to the wielder of the plow, to the crusher with the club, and to the one of great laughter.
To him who holds the noose of death in his hand, who wears Takṣaka as his sacred thread,
whose vehicle is the cloud with lightning, and likewise to him who rides upon a bull.
To the one who dwells in the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, who resides on Mount Meru, who dwells in Kailāsa, and who is the friend of the Lord of Wealth; // SkP_21.36 //
To him who has been given half of Viṣṇu’s body, to him who is the granter of boons to that very [Viṣṇu],
to him who is unequaled by any being, and who is compassionate toward all beings.
Salutations to him who has internalized the elemental beings, who bestows life upon living creatures,
who is the mind that conceives thoughts, and indeed who transcends all pride.
Homage to the one who is awakening and the awakened, to the seer and indeed to the eye;
homage to you, the toucher, and likewise to the sense of touch.
Salutations to the Taster and likewise to the Sense of Taste;
salutations to the Smeller and to the Sense of Smell, and indeed to the Hearer and to the Sense of Hearing; salutations to the Grasper and to the Hand, and likewise to the Walker and to the Foot.
Salutation be to the creator of bliss and salutation indeed to bliss itself;
salutation to Speech and to the eloquent one, and to the Great Soul who is the subtle element of that.
Salutations to the subtle and to the gross being, to Rajas; and constant salutations to Tamas, to the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña), and to the Unconquered.
Salutation to Viṣṇu, the sustainer of the world and the lord of creatures;
salutation to Manu, the seven seers, who are performing austerities and are full of fervor.
Salutations to the one devoted to Brahman, to the pure one, and likewise to Durvāsas;
salutations to the artisan, the lord of craftsmen, the wise Viśvakarman.
Salutations likewise to Atri, to Bhṛgu, and to Aṅgiras;
and to Pulaha, Pulastya, Kratu, Dakṣa, and Anala.
Salutations be to you, Dharmaruci, and to Vasiṣṭha;
salutations to the Being, the Lord of Beings, and the Lord of Kuṣmāṇḍas.
He stands and he flows, he sings and he dances as well;
to the one who is beyond necessity, beyond destruction, ageless, and immortal.
To the one who is imperishable, undecaying, and likewise unimpeded;
to the one who cannot be entered by anyone, who is visible yet possesses an invisible form.
To you who are subtler than the subtle, the all-pervading Great Self—salutations to you, O Blessed One, three-eyed one; salutations to you, O Blessed One, Śiva;
salutations to you, Lord of all worlds; salutations to you, Creator of the world.
O Lord of Gods, neither through sovereignty over the gods, nor again through the state of Brahmā,
nor through being Viṣṇu, O Lord of Devas, nor even through the status of Indra, O Protector of Beings, do I desire anything else; O Īśāna, I desire only your eternal and imperishable state as a Gaṇa.
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to see you forever—along with your attendants, Ambā, and your retinue—in a state of grace; let this boon be granted to me."
O Lord, you alone have been our refuge in the past; you alone are the sovereign protector of the distressed, and you alone are our shelter—I never see any other.
And for one abandoned by you, destruction will surely come swiftly; there is no doubt in this matter.
I see no other course that leads to ultimate well-being.
"O God, accept me who am devoted, loyal, intent upon you, and taking refuge in you; let this be the boon granted to me forever."
Sanatkumāra said: That man who, rising early in the morning, recites this with an undistracted mind, shall,
upon the dissolution of the body, become equal to Nandīśvara.
Whoever should constantly hear this, or cause it to be heard among the twice-born,
shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and be glorified in the world of Rudra.
O Vyāsa, having heard even once this hymn that destroys all sins, one shall not fall into an evil rebirth, regardless of where one dies.
For one who, having constantly studied this foremost hymn, always worships the God with self-restraint—
what need has he for various sacrifices, gifts, pilgrimages, or likewise for well-performed austerities?
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter of the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the Lord of the Gods [beheld him] endowed with supreme devotion,
his eyes filled with tears, wretched, and bowing his head at his feet.
Taking hold of her with his two very gentle hands, the Moon, the remover of supreme suffering,
raised her up and wiped away her eyes which were filled with tears.
Then the Lord, together with the Goddess, having looked upon all the leaders of the Gaṇas, spoke to him with a satisfied soul, as if nourishing him with his very words. (SkP 22.3)
The God said:
"O sinless one, I know your devotion to me, and I know your distress;
O Śailādi, listen now to the outcome of all this."
Immortal, abandoned by old age, eternally free from suffering,
inexhaustible and indeed imperishable, he was together with his father and his circle of friends.
He shall be my beloved Gaṇapa, possessing my own vigor and my own prowess;
he shall always be dear to me, always remain by my side, and,
endowed with the power of great yoga, he shall indeed become like my very own form.
I grant you this island, possessed of supernatural powers, with the Ocean of Milk as its source of nectar; I provide you a dwelling there, where you shall always take delight.
Then, having removed from himself a garland made of lotuses,
the one of great splendor fastened that divine-looking wreath upon Nandin.
With that garland fastened around his neck,
Nandin shone like a second Śaṅkara— the glorious, three-eyed, ten-armed one.
Then the Blessed Lord Hara, taking him by the hand, said:
"Tell me, what supreme boon shall I grant you today?"
And this hermitage, thoroughly sanctified by your asceticism,
shall become my secret sanctuary known as Japyeśvara.
For a league in every direction, the field will be divine, surrounded by hosts of gods,
crowded with siddhas and cāraṇas, and frequented by throngs of apsarases;
it will become a supreme, secret field of accomplishment— of this there is no doubt.
Whatever a person performs here by deed, thought, or word—
whether it be auspicious or inauspicious— all that shall become auspicious.
The mental recitation shall indeed be equal to that of the Rudras;
wherever mortals die, they shall go to your world.
Then, taking the water dripping from his matted locks—which was as pure as a pearl necklace—the one of great asceticism said, "Become a river! and released it.

Then that great river flowed forth— divine in its waters, meritorious, auspicious with its jewel-like water, crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, adorned by ruddy geese, and endowed with groves of lotuses and water lilies.
Assuming the form of a woman, with palms joined in reverence and bowing her head,
she whose eyes had the luster of lotus and water-lily petals stood before Mahādeva.
Then the God spoke to that river who had appeared before him:
"O Goddess of auspicious countenance, since you have issued forth from the water of my matted locks (jaṭodaka),
therefore you shall be known by the name Jaṭodā, O best of rivers."
Whoever performs a bath in you, being pure and with a restrained mind,
shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice and be glorified in the world of Rudra.
Sanatkumāra said: Then Mahādeva, having declared to the Goddess, "This is your son," who was exceedingly radiant like Nandīśvara, caused him to bow at her feet.
Having smelled him on the head and stroking him with both hands,
the Goddess, gazing at the God out of love for her son, bathed him with the three streams of milk flowing from her breasts, white as a conch shell.
"Her three streams have flowed forth like a river possessing a flood;
therefore, Hara called that auspicious river Trisrotasī."
Seeing the river with its three streams, Vṛṣa was supremely delighted;
he bellowed, and from that sound another river came into being.
Since that great river originated from the roar of the bull,
the one whose banner is the bull (Śiva) indeed spoke to her as Ḍhittkirikā.
And the god fastened upon him his own wonderful crown made of Jāmbūnada gold, most marvelous to behold, as well as two earrings born of nectar.
Seeing him thus honored in the sky, the cloud Prabhākara— the mount of the gods— rained down with a roar, accompanied by flashes of lightning.
When he had been consecrated, two streams then began to flow intensely;
because one river issued forth from the gold,
Mahādeva addressed it by the name Svarṇodakā.
Because a holy river flowed forth from that second auspicious crown made of Jāmbūnada gold, they called it the river Jambū.
This place named Pañcanada, situated near Japyeśvara,
has been described by the Great-Souled One as having the same fruit as those [five rivers] at the Jaṭodā.
Having gone to that divine Pañcanada and to that Lord Japyeśvara,
and having fasted for three nights, one should bathe and worship the Wielder of the Trident (Śūlin).
He shall become an attendant of Nandīśvara, dwelling in the Ocean of Milk.
But whoever gives up their life-breaths, so difficult to abandon, at Japyeśvara—
whether by means of a formal vow or otherwise— he shall become a Gaṇapati unto me.
Equal to Nandīśvara, he is eternal, perpetual, undecaying, and immutable; never departing from my side, he is beloved and highly esteemed.
Any man who, having gone to Japyeśvara and Pañcanada, casts off his body there,
shall always be my most excellent attendant (gaṇapa), equal to you, and eternally possessed of splendor and a beautiful form.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. Sanatkumāra said:
The Blessed One, the Lord of the gods of gods, Hara, the master of all beings,
spoke to the goddess Umā, the daughter of the mountain king, O Master of Speech.
"O Goddess, I shall consecrate the god Nandīśvara, the lord of beings; I shall summon the Gaṇas. What do you think, O Imperishable One?"
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, my eldest son Nandin deserves all this— the sovereignty over the seven worlds as well as that of the lords of the Gaṇas."
Sanatkumāra said: Then that blessed Lord, the destroyer of the enemies of the gods,
facing the east, performed the invocation of the lords of the Gaṇas at that time.
Then, O great sage, listen as I describe how thousands of leaders of the Gaṇas, the lords of all the worlds, arrived there filled with joy.
Then [he appeared], with formidable teeth, his face adorned with a frown,
white as a conch shell, a pearl necklace, or water, possessing tusks, wearing a garland, and having three eyes.
With a thousand matted locks rising from his head, hair like flames, and large jaws,
he had eyes like glowing embers and a girdle bound with serpents.
With a tongue like lightning and a massive body, he likewise has his penis turned upward;
he wears a serpent as a sacred thread and likewise carries an axe.
With a girdle of muñja grass bound by serpents and bracelets likewise made of snakes,
emitting loud bursts of laughter resembling the fall of thunderbolts,
the leader of the Gaṇas known as Diṇḍi was seen.
Surrounded by ten crores of those who were like himself—
leaders of the Gaṇas, lords of the gods, and yogins of blazing splendor— [he set forth].
After him was Mahākeśa, who had a massive body and an erect penis;
he had three eyes, resembled a hundred fires, and roared like the falling of thunderbolts.
Dancing, singing, and performing various dramatic dances many times over,
he had flaming fangs, a great laugh, broad shoulders, and carried the Pināka bow.
Together with twenty million hosts of great-souled beings of diverse forms, he appeared all at once.
O Vyāsa, that leader of the Gaṇas named Aṣāḍhi arrived there, accompanied by those with the faces of lions and elephants, the faces of cranes, and the forms of leopards and tigers.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then another arrived, O Vyāsa, possessing the radiance of the sun at the end of an eon,
with arms a hundred yojanas long, naked, and with his organ turned upward.
He was exceedingly tall with an oversized penis, hanging eyebrows, and a thick nose;
he had a round face and large eyes, and his countenance was knit with a frown.
It was five yojanas wide and likewise long;
it bore four fangs in its mouth, as white as a conch shell or the moon.
With five tongues and ears on top of his head, holding a noose in his hand and possessing the speed of thought,
he was seen surrounded by a hundred crores of beings exactly like himself.
Renowned as Bhārabhūti and endowed with the power of great yoga,
that leader of the Gaṇas approached the presence of the God of gods.
Then [he saw the Lord], who possessed the luster of a kunda flower, the moon, or a conch shell, resembling a mass of snow or water,
shining like a lotus stalk or crystal, and wearing a girdle of ashes.
And having seized Aśanīhāsa— who had three feet, was clothed in rags,
possessed a hundred bellies, three heads, three eyes, and hair standing erect— [he subdued him].
His hair was crowned with garlands of flames, he wore a tiger skin as his garment,
possessed the speed of the wind, had a great laugh, and was girt with a belt of serpents.
Afflicted by the Mahoragas, with spike-like ears and an upward-pointing penis,
having ashes as his weapon, possessing great fangs and a massive jaw.
He beheld that heroic Mahāgaṇapati, renowned as Jvara,
who was surrounded by a hundred crores of attendants.
Then another appeared, gentle in form, his limbs smeared with ashes,
holding a trident in his hand, naked, and endowed with the power of great yoga.
Wearing many disguises and devoted to the yoga of meditation,
the lord known as Somavarṇa, surrounded by hundreds of millions,
came when summoned by the God as a leader of such hosts.
Then another appeared, massive in body, spear in hand, and possessed of great strength; resembling the fire at the end of an eon, he was steadfast, with the power of enduring fame.
He has the moon as his crest-jewel, possesses great hair, has four arms, and is deep red;
he is accompanied by those who are one-footed, of massive body, three-eyed, and hold tridents in their hands.
Surrounded by a hundred crores,
