Rudra— the destroyer of all asuras— appeared there together with his great assembly of attendants, like a pillar.
Then another appeared, pure, with short feet and belly,
wielding a spear, possessing a thousand arms and feet, a thousand eyes, and great majesty.
He has formidable fangs, wears black serpents as garments,
possesses three eyes, bears the moon as a crest-ornament, and is adorned with a garland around his neck.
Known as Ugrasena and surrounded by a hundred crores [of followers],
he, the lord himself, having been summoned, came into the presence of the god.
Then another approached the god who bears the crescent moon—
the Lord of great splendor, four-faced and possessing twenty-four eyes.
He has a thousand arms, a mouth of flames, great eyes, and an upward-pointing penis;
he has formidable teeth, spike-like ears, and large claws.
The sword-handed one of great splendor, the hundred-footed, the hundred-bellied,
the lightning-haired, the excessive-laughter, and likewise the one who moves in both directions.
Known as Ajaikapāda, he was surrounded by a hundred crores [of followers];
rich with golden rocks and trees, he was like a mountain shrouded in clouds.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O Vyāsa, another Gaṇapa of great strength arrived;
he was glorious, with faces on all sides, and possessed hands and feet everywhere.
With short arms, thighs, and feet, bearing a beautiful thunderbolt,
he was surrounded by eight hundred million attendants equal to himself;
known as Nikumbha, he possessed a hundred feet, a belly, and a face.
Then another one of great strength arrived, Vidyutkeśa,
who was terrible, wearing a garland of moons, laughing and shaking [the earth].
Holding a staff, with a massive face and the luster of a conch, a jasmine flower, or the moon,
he was surrounded by hundreds of millions of attendants and was supremely scorching to his enemies.
Then another one of great asceticism, surrounded by a host of a thousand koṭis, arrived wearing a garland of suns.
He, named Sūryāpyāyana, was the supreme favorite of the god;
with bow in hand, he possessed great energy, was renowned, and was exceedingly resplendent.
Likewise, there was another named Sarpamāla and Cakrābharaṇa;
the latter, possessing great splendor, had a discus as his weapon and short feet and waist.
He was renowned in the world by the name Grahāpyāyana; surrounded by six hundred million attendants, he pursued [him] closely.
The mighty Śaṅkukarṇa approached with ten million attendants,
as did Nandika with ten, Piṅgākṣa with eight,
Vināyaka with sixty-four, and the one renowned by the name Kuṣmāṇḍa.
Hiraṇyavarṇa with six, Ekapāda likewise;
Dhūmrakeśa with twelve, and Patākī with ten.
Sahasraghaṇṭa was surrounded by eighteen [attendants], Tapa by five,
Sahasraśīrṣa by six, and Bhava was encompassed by hundreds of millions.
Vara approached with ten [attendants], Kumbhakarṇa likewise with eight;
Viṣvaksena with a thousand, and Annada indeed with a hundred.
Āveśanī is likewise [accompanied] by eight, and Pravartana by seven;
Mahārava is surrounded by a host of a thousand crores of attendants.
Caturmukha with twelve [arms], as well as Bāhūpahāraka;
Mahākāla with a hundred [arms], and likewise the Gaṇa Agniśikhara.
Ādityamūrdhā with ten million, likewise Dhanāvaha with ten million,
Saṃnāma with one hundred, and Kukkuṭa with eight.
And Kunda with fifteen [crores], as well as another, Saṃkoṭaka;
Amoghabhūti with ten million, and likewise two Meghabhūtikas.
Ekapāda with sixty, and likewise the group of Saptashiras;
Mahābala with nine, and the well-known Apasmāra.
Nīla, the lord of the gods, as well as Pūrṇabhadra and Nirṛti,
approached together with seventy crores.
There, twenty hundred thousand times ten million *ītis*,
endowed with the power of great yoga, arrived.
The Bhūtas with ten billion, the Pramathas with three billion,
Vīrabhadra with sixty-four million, and the exceedingly powerful Vṛṣabha.
Megha, surrounded by ninety [attendants] including Saudāminīmālā, approached;
as did Prabhākara with twenty, and the very powerful Viṭpati.
Girika, Meghanāda, Udara, Maṇi, the divine-souled Kāṣṭhakarṇa, and the renowned Bilvarūpa; ||| SkP_23.58 |||
Śatamanyu, as well as the valiant Pañcākṣa,
Tālaketu, Ṣaṇḍa, Kāpālī, and Gajanāśana.
Likewise Saṃvartaka, Caitra, Trailokyadahana,
Lokāntaka, Dīptātman, and Hemakuṇḍala.
Mṛtyu, Yama, Kāla, Viṣahara, Śatamāya, Mahāmāya, Sarvatrāśaraṇa, the renowned Ekaśṛṅgin, and he who is Bhṛṅgiriṭi; ||| SkP_23.61 ||
These and other leaders of the Gaṇas, who are secret and possess great strength,
all arrived there filled with joy, fighting with various weapons.
Singing, running, and dancing, those of great strength likewise made the sounds of mouth-organs and cymbals resound.
Some were mounted on chariots, elephants, and horses; others had the wind, monkeys, tigers, lions, cats, serpents, and even birds as their vehicles.
Likewise, some were mounted upon various auspicious beasts of prey and other diverse creatures,
while others were mounted upon celestial chariots, and still others among human beings.
With kettledrums, conchs, and clay drums; with small drums, tabors, and cow-horn trumpets; and with various musical instruments such as large drums and single-headed drums.
With the resounding blasts of kettledrums and jharjharas, with āḍambaras and ḍiṇḍimas,
with maḍḍukas, flutes, lutes, and even with vivṛṣas and tuṇavas.
To the assembly of the gods came the great yogas, accompanied by the sounding of dardura drums, tāla-claps, tortoise-shells, and paṇava drums.

Those [gods], who were as radiant as the likeness of the thousand-eyed one, bowed down to Viśvakarman— the subduer of enemies, the lord of all, the single-syllabled, and the imperishable— and cried out loudly in praise.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: [Chapter Twenty-four of the Skanda Purāṇa]
All those lords of the Gaṇas, beings of great power and sovereigns over the lords of the gods, bowed down to the God and the Goddess and spoke these words: SkP_24.1 //
O Blessed One, O Slayer of the Enemies of the Gods, O Lord of the Goddess of the Gods!
For what purpose have we been summoned? Command us; it shall be done.
"Shall we dry up the oceans, or shall we strike down Yama along with his servants?
Shall we slay Death itself, so that today the Lotus-born One may not exist?"
"Either we shall bind Indra along with the gods, including Viṣṇu and Vāyu,
or, being thoroughly enraged, we shall bring back the Daityas together with the Dānavas."
"Whose terrible calamity shall we bring about today by your command?
Or whose festival, O Lord, filled with the fulfillment of all desires, shall we provide?"
To all of them who were speaking thus and bowing down, the god Bhava, the Lord of Ganas, affectionate toward his devotees, spoke after first honoring the Ganas.
The god said:
"Listen, you who are devoted to the welfare of the world, why you have been summoned here;
having heard it, perform that task with a disciplined mind and without hesitation."
"This Nandīśvara is our son, the Lord of all lords;
he is your beloved leader and a composed commander of the army."
Therefore, by my command, all of you who are in agreement should consecrate this great lord of yoga as the commander-in-chief and your husband.
"From this day forward, this auspicious Nandīśvara shall be your beloved, respected, and authoritative non-human commander-in-chief."
Sanatkumāra said:
When this had been spoken by the Blessed One, all those leaders of the Gaṇas,
having deliberated and agreed, saying "So be it," then brought together the necessary materials.
Then they brought for him a divine, beautiful seat made of Jāmbūnada gold, resembling Mount Meru in splendor and enchanting to the mind.
It was also made of gold, possessing the luster of beautiful refined gold,
hung with strings of pearls, and illuminated by precious gems.
Having constructed a pavilion facing all directions, adorned with pillars made of lapis lazuli, covered with networks of tinkling bells, and endowed with beautiful jewels,
they then fashioned an auspicious and excellent seat in its center.

In front of him, they prepared a blue footstool illuminated by diamonds for the purpose of placing his feet, and two jars filled with the finest water and their mouths covered with lotuses were placed at his sides.
Having established the fire in front, and having placed a bull at his side,
he should then place Surabhi with her calf on his right side.
And there was an auspicious parasol with a hundred ribs, made of Jāmbūnada gold,
its back resplendent with a conch-shell necklace as white as water.
A beautiful fan, white as the moon and with a golden handle;
and a garland of lotuses frequented by swarms of bees.
There, the leaders of the hosts brought golden *nandyāvarta* designs,
as well as two fish from the abode of Varuṇa, representing the lunar mansions Punarvasu and Puṣya.
The svastika, the vardhamāna, and the golden śrīvatsa;
likewise, the kīcaka bamboos and the highly honored maiden.
These two elephants, Airāvata and Supratīka, are honored;
as are the divine banner and the conch shell, which possesses the luster of the moon.
And there were a thousand golden jars of great luster,
as well as a thousand silver ones and likewise earthen ones.
Then he gave a thousand divine copper vessels with the brilliance of fire,
as well as a pair of garments made from tree-bark, which were stainless and exceedingly fine.
A golden crown, well-crafted by Viśvakarman,
as well as two stainless, divine earrings, and the thunderbolt, that supreme weapon.
The great divine sword Paṭṭiśa, the trident, and the thunderbolt,
as well as a thread made of Jāmbūnada gold and a pair of armlets.
And [the regions of] Hāra with its limbs variegated by jewels, as well as Rocanārucaka, Nalabhā, Pāriyātra, and Kaṅkaṇi.
The leaders of the Gaṇas, esteemed by the gods, remained unperturbed as they brought from all sides divine Darbha grass, sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and incense.
Then the quarters, the oceans, Varuṇa together with the Lord of Wealth, Yama, Agni, and the Vasus, as well as the Moon and Sun along with the planets; SkP_24.28 //
All the stars in the form of constellations, as well as Dhruva,
the Rudras, the Rākṣasas, the Yakṣas, the two Aśvins, and the Daityas and Dānavas.
The Gandharvas and Apsarases, as well as Nārada and Parvata;
the Earth and the oceans, the rain-clouds and the mountains likewise.
The trees, the creepers, and the mighty medicinal herbs,
as well as all the rivers and all the animals from every quarter, assembled there.
The mothers of the world, the earth, heaven itself, the elements, primordial nature, and all the sense organs; SkP_24.32 //
All sacred fords, various kinds of gifts, the Ṛg-veda verses, the Yajur-veda formulas, the Sāman chants, and also the Atharva-Aṅgiras hymns; 24.33.
Sacrifices, ritual ceremonies, offerings, and religious observances; all the Vedic meters as well as the Piśācas and the divine origins;
Brahmā, the sages, and Viṣṇu together with his attendants.
When they had all arrived, the Blessed One, whose banner bears the bull,
commanded the Grandfather (Brahmā) to perform the ritual for all the necessary tasks.
Having prepared each individual jar there, provided with all medicinal herbs, filled with water, and covered with a lotus upon its mouth; SkP_24.36.
Jayā and Vijayā, as well as Siṃhī and Vyāghrī,
Suvarcalā, Śaṅkhapuṣpī, Viṣṇukrāntā, and Punarnavā.
Kumārī, Candrakāntā, and Mṛtasañjīvanī as well,
Ādityavarcas, Amṛtā, and Śrīniketanā.
Likewise, O Vyāsa, they then cast the kumudvatī plant and all the medicinal herbs into those earthen vessels; at that time, all the lords of the Gaṇas were present.
The Blessed One established all the various sacred fords (*tīrthas*) and all the acts of giving (*dāna*) within all those golden [images].
And within the shining jars, he placed the mantras and the Vedic meters,
as well as various other sacrifices, both optional rites for specific desires and those of other kinds.
In all the Audumbara regions, the Blessed One likewise deposited the rivers, the oceans, as well as ascetic penances and religious observances.
Having filled each jar there and consecrated them with mantras,
and having bound them with thread, the Lord presented them to the gods.
Then Brahmā, the Grandfather, took one jar for himself,
gave one to Viṣṇu, and one to the wise Indra;
likewise, he gave others to the Gaṇapas and to the sages.
Then, having seated him upon that throne and having honored him, the high-minded Brahmā himself consecrated him.
Then Viṣṇu, then Śakra, the ṛṣis together with the immortals,
and all the lords of the Gaṇas consecrated Nandin.

He himself gave him a pair of divine garments and likewise divine perfumes; he also gave him armlets, earrings, a crown, and a necklace, as well as a sharp-edged spear, a trident, a thunderbolt, and a lightning bolt.
The Lord of the Gods took up the parasol, and Vāyu the fan;
and the sages, led by the Grandfather, offered hymns of praise.
Viṣṇu said: Salutations to the King of Kuṣmāṇḍas, who holds a raised thunderbolt in his hand,
the grandson of Śālaṅkāyana, and who has arisen from the path of the plow.
Salutations to the son of Śilāda, to the one who performs the recitation of the Rudra-hymns,
to the devotee of Rudra, to Deva, who reclines within the waters.
Salutations to the Lord of the hosts and the Lord of all beings;
salutations to the divine son of Umā, who bears the *paṭṭiśa* weapon.
Homage to the one with terrifying fangs and the eye on his forehead;
to the one who torments, the most excellent, and the one dedicated to Īśāna.
Salutations to the guardian of the gate, the hero, the lord of great fame;
salutations to him who wears a preeminent garland and whose abode is the Ocean of Milk.
To the great lord of the host, the great master of yoga,
to Diṇḍimuṇḍa, to Caṇḍa, and to the one who delights in the single syllable.
To the one who is imperishable, the immortal, the ageless, and the deathless;
to the Lord of Creatures, and likewise to the conqueror of Death.
Homage to the one with the speed of the wind, to the omniscient, and to the unconquered;
to the one with many heads and indeed to the one with many feet.
O god who wears a crown and earrings, whose arms are like great iron clubs, protect all the hosts of gods; O god, homage be to you!
Sanatkumāra said:
Having thus praised him, O Vyāsa, the god then, becoming composed and with palms joined in reverence, uttered the cry of "Victory! to that high-souled one.
Then the hosts said, "Victory! Then the gods, then the asuras, then all beings, and likewise Brahmā and Śakra.
Then [he sounded] conchs and kettledrums, as well as paṭahas and āḍambaras, flutes and cymbals, and also kṛkavāks and cow-horns.
The leaders of the Gaṇas, filled with joy and delight, played ḍiṇḍimas, veṇukas, and mardalas on all sides.
Sanatkumāra said:
That mortal who constantly recites this hymn composed by the gods for Nandīśvara shall go to my world.
Having uttered "Homage to Nandīśvara," whoever performs the ritual of sleep shall have no fear whatsoever from the Kuṣmāṇḍa kings.
O Vyāsa, wherever this supremely honored hymn is constantly established,
there is never any fear from the planets.
Those mortals who constantly bow down to Nandīśvara, their senses ever serene and their being pure,
become beloved and most excellent attendants of the God of gods together with the Daughter of the Mountain.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa. Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having honored the gods who had arrived there, Bhava, the lord of the deities and master of the existent and non-existent, spoke to the Maruts regarding the maiden.
The Lord, together with Śakra and the Grandfather, addressed by name those Maruts who possess great speed, great being, and great splendor.
"O you of great strength, you ought to give me that daughter of yours, Suyaśas— fortunate and of divine form— as my daughter-in-law, she who possesses beautiful eyebrows."
The Maruts said:
"O Lord of the three worlds, you are the sovereign power over us, over her, and indeed over the entire universe; therefore, it does not behove you to make a request."
"You alone must give and you alone must receive; you are our unsurpassed refuge.
Do not distress us with requests for the dwellings of others."
Our father is the illustrious Kaśyapa, and Marīci is our grandfather;
Brahmā is the grandfather of our grandfather, and you are his grandfather as well.
As such, you are our great-grandfather; it does not behove you to turn away from us.
Thus addressed by the Maruts, the best of gods,
the Lord of the Gods immediately brought Suyaśas, the daughter of the Maruts.
He himself was the Hotṛ priest there, while the Grandfather of the worlds was the Brahman; Kaśyapa was the Udgātṛ, and Atri himself sang the Sāman;
furthermore, the two gods Atharvan and Aṅgiras performed the office of the Brahman.
Nārada and Parvata, the singer Citrasena, Viśvāvasu and Ruci, as well as Hāhā and Hūhū.
Likewise, Śāliśiras, the renowned Gaṇḍamaṇḍaka, Īti, Indravāha, Yajñavāha, and Dakṣiṇa—
these and other Gandharvas sang with sweet throats.
Urvaśī, Rambhā, Ghṛtācī, Pūrvacitti,
Tilottamā, Viśvācī, and other auspicious Apsarases danced there, O fortunate one,
performing a dance most enchanting to the gods.
Sanatkumāra said: O Vyāsa, such was the incomparable and irreproachable wedding of that wise one, Nandin, the chief of the Gaṇas.
Then, having performed the marriage, the high-minded Nandin went and prostrated at the feet of the God, the Goddess, and Brahmā;
and that lord of the world, endowed with supreme splendor, also paid homage to Śilāda.
The God said:
"Choose a boon, my son; and this dear daughter-in-law of yours as well.
O child, I grant you both a boon together with her, whatever you desire."
Nandin said:
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased, let my devotion toward you be firm;
and may you, together with Ambā and the lords of the Gaṇas, always remain gracious toward me."
O Lord, O Granter of Desires, you ought to unite this father of mine, my progenitor, with a favor endowed with grace. (SkP 25.16)
The God said:
"O wise one, O Nandīśa, lord of the hosts, I am always well-pleased with you along with Pārvatī; listen now to these words of mine."
He is beloved, most excellent, and endowed with supreme sovereignty;
he is a great yogi, a mighty archer, and possessed of great strength and prowess.
May you always be unconquerable and a conqueror, worthy of worship and a worshipper;
wherever I am, there you shall be, and wherever you are, there I shall also be.
And this father of yours, O Brahmin, endowed with supreme sovereignty,
shall become a leader of my Gaṇas, Mahāgaṇapati.
And I shall give him Mount Vaibhrāja, which moves at will, is made entirely of gold, filled with divine palaces, and crowded with people;
by means of it, he shall travel through all the worlds as he desires.
And his place of residence shall be on Śrīparvata, where he will be highly honored.
Furthermore, that righteous person who gives up their life at that Bhṛgu-gorge shall become a leader of the Gaṇas in Vaibhrāja, moving according to his own will.
Sanatkumāra said: Then the highly fortunate goddess granted a boon to the son of Śilāda;
he said, "May my devotion toward you always remain unfailing."
Then the daughter of the Maruts, urged by both of them, replied to them as follows: "Choose a boon indeed according to your desire."

"O Lords of the Gods, givers of thousands of boons, I desire this boon from you both: may my devotion be toward you as well as toward my husband; and may my supreme mind be ever-constant in righteousness."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O lady of pure smiles, those two gods, being delighted, spoke thus to that daughter-in-law of excellent complexion: "It shall be so for you."
Then all the hosts of great beings, having approached him with the desire to please the gods, granted him a boon; he, Kāñcanaprabha, chose it.
My devotion to you and my sovereignty are highly esteemed;
you are all under my control, and I am dear to you as you are to me.
The Gaṇas said:
"You are the thinker and the one who authorizes thought; you are the goal and the means of arrival. You are the lord of us all, and the sovereign even of the gods."
You are the most excellent among the Kuṣmāṇḍas, you are the one of great strength among the Rudras,
and likewise the gatekeeper of the calamities as well as of the Pramathas.
You are indeed considered by us to be the one of great strength, the great yogin, and our commander;
you are the being, the leader of beings, the guide, and the supreme conductor.
You are the lord of the planets and likewise the wielder of the fierce rod;
you are the foremost warrior, the slayer of enemies, you are the hero, and you are the lord of heaven.
You are indeed possessed of great majesty, you are the abode of the Milky Ocean,
the dwelling place of Japyeśvara, and you are manifested by Japyeśvara.
O nourisher of all beings, giver of boons, worshipped by the givers of boons;
O Lord of Beings, O Master, be a giver of boons to us as well.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus praised by all the lords of the Gaṇas, the omnipresent Lord Nandīśvara spoke to them as they bowed down: "Tell me, what shall I do for you?"
Thus addressed, all those leaders of the Gaṇas, who were possessed of great strength and knew the divine nature [of the Lord], spoke to him in the presence of the God of gods.
"You have been appointed by Lord Śambhu as the leader of our host;
you have been consecrated by us as our guide and bestower of the Dharma."
Therefore, being auspicious and gentle, endowed with virtues even amidst those devoid of virtue,
and possessed of patience, purity, and self-restraint, always do what is pleasing to us.
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus, he then bowed to all with great reverence;
placing his joined palms upon his head, he then praised the leaders of the Gaṇas.
Nandin said:
"Salutations to you all, O beings; salutations likewise to the yogis;
salutations also to those without abodes, and salutations to the lords of yogis."
Homage to those who move at will, and homage indeed to the fierce ones;
homage again and again to the Deaths, to the Yamās, and to the Times.
Homage to those with golden garlands and to all who possess dharmas;
homage to you who are both slayers and likewise those who are not to be slain.
Homage to the supreme yogins and homage again and again to those with matted hair;
homage to you who possess invisible forms and likewise to those who are deformed.
Homage to those who dwell in bark garments and to those who dwell in animal skins;
homage to those with white robes and garlands, and to those with variegated garlands—homage, homage!
Homage, homage to those who are running, to those who are rushing, and to those who have set out;
homage, homage to the sages who are singing and to those who are reciting prayers.
Homage to those in the form of śarabhas and to those in the form of śatarūpas; homage to those dwelling in the mountains and to those in the form of tigers.
Homage to those in the form of cats, and likewise to crows and cranes;
homage to those in the form of deities, and similarly to the winds.
Homage to the fires and likewise to the waters, and likewise to those who are Varuṇas;
homage to those who have the form of the Lord of Wealth, and indeed to those who possess every form.
Homage to those with bellies for faces and to those with faces on every side;
homage to those of dwarf form and to those of beautiful forms.
Salutations again and again to those who nourish the gods, asuras, and humans;
salutations to you all beings, and salutations to you from every side, O auspicious ones!
Salutations be to you, O planets; likewise, salutations to the liberations.
Salutations be to you, the auspicious ones, and likewise to those that are inauspicious.
May these leaders of the hosts be gentle and auspicious toward me.
Thus praised with auspicious words, may these Gaṇapas of great strength, the destroyers of the enemies of the gods,
grant me incomparable happiness, and may they, the bestowers of bliss, grant me strength, valor, and steadfastness in battle.
May the lords of the gods grant me inexhaustible ascetic power, an incomparable state, as well as fame, the foremost rank, abundance, constancy in dharma,
everything desired by my mind, and likewise unsurpassed prosperity.
Sanatkumāra said:
He who constantly studies these two hymns to the lords of the hosts of Nandins is liberated from all sins, just as one is purified by the final ablution of a horse sacrifice.
By reciting during the latter twilight, one abandons the sin committed during the day;
likewise, by reciting during the former twilight, one abandons all that was committed during the night.
Sanatkumāra said: Then all those leaders of the Gaṇas, having been praised by that wise one,
were dismissed and departed after bowing down to the bull-bannered Lord.

Then the gods and all the worlds departed; thereafter the high-minded Lord himself, having created the abode of Nandīśvara and bestowed it upon him, went together with the Goddess to his own imperishable station, which is desired by all.

That Brāhmaṇa who recites or causes others to hear this account of Nandin’s birth, as well as his granting of boons, his consecration, and his marriage, goes upon death to the same world as Nandīśvara.
But whoever, with a restrained mind and full of devotion to Bhava, should recite this entire [text] with humility,
he too, having departed for the next world, shall become like Nandi and indeed my own attendant.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
"O Vyāsa, in this manner Nandīśvara was born as an attendant."
He was consecrated to the office of general of the God of gods.
Vyāsa said: Then, seated there with the Goddess, what did the Blessed One Mahādeva, the granter of desires, do? This I wish to know.
Sanatkumāra said: On a peak of the Himavat, the Blessed Lord Śarva, desiring to please the Goddess,
repeatedly produced laughter through his attendants of various forms.
And the one whose forehead-mark is the young crescent moon delighted and sported with the goddess,
accompanied by those auspicious ones who were high-souled, omniscient, and capable of assuming any form at will.
Then a certain goddess approached her mother, the Supreme Goddess,
who was seated upon a splendid, golden, and most highly honored throne.
Then, seeing the goddess Satī arrived in her beautiful form,
he offered the blameless lady a highly precious seat.
And as she sat there, Menā, the beloved of Himavat, said to her:
"O daughter of auspicious gaze, it has been a long time since your arrival today;
for you have come together with your husband, playing with the toys of the poor."
Those who were once poor and likewise without refuge—
both of them now sport in this manner, O auspicious lady, just like your husband.
Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus by her mother, she was not at all joyful in mind;
filled with great indignation, she said nothing to her at all.
Then, having been dismissed by her mother, she went and spoke to the God:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, I shall not dwell here on this mountain;
O Lord of the World, O You of Great Splendor, choose another abode for me."
The God said:
"O Goddess, although you were constantly being urged by me for the sake of a dwelling, O Sovereign Lady, you never once took pleasure in residing elsewhere."
"Now, O auspicious goddess, why do you yourself seek to dwell elsewhere? Tell me that, O lady of pure smiles."
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, today I went to the house of my high-souled father;
and there, in a secluded place, I saw my mother, the creator of the worlds."
Having honored her with a seat and other offerings, she spoke to me thus:
"O Umā, O auspicious one, your husband always plays with the toys of the poor;
for the play of the gods is not of such a kind."
O Mahādeva, O bull-bannered one, that you take delight with various auspicious Gaṇeśas is indeed disagreeable to me and my mother.
Sanatkumāra said: Then the Lord, the master, laughing, spoke to the Goddess in order to make her laugh: "It is exactly so; there is no doubt. Why has anger arisen in you?"
Clad in a hide or indeed naked, dwelling in cremation grounds, homeless in the forests and in mountain caves,
I wander surrounded by naked hosts, O lotus-eyed one.
"Do not be angry, O Goddess; your mother spoke the truth to you.
For there is no kinsman equal to a mother for living beings, O beautiful one."
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of the foremost of gods, I have no need for my kinsmen.
O Mahādeva, act in such a way that we may dwell elsewhere."
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by the Goddess, the Lord of Gods, the sovereign master,
spoke to the leader of the Gaṇas standing at his side, the one renowned by the name Nikumbha.
O Nikumbha, lord of the Gaṇas, go to the auspicious Vārāṇasī and,
O mighty-armed one, make it empty by means of stratagem alone, not by force.
There dwells the powerful King Divodāsa,
who is righteous, devoted to me, a great yogi, and possessed of great strength.
Therefore, you should act in such a way that you do not offend him;
by his very offense alone, make Vārāṇasī empty.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed in this way, the radiant Nikumbha, the best of the Gaṇas,
bowed down with joined palms and a joyful countenance, and spoke to the God.
"I shall do so, O Lord of Gods, that indeed that king shall become a lord of sinners, you shall be satisfied,
and Vārāṇasī itself shall become empty; of this there is no doubt."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus and bowing his head to Hara,
that lord Nikumbha departed for the holy city of Vārāṇasī, renowned throughout the worlds.
There, that Gaṇa granted an audience in a dream to Maṇḍūkākṣa the barber and then revealed his own form to him.
Nikumbha said: "Maṇḍūkākṣa, I am Nikumbha, the leader of the Gaṇas and the destroyer of grief;
I have come here to bestow grace upon you, so do what I tell you."
"Establish my abode at the gateway of Divodāsa’s house,
and install there an auspicious image that resembles my own form."
"I shall grant you wealth, as well as sons and good fortune; moreover, I shall grant you popularity everywhere and, finally, the supreme state."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus by Nikumbha, the barber then went to King Divodāsa—
who was like Indra or Vaivasvata— and spoke to him.
The barber said: "O Master, I shall fashion a Gaṇapālaya at the door of your house;
I shall also install Gaṇeśa there, so you should grant me permission for this."
Saying "So be it," he was granted permission and then constructed a temple there; he installed the image exactly as he had seen it.
The Great Being performed a magnificent and beautiful worship of Gaṇeśa, and he accepted it.
By that ritual act, the Lord bestowed upon him whatever wealth he desired,
as well as cattle, sons, and good fortune.
Having observed that incomparable prosperity of the barber,
the people, desiring to propitiate him, indeed offered him worship.
Some undertook journeys, while others observed fasts;
likewise, others performed fire-offerings and recitations, and still others performed worship for the sake of obtaining boons.
Similarly, some offered oblations, and others engaged in song and dance.
To them who had thus approached him, the highly illustrious Nikumbha granted all the desires that each of them wished for.
O Vyāsa, having thus recognized him as the granter of desires, King Divodāsa then spoke to his queen at one time out of a longing for a son.
"O Goddess, he grants all desires to people;
you too should propitiate this Lord of the Gaṇas for the sake of offspring."
Thus addressed, that beautiful woman then went and, having reached Gaṇeśa, said: "O Blessed Lord, O God, O Sovereign, I am childless."
"I shall observe a fast for the propitiation of you, O God;
I will not eat until a boon has been granted to me by you, O Lord."
"O Lord of Herds, once a son is born, I shall give one thousand cows to the twice-born on your account."
Likewise, with a thousand jars of curd, of clarified butter,
of milk, and of the five products of the cow, I shall perform your ritual bath.
"When your son is born, I shall undoubtedly feed a hundred thousand well-honored brahmins before you. (SkP 26.45)
The king will grant many villages and likewise female slaves;
O Lord, he will always perform sacrificial sessions and worship for you.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus to him, O Vyāsa, she remained established in her observance;
fasting at that time, she performed a great worship for him.
To her as she remained thus, that god, the lord of the Gaṇas, said:
"Arise; you shall have no son; do not indulge in vain grief."
Thus, being addressed repeatedly by that high-souled Gaṇeśa Nikumbha, she desisted from her observance.
Then the queen, dejected in mind, spoke to the lord of men:
"Noble son, that leader of the Gaṇas does not grant me a son;
he says, 'You have no son,' so do not practice vows in vain."
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by the queen herself,
O King, that lord of men remained constantly restrained in his observances before Gaṇeśa.
Nikumbha spoke to that king who was established in his vow:
"O King, do not remain here in vain; I will not give you a son."
Thus addressed by Nikumbha, that mighty lord of kings,
his eyes red with rage, rose up and spoke to the lord of the Gaṇas.
The king said:
"Whether you are a Gaṇa, a Piśāca, a Bhūta, or even a Rākṣasa, you are undoubtedly ungrateful; you do not deserve worship here."
"He has been honored by the citizens at the very door of my own house;
he resides within my domain, yet you do not grant him a son."
Therefore, you are not worthy of worship; instead, you deserve punishment from me, for you are cruel, arrogant, harsh, and filled with envy.
Then he caused his dwelling to be broken open by the leaders of elephant herds;
he quickly shattered the sacrificial altar and set ablaze the radiant image.
The lord Nikumbha, having achieved his purpose, remained stationed in the sky and spoke to Divodāsa as if burning him with his splendor.
The gods grant whatever desired boon one wishes;
if that [boon] was not granted, what cause for anger did you have in that matter?
"Since you have destroyed the abode of me, who have done you no harm,
therefore your city shall remain empty for a thousand years."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus to the king, the self-possessed Nikumbha informed the Lord of the Gods and stood by the side of his master.
And the king, having indeed encountered supreme shame because of his words which were both true and meaningful, then returned home.
Then, by that curse, the city of Vārāṇasī quickly became empty, purified, and frequented by deer.
Having realized that it was empty, the wielder of the Pināka bow, possessed of great splendor, arrived there together with the Goddess, his attendants, and Nandin.
There, the god mentally fashioned a divine celestial chariot, radiant as the sun, possessing incomparable qualities.
My wisdom does not suffice to describe that [reality] in its entirety;
only this much can be said, for it possesses qualities beyond comparison.
The Lord created a glorious garden that was far superior to those delightful celestial gardens, such as Nandana and others.

In that celestial chariot, endowed with every supernatural power and beyond the reach of words, the goddess— the daughter of the King of Mountains— delighted with eyes like blooming blue lotuses, and she no longer remembered her mother’s words.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now, while the daughter of the mountain and the bull-bannered Lord were seated comfortably there, [the following occurred].
Upon a divine golden seat, adorned with various jewels.
Then the goddess, the daughter of Acala, seated comfortably during the night,
the daughter of the Lord of Mountains, spoke to her husband, the Lord of all the worlds.
O Blessed One, destroyer of the enemies of the gods, adorned with a portion of the moon,
O All-pervading Lord, bestower of honor, tell me that which I ask of you.
O Lord of Gods, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, what fruit do those obtain who, out of devotion, perform any act for you with a specific result in mind? SkP_27.4 //
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by Umā, the trident-bearing god whose banner is the bull, the God of gods, remained unperturbed and spoke of everything, both auspicious and inauspicious.
Vyāsa said:
What did that blessed Lord, the god of great asceticism and the imperishable one, say when he was asked out of affection by the Goddess at that time?
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, O Brahmin, I too previously questioned the lord Nandīśvara regarding this; I shall relate to you exactly what he told me.
I, composed and undistracted, questioned the highly fortunate Gaṇeśāna, who possesses a splendor equal to ten thousand suns— the immensely radiant Nandīśvara.
O best of the Gaṇas, tell me exactly as it happened that which was previously told by Īśa to the Goddess; for my curiosity is indeed great.
Nandīśvara said:
Listen, O great sage, as I shall tell you that which was spoken of old by the God of gods for the benefit of Pārvatī, in response to your question.
The God said:
"Listen, O lady of excellent vows; I shall tell you that which you ask of me.
For the benefit of my devotees, O Goddess, I shall answer what you have asked."
O Goddess, O blameless one, for whoever shall build a bright palace for me,
I grant him an imperishable Arjuna house in the city of Śiva.
Whoever installs my *liṅga* according to the prescribed injunctions as described shall always move about together with me, endowed with the eight supernatural powers (*aṣṭaguṇa*).
To whoever gives me even a single *tuṭi* of gold, or even much more,
I shall grant an excellent dwelling upon the peak of the Himavat.
"To whoever would give me cows or gold with a joyful heart for my pleasure,
I shall grant him worlds endowed with all desires."
Whoever should present a bull, whether white or even blue,
shall deliver twenty-one generations of his lineage on both sides.
Or even he who would give me land the size of two cow-hides,
having reached my city, rejoices together with the lords of the Gaṇas.
Whoever should give me the fruit of their merit previously acquired by themselves,
that person obtains infinite fruit and rejoices in the third heaven.
He who performs a procession for me on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in a chariot yoked with bulls rejoices in my world.
To him who honors me with marks of greatness, ritual services, and recitations,
I grant a highly honored residence in the world of Brahmā.
"O slender-waisted one, he who thinks in his mind, 'I shall worship Hara,' yet is unable to do so because he lacks the necessary materials, [is not at fault]. (SkP 27.21)
Purified by that faith and liberated from all sins, he attains my world upon the dissolution of the body; of this there is no doubt.
He who, having bathed at the morning twilight, always approaches me,
becomes a powerful Yakṣa, a friend of the King of Yakṣas.
Sweeping is worth five hundred [gold pieces], smearing with cow-dung is worth a thousand;
perfumes are worth ten thousand, and worship is said to be infinite.
The anointing should be performed one hundred and eight times, the bathing three hundred times;
likewise, the perfumed water and the five products of the cow should each be used five hundred times.
O Goddess, milk should be five times that amount, and Kapila [cow's milk] even more than that;
likewise, a bath with clarified butter should be five times that amount.
"O Goddess, I forgive his many offenses here;
this secret sprinkling with ashes is my desired end, leading to infinity."
Ten thousand units of agaru, six thousand of sandalwood,
and fourteen thousand of kālāgaru are prescribed as incense.
Unbroken grains of rice and barley, two hundred measures of śāli rice,
and guggulu resin, well-incensed with clarified butter, are prescribed for the sake of infinity.
O Goddess, he who would burn two thousand palas of mahiṣākṣa for a full year shall become equal to Nandin unto me.
He who, for one year, offers milk-rice with ghee to the auspicious image on the south side shall become equal to Nandin.
There were ten thousand carus, and the yāvaka was four times that amount;
all the remaining carus were equal to half of the yāvaka.
One who gives an incalculable vessel of clarified butter attains eternal bliss both in this world and after death; he gratifies all the ancestors and rejoices in a celestial chariot.
Furthermore, he who gives an umbrella likewise shines with splendor in heaven.
On both the thirteenth and the eighth days of the lunar fortnight,
one who observes a fast and approaches me with devotion,
offering a gift, O blameless goddess— being pleased, I shall grant him my own eternal world.
If he has always worshipped me with devotion using red and yellow garments as well as various kinds of flowers, I regard him as my own son.
And to that mortal who stands offering a lamp for a single night,
I grant the fruit of all sacrifices as well as prosperity itself.
All the worlds, including both the ignorant and the learned, are deluded by me alone;
blinded by passion and overwhelmed by dense darkness, they do not perceive me.
Those who are meditative, ever-disciplined, devoted to the true Dharma,
one-pointed in mind, and self-controlled— they behold me at all times.
Those who are my devotees, who are always proficient in Sāṃkhya and Yoga,
see everything in me and me everywhere through the power of yoga.
Having transcended the three worlds as well as the world of Brahmā,
they go to my own world, having pierced through the darkness that is so difficult to pierce.
I cannot be seen even by hosts of sages endowed with ascetic power;
O Goddess, only the wise who are meditative and ever-disciplined behold me.
O fair-hipped one, whatever sacred fords and shrines of the deities exist in the worlds, they are always present at my feet.
With his mind constantly offered unto me and likewise permeated by my nature,
he is liberated from all sins through my very power alone.
O Goddess, whatever way a man may live, if he should always remember me,
that doer shall never be joined with impurity.
Even if he is a wicked soul in every respect, whoever constantly worships me with a mind fixed on knowledge shall become equal to my own self.
And whoever always worships me through the sixfold yoga shall quickly enter into me; there is no doubt about this.

O Goddess, even one who delights in the company of the wicked, who is born of an improper womb, and who is always possessed of sinful deeds— even he goes to an inconceivable state if his mind is fixed on me and he is dedicated to me.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, the auspicious goddess again [addressed] her husband, the lord of vows.
Honored by hundreds of fruits, she asked about the fruit connected with the vow.
O Maheśvara, O Lord of the Three Worlds, tell me what the fruit of vows is—whether it be small or great—and what kind of vow it must be. SkP_28.2.
The god said:
"O auspicious and blameless one, listen to what kind of vow has been prescribed, whether it yields great fruit or even small fruit."
On the fourteenth and likewise on the eighth day of both fortnights, being pure for a year, tranquil, self-controlled, and having conquered his senses, he should fast.
Whatever fruit belongs to those who perform the sacrificial session (sattra) and to those who speak the truth and approach their wives during the proper seasons—
that very fruit he obtains, and he does not see Yama.
He who has taken refuge in me, yet remains on his bed or seat amidst women, attached to pleasure and delighting in comfort— he burns constantly from the tips of his nails to the very end.
My devotee, endowed with austerity, attains me alone;
his worlds are imperishable, O Goddess, even if he should be a perpetrator of great evil.
O Goddess, that man who always eats from an earthen vessel on the sacred festival days (parvan) obtains the fruit of a three-night fast by means of a single day and night.
He who, indeed, for a full year eats [only what is] always offered to the ancestors and the gods, remaining ever untiring, shall become the sole sovereign of the earth.
O Goddess, that self-controlled man who does not eat on the ninth, the eighth, the full moon, and the thirteenth day throughout the year [attains great merit].
O blameless one, he attains lordship over the Gaṇas without rival;
he becomes beloved by all beings and assumes a divine form.
One should offer a śrīvatsa mark made with flour and a beautiful golden fruit;
one should scatter black sesame seeds there, as well as rice and unbroken grains (akṣata),
along with various kinds of fruits of diverse shapes, as they are available, and endowed with flavor.
Indeed, for sixty-two thousand years, he rejoices in heaven,
assuming a divine form, endowed with splendor, and constantly accompanied by the deities.
Whoever would give me their own image made of gold, well-prepared with all kinds of perfumes, essences, and exudations; ||| SkP_28.14 ||
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should offer various kinds of foods and edibles here in the southeast,
as well as in the northwest.
On the sides, one should indeed offer yellow orpiment, black agallochum, realgar,
and sandalwood, each worshipped in its respective order.
O Goddess Mattakāśinī, hear from me the fruit of his merit:
he shall be liberated from all diseases and likewise become free from all blemish.
Having enjoyed great happiness in heaven for eight hundred million years,
he is born happy in this world and attains me alone.
Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even a woman, whoever should give this Ratnāvalī shall attain supreme happiness like mine in my world.
Furthermore, if one uses white mustard seeds for the purpose of the *argha* offering, whether in rites for the gods or for the ancestors,
he shall satisfy even the ancestors for thirty thousand years.
He attains a perfect form, equal to that of the sages and all the gods;
for a Manvantara, he is honored by the daughters of the cow-herds in Goloka.
All the gods, as well as Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the sages, indeed provide their presence for the arghya offering; know that it has issued forth from them.
O Goddess, he who knows this supreme secret is a man of great austerity;
by its power, he shall become wealthy, pleasing to behold,
endowed with wisdom, beauty, and virtue, and live for ten million years.
If anyone should constantly bathe me three times a day with milk, being diligent,
I shall forgive even a thousand offenses of his.
And whoever should behold that bathing ceremony is liberated from all sins and shall obtain the fruit of a thousand recitations of the Mānasa hymn.
He who, being pure, performs the ritual bathing with milk for one year,
attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas and constant favor.
The man who, with an undistracted mind, performs an anointing of me with clarified butter shall obtain the fruit of two thousand mental recitations.
That best of men shall become worthy of being approached by the gods,
and he shall obtain the fruit of a thousand pieces of gold and refined gold.
To him who performs the sweeping while observing this vow for a year,
I grant a beautiful world that is eternally auspicious and firm;
O Goddess, even when all worlds perish, there is no destruction for him.
O Goddess, he who, firm in his vows, performs the worship of my *liṅga*,
rejoices in heaven for a hundred thousand divine years.
Śaṅkara smells the fragrance of four kinds of flowers:
the arka, the karavīra, the bilva, and the buka.
Indeed, it is said that in every flower there is a golden coin (suvarṇaniṣka).
Whatever fruit is said to be obtained by giving a thousand arka flowers,
that same fruit is indeed obtained by giving a single karavīra flower.
Whatever fruit may result from giving a thousand *karavīra* flowers,
that same fruit is said to result from giving a single *padma* flower.
Whatever fruit is obtained from giving me a thousand lotuses,
that same fruit one obtains by giving a beautiful leaf of the *bilva* tree.
Whatever fruit is traditionally said to be obtained by giving a thousand bilva leaves to me,
one may obtain that same fruit by giving a single bukā flower to me.
Whatever fruit there is from giving me a thousand *buka* flowers,
one obtains that same fruit by giving a single flower of the *dhuttūraka*.
For whatever man— whether impure, one who has broken the bounds of propriety, or one possessed by sin— shall constantly bear my floral remains upon his head.
Self-willed, likewise unrighteous, and excluded from the religious observances,
he shall fall into a terrible hell and be reborn in the womb of an animal.
O observer of the great vow, if one who has become pure through the practice of celibacy wears the remains of an offering,
I shall swiftly destroy his sin.
He who indeed creates a garland of lamps for me during the month of Kārttika,
and at the conclusion of the lamp-offering, being pure, gratifies the Brāhmaṇas—
he attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas and shines like the sun.
One should offer black sesame seeds together with white mustard seeds;
O Goddess, he who always places these upon my head shall be equal to Nandin unto me.
For those who are called white mustard seeds, as well as those black sesame seeds—all of them consist of you, O Goddess; this secret has been declared by me.
There is a host named Citra; with him he rejoices.
Even when the universal dissolution occurs and the destruction of the three worlds has arrived, having abandoned all sufferings, he attains me alone.
O Goddess, daughter of the mountain, I am not as satisfied by being worshipped through an image as I am exceedingly pleased when the Liṅga is worshipped, O Pārvatī.
Whether he is addicted to all the senses or joined with all sins,
O Goddess, he who worships my Liṅga here goes to heaven.
Having abandoned all sins, free from the pairs of opposites, and with his impurities burnt away,
he who eats my food and offers me salutations attains to me alone.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the Blessed Lady again questioned her husband, the Lord of all the worlds: "O God, by what means are you pleased? (SkP 28.47)
Then, with a smiling face, the Blessed One, the Lord of the lords of all worlds, spoke these words out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds: *SkP_28.48*
The God said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the truth of how all living beings in the three worlds who are my devotees, O fair-faced one, attain an auspicious state.
Whatever is that supreme secret, all of that resides within you;
for whoever knows it in its true essence is completely liberated from saṃsāra.
A man should not reveal this secret; rather, rising in the morning with palms joined in reverence, he should always recite your name as "the All-enduring One."
And from that recitation, one shall utterly burn away all evil;
having attained fame and renown, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Whoever should constantly offer all kinds of garlands upon all the forms,
according to the rule and with the mantra, his meritorious fruit shall be great.
O Mantra,
salutations always to the all-pervading Lord of the gods, who consists of all the deities, and to the Blessed One, the secret of secrets.
To Soma, the lord of beings, to Bhāvana and to Bhava;
to the one who is all secrets, Svāhā, and to the one whose nature is the secret of the gods!
The mantra consisting of all secrets is: "Svāhā to Soma indeed, and svāhā to Kaṭaṅkaṭa, svāhā to the powerful god."
Whoever should constantly offer flowers with this mantra,
by him a thousand recitations of the mental mantra have been performed.
Then, on the new moon day, with a concentrated mind and palms joined in reverence,
O Pārvatī, he worships according to the rule and offers, as available, black sesame seeds and mustard seeds.
And one should utter these words: "Sūrya" and "mine.
Such a man, liberated from all evil, shall go to the heavenly world.
And having worshipped me, O Goddess, whoever shall proclaim my names on the fourteenth or the eighth day of both fortnights,
he too, O Goddess, shall behold me; he does not go to a base womb.
O Vāmadeva, O Sudeva, O Hara, O Gupta;
O Lord of Umā, O Blue-throated One, O Peaceful One, O Śrīkaṇṭha, O Lord of Cows!
One should proclaim the secret names: Śarva, Bhīma, Paśupati, Śaṅkara, Ugra, Bhava, and likewise Mahādeva;
by doing so, one is liberated from all sins and is honored by the gods in heaven.
Whoever should either speak of or read even one of these,
having pierced through the path of the body, attains me alone—
thus has it been proclaimed by me with every prostration.
O my beloved, he who daily burns guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter and milk on the new moon day attains the imperishable state; by my grace, there is no doubt of this— this is my secret.
And this supreme secret, O Goddess, whoever should offer to me—
a vessel made of arka leaves filled with ghee together with honey—
having offered it according to the rules with devotion, is liberated from all sins.
And, O highly fortunate lady, whoever should proclaim these names of mine—
whether he dwells in a cremation ground, is naked, lies upon ashes, or is firm in his vows— [he shall attain success].
Vāmadeva, the profoundly peaceful, he whose phallus is motionless, the three-eyed one,
who delights in the left, the right-hand one, the multiformed, and the end-maker of the end-maker.
He is the ancient one, invoked by many, the death of death, and the conqueror of the senses;
he is without senses, yet beyond the senses, abiding in the hearts of all beings.
He is the wheel of saṃsāra, the one whose self is yoga, the Kāpālī, and indeed Diṇḍira;
he is Mahādeva, Mahādeva, and truly Mahādeva.
One who possesses self-restraint should either recite this or listen to it constantly;
upon the dissolution of the body, he shall become a leader of the Gaṇas, with his soul perfected through yoga.
Sanatkumāra said: A devoted person should never recite this meritorious [text] to one who is inauspicious, nor to a sinner, nor to a liar, nor ever to one who observes no vows.
It is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life, bringing about peace and prosperity,
beautiful, pure, supremely sanctifying, and the most auspicious of all auspicious things;
it should not be heard by everyone, nor should it be given to anyone at all.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus reached his dwelling in Vārāṇasī in the course of time, [he remained there].
The two gods, the parents of the world, have done this; what more could be done beyond this?
Sanatkumāra said: Then that Blessed Lord spoke to the Goddess, the daughter of Himavat:
"O Goddess, let us go see the garden, if it pleases you."
The Goddess said:
"So be it, O Lord of Gods, just as you have spoken, O Bull-bannered One;
for I must not go anywhere beyond the garden, O Hara."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, O Vyāsa, the Bull-bannered Lord, together with the Goddess, wandered everywhere in Vārāṇasī out of a desire to see the divine gardens.
In that eastern quarter, the God who wields the Pināka bow showed the Goddess a garden adorned with various kinds of flowers.
It was crowded with *campaka*, *aśoka*, *puṃnāga*, *priyaṅgu*,
and mango trees, as well as with *bilva*, *arjuna*, *kadamba*, *nyagrodha*, and *udumbara* trees.
And with fragrant flowers— jāti, kesara, and ketakī—
as well as delightful, sweet-smelling blossoms frequented by swarms of bees,
the entire forest was magnificent, resembling the Vaibhrāja grove.
Having reached that garden, the Lord of the World said to the Goddess:
"O beautiful Goddess, in former times, while I was staying in this place..."
Above, as the cows established in Goloka were drinking their milk with great speed by means of their self-manifested calves, froth fell upon his head.
Then I beheld those cows situated near Soma;
as they were gazed upon by me there, those cows then became scorched by his splendor, assuming many colors and being severely afflicted.
"O Goddess, these cows were formerly of a single color, born from the Kapila breed; they were not of many colors when they were first beheld by me."
O Daughter of the Mountain, having recognized their capacity to provide refuge, Soma came to me and, taking shelter with me alone along with the cows, did not abandon them.
Then, as the cows were thus distressed, Brahmā spoke to me:
"O Lord of Gods, honored by all the deities, show favor so that Surabhi may not perish instantly through your splendor."
Then, O Goddess, I myself established myself in this very place,
renowned as Goprekṣaka and praised by all the deities.
Having gone to Goprekṣeśvara, having seen and worshipped it,
a person does not fall into a miserable state and is liberated from sins.
Then, while I was gracious, those cows, being scorched, approached this lake and fell into it; having become cooled, they shone forth at that time.
From that moment on, it has been called the Kapilāhrada.
"In this matter as well, O Goddess, I myself, known as Vṛṣadhvaja, have established my presence; let him be seen standing here."
Having bathed at this sacred ford of the Kapilā lake with an undistracted mind,
a man who beholds this Bull-bannered Lord shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices.
Having worshipped me here, even after death one attains residence in the same world;
and upon the dissolution of the body, one obtains the state of being a Gaṇa, which is exceedingly difficult to attain.
In this very place, moreover, all those cows were themselves milked by Brahmā for the sake of the peace of all the worlds; [the milk was] nectar.
From their milk this enchanting lake was produced;
it is known as Bhadradoha, a meritorious and auspicious divine forest.
"O Goddess, I have been propitiated in this place by all the gods;
go to tranquility, O Lord!"—thereupon he became Upaśāntaśiva.
Remaining here, I am established in this place; even the sight of it is meritorious.
Having seen it with a disciplined mind, a mortal shall attain the heavenly world.
"Here I was brought and established by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord;
and having taken me from Brahmā as well, I was established once again by Viṣṇu."
Then Viṣṇu was addressed by Brahmā, whose mind was filled with agitation:
"Why have you installed this liṅga which was brought here by me?"
Viṣṇu spoke again to Brahmā, whose face was clouded with anger:
"In former times, my devotion toward the god Rudra was exceedingly great."
"By me this has been established; therefore, it shall belong to you by that name as Hiraṇyagarbha. Thus I am firmly established here. Even by seeing this Lord of Gods, a man shall go to my world."
Furthermore, O auspicious one, Brahmā then installed this *liṅga* of mine according to the prescribed rites, endowed with supreme devotion; thus,
I myself am established here as Svarlīneśvara.
Dissolved within myself, who am beyond the other, in Pradhāna, my cause;
therefore, this secret field of mine is remembered as "Svarlīna."
Having abandoned the vital breaths here, a man is not born again anywhere;
that is his infinite goal, and it is likewise remembered as the goal of yogins.
In this very region as well, a powerful and arrogant Daitya, a thorn to the gods, was slain by me after he had assumed the form of a tiger.
Therefore, he is renowned as Vyāghreśvara; I am always established here.
Having seen this Amareśvara, one does not go to a state of misery again.

O auspicious one, those two Daityas, Utpala and Vidala, who were created by Brahmā in the past and were arrogant enough to be slain by women, were killed by you here with a ball in a manner that showed them contempt;
this is the mark established there.
"Having come here at the beginning, I remained together with the lords of the Gaṇas;
therefore, this is my preeminent station, and its sight is meritorious."
Having seen this linga of mine, which is situated at Jyeṣṭhasthāna, a mortal no longer grieves; perfected, he is liberated from birth and death.
Indeed, lingas have been established on all sides by all the deities;
having seen them, a mortal who is self-restrained shall become a member of the Gaṇas upon the dissolution of the body.
"Now that I have come here and established myself in person,
and because it has not been abandoned by me, this sacred field of Vārāṇasī shall henceforth become a bestower of liberation; therefore, it is called Avimukta."
Indeed, whatever person shall behold me here as Avimukteśvara,
his destination shall be that of the Gaṇas, wherever he may die;
but by renouncing his life-breaths right here, he shall attain the highest liberation.
In former times, your father Himavat, the king of mountains,
having himself recognized that this place was dear to me, installed a linga here.
"Behold this place known as Śaileśvara, which stands here;
having seen it, O Goddess, a man shall not follow the path of misfortune."
And this river Vārāṇasī is holy, liberating one from sin;
having adorned this sacred field, it has joined with the Jāhnavī.
At this confluence, Brahmā established an excellent Liṅga;
let it be seen in the world as renowned by the name Saṃgameśvara.
For that pure person who, having bathed at the confluence of the two divine rivers,
worships Saṅgameśāna— whence can there be any fear of rebirth for him?
This is another great field, the supreme abode of yogins,
in the midst of which I myself am established,
renowned among all gods and asuras as Madhyameśvara.
This is indeed the abode of the Siddhas who observe my vows,
of the Yogins seeking liberation whose selves have conquered birth and death;
having seen this Madhyameśāna, one does not grieve over rebirth.
And this Liṅga has been installed by your son Śukra;
it is named Śukreśvara, worshipped by all the Siddhas and the immortals.
Upon seeing this, a human being would immediately be liberated from all sins;
and having died, that man would not undergo rebirth in saṃsāra.
Formerly, the Asuras, who were thorns to the gods, having assumed the form of jackals and having obtained a boon from Brahmā, became apprehensive of being killed by a vulture.
O Daughter of the Himavat, because I have slain Jambukeśa,
I have become renowned in the world and am honored by gods and asuras;
even by beholding this Lord of Gods, one shall obtain all desires.
Indeed, these have been established by the planets, with Venus at their head;
behold these meritorious lingas which grant all desires.
Thus, O Pārvatī, these meritorious abodes of mine have been described to you in this sacred field; now hear this other secret.
This field is proclaimed to extend one krośa in each of the four directions;
know, O lady of beautiful limbs, that it bestows immortality at the time of death for a distance of one yojana.
Established at the site of Mahālayagiri and at Kedāra, one attains the status of a Gaṇa by seeing [the deity] in this sacred field; liberation is attained there.
O auspicious one, because that liberation is supreme even compared to the station of the Lord of Ganas (Gaṇapati),
this field of Avimukta is remembered as the most meritorious, surpassing even Mahālaya and the middle Kedāra.
In the central place of Kedāra is the Mahālaya shrine;
among all my meritorious sites on the earth, this one is indeed the most excellent.
Since the worlds were created from this place, this field is auspicious;
because it was never abandoned by me at any time, it therefore became known as Avimukta.
Having beheld the Avimukteśvara Liṅga here,
a human being is instantly liberated from sin and released from the bonds of Paśu.
Śaileśa, Saṅgameśa, Svarlīna, Madhyameśvara, Hiraṇyagarbha, Īśāna, Goprekṣa, and he who has the bull as his banner; ||| SkP_29.58 |||
Having beheld Upaśāntaśiva, who dwells in the Jyeṣṭha-sthāna,
as well as the renowned Śukreśvara, Vyāghreśa, and Jambukeśvara,
a mortal is not born again in this ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra.
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva gazed in all directions;
and when the Great Lord, the God of gods, had finished looking and remained still, [the world was restored].
Suddenly, that entire region became as if ablaze;
filled with the sound of thundering lightning and as if ten million suns had risen at once,
it was completely suffused with splendor, like a confluence of fire and the sun.
Then there were the perfected Pāśupatas, white with the luster of smeared ashes,
great-souled masters of yoga, as well as those who observe the sacrificial vows.
And many others, hundreds in number, who bore unmanifest signs yet shone with the radiant splendor of Śiva-yoga, approached and paid homage to Maheśvara.
Having gazed again upon the Lord of Gods and having fully practiced the yoga of meditation,
they stood with their souls centered, as if merging into the Lord.
While they were thus standing there, that Lord of Uma, the God of gods,
having reflected upon his supreme form, became the Lord Puruṣa.
The twenty-sixth is the Lord, the Unmanifest, possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns;
he stands as if about to bring the entire world into a single state.
As the Lord of the World remained in that supreme form,
the Daughter of the Mountain King, her hair standing on end with joy, was unable to behold his body.
Then, having realized that she had been created by him and was established within primordial nature (prakṛti),
she assumed the form of primordial nature through yoga; as one whose essence is the Supreme Self,
she was able to behold the body of that Puruṣa, the Supreme Self.
Then, having attained dissolution within that Puruṣa, all those yogins, whose seeds of saṃsāra had been burnt away, entered his heart.
Then, having favored all those Siddhas, the most excellent among men,
he again assumed his auspicious body abiding in the form of Nīlalohita.
Seeing him, Śailajā, her every hair standing on end with joy, went before his feet and, offering praise, asked: "O Blessed One, who are these? (SkP 29.71)
Then the best of the gods spoke to that goddess, the daughter of the mountain king:
"By those most excellent twice-born ones who, having undertaken my vow, practice yoga here with devotion, [liberation] is attained in a single birth."
"By the power of this sacred field and through my sincere devotion,
I indeed bestow such grace as this, which always grants liberation."
Therefore, this great field of mine is frequented by Brahmā and the other gods,
by the foremost of Brahmins learned in the Vedas, and by perfected ascetics.
Every month on the eighth day and every month on the fourteenth day,
O Goddess, in both fortnights, at Vārāṇasī, my own abode, [one should worship].
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, and especially on the full moon day of Kārttika, on all meritorious festival days (parvan), at the equinoxes, and at the solstices; SkP_29.76.
All the sacred fords on earth are present in Vārāṇasī,
as well as the meritorious Jāhnavī, which flows northward and has issued from my crest.
O fair-faced one, listen as I describe those auspicious rivers that flow from your father, the king of mountains, Himavat, and which all people approach from every direction to worship. SkP_29.78.
Kurukṣetra with its hundreds of sacred fords,
as well as Puṣkara, Naimiśa, and Prayāga along with Pṛthūdaka, are present there.
The Sandhyā, the Saptarca, all the rivers, the lakes,
and the seven oceans— all these divine tirthas shall come here in their entirety to the Bhāgīrathī, which flows toward Kāśī, on all festival days.
O daughter of the Mountain, all the meritorious sacred sites (āyatana) that exist on earth always come to me, Avimukteśvara, who am stationed in Kāśī,
and enter me during every auspicious festival.
The liṅga that is at Kedāra, the liṅga that is at Mahālaya, the one situated at Madhyameśvara, and likewise Paśupatīśvara; ||| SkP_29.82 |||
Both Śaṅkukarṇeśvara and Gokarṇa,
as well as Drimicaṇḍeśvara and likewise Bhadreśvara.
Then there are Sthāneśvara, Athaikāmra, Kāleśvara, Ajeśvara,
Bhairaveśvara, Īśāna, and likewise the one situated at Kārohaṇa.
And whatever other meritorious sites there are of mine upon the earth,
they all enter into me without exception within the city of Kāśī.
This secret has been proclaimed for all meritorious festival days;
by means of it, even a creature who has met with disaster attains the immortal state in this world.
O auspicious lady, by merely seeing me after I have bathed in the Gaṅgā,
one immediately obtains the fruit equal to hundreds of thousands of desired sacrifices;
what indeed could be greater than this?
O Goddess, understand that there is nothing superior to this in its entirety— whether among the foremost of all abodes in heaven, on earth, or even upon the mountains.
This supreme place is always frequented by Brahmā, Arka, Vaiśvānara, Śakra, and Candra, as well as Jaleśa, Vittādhipa, and Vāyu, together with the hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Siddhas.
"O Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, this place of mine is always secret; this field is exceedingly meritorious.
Indeed, ascetics awakened to reality declare that it bestows the fruit of the perfect attainment of liberation."
Those virtuous men who dwell in this field, who always behold me with reverence day after day, being pure, bathed, and ever devoted to me—
they mortals, freed from fear, sin, and suffering, and having purified their ritual actions, pierce the dense web of worldly existence and attain supreme liberation.
Thus is this lake-filled, most secret field of mine, adorned by the Gaṅgā and crowded with various trees and creepers, a place of great merit.
Having reached the Bhāgīrathī here in Vārāṇasī, my own abode,
one obtains the merit of a hundred horse-sacrifices and goes to the world of Brahmā.
O Goddess, there is nothing more meritorious than this, nothing more secret anywhere than this,
nothing more auspicious than this, and nothing dearer to me than this.

Having reached this field of mine, frequented by gods and siddhas, a mortal through the power of his meritorious deeds shall become renowned among all the gods and asuras; and upon death, he shall go to that supreme state.
Sanatkumāra said: Then the God, having described to the daughter of Himavat his gardens and likewise his own abodes, wandered about once more.
Then he saw the brahmin Jaigīṣavya, whose wealth was his asceticism, the son of Śataśalāka, performing supreme penance.
Having installed the *liṅga* of the God of gods, he worshipped it constantly;
lying upon ashes and smeared with ashes, he delighted [the deity] with dances and songs.
Purified and refined by austerity, he [propitiated him] with silent recitation (*japa*), the sounds of the bull, and fervent devotion.
But as he was thus engaged, endowed with supreme devotion,
the Blessed One suddenly approached and spoke these words:
"O Jaigīṣavya of great intelligence, behold me with your divine eye;
I am pleased and am a granter of boons—tell me what is in your heart."
Thus addressed by the god, he beheld the three-eyed Soma;
bowing his head, he prostrated at his feet with supreme joy.

Jaigīṣavya said: Homage to the one who has accomplished all aims; indeed, homage to the one perfected in yoga. Homage to the one who holds the Pināka bow in hand, and to the one whose abode is the Himavat mountains.
Homage to him who possesses the speed of the wind, who is always to be meditated upon by those who practice meditation;
homage to Soma and to Hema, and to the wearer of the golden garland.
Homage to the Lord of the Gaṇas, and homage to him whose senses are tranquil;
to the one who provides assistance in yoga, and to the one who brings about the cessation of violence.
Homage indeed to the remover of death, and homage to the remover of sorrow; homage to the bestower of success, and homage indeed to the one perfected by success.
Homage to the sustainer of all worlds and the lord of all worlds;
homage to the one of fivefold color and the dispeller of saṃsāra.
Homage to him who has reached the further shore of saṃsāra, and who is the supreme beyond the shoreless;
homage indeed to the self-mantra and to the mind that is truly difficult to comprehend.
Homage to the knower of the divisions of time, both to the one with parts and to the partless;
homage to the one who dwells within the principles (tattvas), to the lord of the pretas.
Homage to the one free from anger, homage to the lord of anger;
homage to the ascetic who is beyond fatigue and to the remover of weariness.
Homage to the Knower of the Essence of Wisdom, to the Wise One who removes ignorance,
to him who is devoted to asceticism and intent upon sovereign power.
Homage to Jñāna, the binder who turns back ignorance;
homage to the one possessed of all-pervading power, whose mind follows after all states of being.
Homage to the one enriched with tranquility and self-restraint, the remover of the messengers of death;
homage to the Lord of Śailādi and the protector of the hosts of Śailādi.
Homage to the secret of yoga, homage again and again to the giver of yoga!
O Blessed One, O Lord, grant me all my desires with your whole being.
Sanatkumāra said: Being thus praised with supreme devotion,
he was pleased and, being further gratified, spoke this to him.
The god said: "He is indeed ageless and immortal, free from all sorrow;
he is a great yogi of great heroism, endowed with the sovereign power of yoga."
And by the power of this secret field of mine, which is eternal,
you shall attain the supreme and great eightfold sovereignty of yoga;
O best of the twice-born, you shall become a renowned master of yoga.
Whoever shall worship this *liṅga* fashioned by you according to the rule,
having passed through seven wombs, shall attain union (*yoga*).
And that twice-born man who, having reached this cave of Jaigīṣavya,
applies himself in yoga for seven nights with a disciplined mind, is liberated from all sins.
Within one month, he will know his former birth and what was studied in previous lives;
with one night, he attains pure progress, and with two nights, he delivers his ancestors.
"By means of this three-night rite, one delivers those who have passed away as well as seven future generations.
Beyond this, what more shall I give to you today, Jaigīṣavya?"
Jaigīṣavya said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, grant me that which is in my heart;
therefore, I desire nothing other than the supreme benefit that is imperishable through yoga."
May there be constant devotion toward you, as well as toward Soma, the lord of the Gaṇas;
likewise, may there be freedom from pride, forbearance, tranquility, and self-control.
Nor should you cause me subjugation, nor the disparagement of my splendor;
O God of great luster, I always desire these boons.
The God said:
"These shall be yours, as well as invincibility against yogins;
and whenever you desire it, my very appearance shall be before you."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that blessed Lord Pārāśarya, together with Umā,
Sananda, and his retinue, [appeared] out of a desire to bestow grace upon his devotees.
While the Yakṣa king was performing his austerities with Maheśvara held in his heart,
the Lord of Gods then went before him to grant a boon.
Then, he saw the son of Viśravas, who had three feet and short arms, thighs, and feet, performing severe austerities.
Having seen him, O Vyāsa, the god then spoke to Kubera, who was blazing with splendor,
purified by asceticism, and reduced to mere skin and bone.
The god said:
"O son of Viśravas, I grant you divine vision;
behold Soma, O great being, through this divine eye."
Then, having seen the Lord of Gods accompanied by Ambā and preceded by Nandin, he prostrated himself; being utterly overwhelmed, he was unable to stand up properly.
Observing him to be weak and unable to rise, the Lord said, "Arise;
may it be well with you; let your ancient strength return to you."
Then, rising up, Kubera remained on his knees,
standing while gazing at the goddess with a sidelong glance from his eye.
This is that daughter of the mountain, honored by all the worlds;
she is the mother of these three worlds, endowed with the power of great yoga.
"Oh, the power of her asceticism! Oh, her radiance! Oh, her strength!
For she has become the wife of the Lord of all the worlds."
Sanatkumāra said:
Observing him whose mind was thus disposed and looking toward Pārvatī,
the Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign, understood his state and became enraged.
Enraged, she [consumed] the brilliantly shining left eye of Kubera;
like a flame of fire, she set it ablaze until it was completely withered, as if burning dry underbrush.
Furthermore, she of auspicious countenance, whose source was asceticism, set her mind upon the destruction of Kubera; then Hara spoke to her.
"Do not be angry, O Goddess, with this ascetic Yakṣa who is your devotee;
for he is illustrious and righteous, and especially so because he is devoted to you."
"O auspicious one, O Great Goddess, it was out of curiosity that he gazed upon you; show favor to this child of the Giver of Wealth."
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Master, this one looks at me repeatedly out of immodesty;
why does he stand before me, O God, without measuring my virtues?"
He who, out of delusion, would attempt to leap over those immeasurable splendors,
being of little strength, would perish like a moth that has flown into a fire.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having thus beheld her, whose eyes were copper-red with anger, Śaṅkara spoke these sweet and gentle words to the daughter of the Mountain King.
I speak to you, O highly fortunate one; do not be angry, for you are the friction-stick of the world.
The entire world was created by you; you are primordial nature (prakṛti), O Queen of the Gods. Since this son is yours, O Goddess, you ought not to be angry.
O beautiful one, as he gazes upon his mother,
there is no fault in him, nor is his mind deluded by you.
Therefore, O Goddess, show favor to this Kubera, who is pleased and prostrate before you; grant the Lord of Gods his heart's desire.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by the God of gods, that daughter of the best of mountains showed him favor,
and being pleased, she spoke as follows.
The Goddess said: "O sinless Kubera, that evil of yours has been forgiven by me;
I am pleased with you, so do not again transgress against one who possesses such splendor."
"As for this left eye of yours which was burned by me while you were looking on,
let it likewise become tawny and radiant."
Marked by this in the world, you will undoubtedly become known by the name Ekākṣipiṅgala, honored everywhere.
This conduct of yours, as well as this austerity, shall become imperishable and eternal;
and through my grace, supreme good fortune shall also be yours.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus, the goddess of auspicious countenance then became silent;
thereupon, the Blessed One said to Kubera, "I am the giver of boons."
Then, having been addressed thus by the God, Kubera, with a joyful mind,
praised the God and the Goddess, bowing with his head and palms joined in reverence.
Kubera said:
Homage to the one with a thousand arms, who wears an excellent crown;
homage to the bearer of bracelets and to the bearer of the mirror.
Homage to the one whose every limb is hair; homage again and again to the one with long hair!
Homage to the wearer of the girdle; and homage to the bearer of the muñja-grass belt!
Homage to her who has a blue crest; homage to the wearer of tawny matted locks;
homage to the embodiment of knowledge; homage to the sovereign of all beings.
