Homage to the one who bears the name Tārā; homage indeed to the lion-chested one.
Homage to the bearer of the foremost jewel; homage to the one whose crown is adorned with the crescent moon.
Salutations indeed to Prakṛti, and salutations be to Puruṣa;
salutations indeed to Buddhi, and salutations truly to Ahaṃkāra.
Homage be to Delight and to Bliss, salutation after salutation;
homage to Fame and to Action, to the Beginning and to the Completion.
Homage to the sacrifice, to the mantra, and to the sacrificial fee; homage to the Ṛg-verse.
Homage to the Sāman, to the Yajus, to the meter, and to the ritual action.
Homage to Agni and to the sacrificial altar, homage to Svāhā and to the oblation;
homage to Lakṣmī and to Śrī, and homage to Dharma and to the Creator.
Salutation to desire and to delight; salutation to him who is dispassionate toward worldly prosperity.
Salutation to success, as well as to nourishment, contentment, and patience; salutation, salutation!
Salutations to Svadhā, to Kavya, and salutations again to Havya;
salutations to Vedyā, to Vidyā, and salutations to Śarva and Bhakti.
Salutations to Time and to Death, who exist for the sake of dissolution and creation, for maintenance and for wandering through saṃsāra, and for liberation and final release.
Salutations to you, O Blessed Lord, God together with the Goddess, Lord of the World;
O Lord of the past and the future, grant me that which resides in my heart.
Sanatkumāra said: "Whether he be a Brahmin, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even a Kṣatriya, whoever— having risen in the morning— constantly recites this hymn and mutters it," SkP_29.165.
The Lord of Wealth, being pleased with him, bestows great wealth;
and the blessed Soma, being pleased, grants his desired goal.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus praised by Kubera, the Lord of the World said, "I am the giver of boons; speak, O son of Viśravas."
Kubera said:
"May there be constant grace from you and eternal devotion toward you;
O Blessed One, may I behold you—let this be my boon, O All-pervading Lord."
Saying "So be it," the Blessed Śiva then gave all of that and bestowed upon him eternal friendship with himself.
The god said:
"Take this palanquin, yoked with men and free from attachment;
O Lord of the World, having mounted it, you shall travel through the worlds as you desire."
And take this very divine thunderbolt, characterized by its irresistible nature;
let this weapon be yours, which shall be unbearable for your enemies.
And I shall grant you a weapon;
it shall be known by your name as the Kaubera, which bewilders all embodied beings.
Sanatkumāra said: Then that god, his soul gratified, himself bound upon his head a blameless garland possessing a splendor like that of the sun.
And the Lord of Umā, being delighted, indeed fastened a beautiful garland of blossoming lotuses around his neck.
Having granted him a full vision of himself and the status of Lord of Wealth,
the Blessed Lord Soma then departed for another desired region.
Sanatkumāra said:
He who, being composed, should constantly hear or cause others to hear this entire account of Kubera’s boon-granting to Brahmins, [attains the highest goal].
Upon death, that man is born endowed with wealth, possessed of beauty, accompanied by sons and grandsons, and gifted with noble lineage, knowledge, and strength.
Then the illustrious goddess, accompanied by Śambhu,
reflected upon the five-crested, auspicious Apsarases who were performing penance.
With slender limbs, full of devotion, and with their sins burnt away by asceticism, their hearts drawn by compassion, they addressed these words to the God: SkP_29.179.
"O Lord, as these women perform their penance, you should grant them their supreme and most excellent desired boon; it behoves you to give me your permission for this.
Having heard her request, the Blessed One spoke as follows:
"Act thus, O illustrious one, to grant the desired grace to your devotees.
For these are the Vedic Apsarases known as the Pañcacūḍās;
they perform penance having placed you in their hearts. Let a boon be granted to them."
Then, thus urged by the God of gods,
Pañcacūḍā approached and spoke these words.
"I am pleased, O Apsarases; behold me directly, you of pure smiles! I shall grant you the desired boons that dwell within your hearts."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having been addressed thus by Pārvatī, those auspicious Vedic Apsarases,
beholding the Goddess, bowed their heads at her feet and remained prostrate.
With eyes filled with tears and dejected, they steadied themselves by their own effort;
placing their joined palms upon their heads, they praised him together in unison.
Homage to Siddhi, homage to Tuṣṭi; homage to Kriyā and to Buddhi;
homage to Kīrti, homage to Satī, to Ulkajā, and likewise to Iṣṭi.
Salutation to the auspicious Earth, to Śrī, to Lakṣmī; salutation again and again!
Salutation to Sudhā, to Svāhā, to Svadhā, and to Diti; salutation!
Homage be to Taḍit, and salutations again and again to Saudāmanī;
homage and salutations to Sāvitrī, to Gāyatrī, and to the Mother of the Vedas.
Salutation to the Daughter of the Mountain, to Mati, and salutation to Smṛti;
salutation to the Dwellress of the Mountain, and repeated salutations to Rudrāṇī.
Homage to Prakṛti and to Jyotsnā, homage to Ṛddhi; homage to Śobhā and Dīpti, and to the rays of the sun and the planets.
Salutation to Gatyā and Gatī, to Indrāṇī and Muktī;
salutation to Niyatī and Saritī, to Gaṅgā and Sūti.
Salutation to Heti and to Prīti; salutation to Karaṇavṛtti;
salutation to Saṃnati; and salutation to Irā and to Vṛtti.
Salutations again and again to Vāruṇī, to Śaraṇyā, to Gaurī, and to Kālī;
salutations be to you, Kauśikī, and salutations again and again to Kātyāyanī.
Salutations to Saṃnati and to Mahimā; salutations again and again.
May there be salutation to you, Aṇimā; salutations again and again to Laghimā.
Salutation to you for worship; salutation be to you, O Śitibāhu and Sṛpti;
salutation be to you, O Saṃjñā; and salutation to Gīr and Smṛti.
Salutations be to Sarasvatī; salutations to the tongue and to vision.
Salutations to the slayer of Mahiṣa, and likewise to Sumbha and Niśumbha.
Salutations to her who has a lion-chariot and to the wielder of the trident; salutations again and again.
Salutations to the bearer of the mallet and to the one clad in armor; salutations again and again.
Salutation to the bearer of the quiver, salutation to the supporter of the world;
salutation to the wielder of the bow, and repeated salutations to the one who bears the sword.
Homage to Piñcchadhvajinī and to Dhāriṇī and to Paṭṭisa;
homage be to Bhūtamātṛ and to Skanda—homage, homage!
And also to Viśākha and Śākhā, to Naigameṣa,
to the goddess of all flavors, and to the deity of the forest.
And let there be constant salutation to the Noble One; salutations again and again to Śikhaṇḍinī.
Salutations to Nīlaśikhaṇḍinī; salutations again and again to Dīrghaveṇī.
Homage be to the slender-waisted goddess and to Wealth;
homage to Steadfastness, homage to the Pile, and repeated homage to Fame.
Salutations again and again to Dhāriṇī, who bestows good fortune upon women;
salutations again and again to Rākā, Anumati, and Sinīvālī.
Homage to Action, to Faith, and to Intelligence—homage again and again!
Homage be to Retention and to Discernment—homage again and again!
Salutations to you for the sake of removal; salutations to the primordial source of the *vaṣaṭ* call;
salutations indeed to meditative absorption (*samādhi*), to longing, and to wealth.
Homage be to you for sensation; homage again and again to you, the one of great growth.
Homage to the radiant one, to the pure one, and homage to the purity and the bright one.
Salutations again and again to the consort of Tryambaka and to Vidyā;
salutations again and again to Dīkṣā, to Dakṣiṇā, and to Jvālā.
Salutations again and again to Bhavānī, for the engagement of the senses and the cessation of actions, and for the hearing of all the Vedas.
Salutations to Durgā, the savior from distress, the sustainer of all embodied beings;
salutations to you, the deity of all gods; salutations to you, the creator of the worlds.
Homage to Śānti, homage to Kānti, and homage to the wife of Hara;
homage be to Aditi, to Dānavī, and repeated homage to Vinatā.
Salutations to Śivā and to Kartrī; salutations again and again to Prabhāvā;
salutations to Mṛkaṇḍvī, to Mārdavāhū, and likewise to Suratī.
Salutations again and again to Vinatā, to Lakṣmī, and to Surasā;
salutations to you, O Śitikaṇṭhinī, and salutations to you always from every side. Being well-disposed toward us, grant us everything that resides within our hearts.
Sanatkumāra said:
"The man or woman who, being composed, recites this daily,
shall abandon all sin committed during the nights without exception."
O Vyāsa, whoever, being pure and constantly reciting this while lying down, shall abandon whatever was committed during the day; and having died, he shall go to a happy rebirth.
Whoever should hear this constantly, or should always cause the twice-born to hear it, shall,
upon the dissolution of the body, become beloved by Pañcacūḍā.
And that mortal who, while giving up his life-breaths so difficult to relinquish, should mutter this [mantra],
shall be liberated from all sins and rejoice for ten thousand years in a celestial chariot resembling the sun, served by throngs of Apsarases.
And that man who, observing the rules on the lunar day, recites [the mantra] after worshipping the Goddess with supreme devotion, is liberated from all sins.
When his body is shattered through the mortification of the flesh in Japanāda,
that devotee becomes an attendant of the Goddess and is glorified in a holy world.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus praised by them, the goddess stood in the presence of the Lord;
then Pañcacūḍā, her face beaming with joy, spoke these words.
Listen, all you Apsarases, to the great fruit of this asceticism,
and also to the fact that you, O beautiful ones, have sought refuge in me with supreme devotion.
By my command, you shall be free from old age and sorrow, with minds eternally joyful, and beloved by the entire world.
Speak without hesitation whatever else resides in your hearts;
I shall grant you all of that. Let it be told without delay.
The Pañcacūḍās said:
"O Goddess, it is known to you that all women exist for the sake of men's purposes;
they are our clients as long as their business is not completed."
And when that task is completed, they become as if strangers to us.
Therefore, O Goddess, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to us,
O Great Goddess, let all men be under the control of all women.
The Goddess said:
"From this day forward, among all women in the worlds, men shall always be under their control and shall indeed perform every task for them."
"In the beginning and at the end, let them give gold, cattle, women, and all objects of enjoyment from all [the goddesses]; and let them remain entirely under one's control in every way."
Even if they commit many various offenses,
they will remain beloved, and no evil shall ever befall them.
Having fallen under the sway of women, they will commit improper acts even toward their mothers, fathers, brothers, friends, and even their sons.
Even though they behold falsehoods, faults, and deformities,
those men, their senses deluded by my boon, shall not see them at all.
Sanatkumāra said: Then that wife of the God of gods, the daughter of Himavat,
of auspicious countenance, took a garland and began to whirl it about.
"Be a noble woman," said the imperishable one, smiling at her beloved.
As Dāman wandered about, those flowers which fell shattered upon the ground became women with lotus-like eyes.
She said to them: "O immortals, you are devoid of old age and decay;
you cause delusion in the world and bind the hearts of men."
Entering into the world through the play of sight and touch,
you shall delude men and bring them under your power as women;
all men shall always be devoted to you.
And by my splendor, the conduct of all women shall become auspicious,
for the sake of men’s attainment of sexual enjoyment and for the sake of women’s pleasure.
Ritual actions, purifications of the auspicious limbs, and those things divine and human—
assuming many forms, they entered all the women.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having thus created those goddesses at that time and having dismissed them, she spoke to the Apsarases: "Tell me, what more shall I do for you?"
With contented minds, they said, "O Vyāsa,
may we be unslayable by gods, humans, and even by Rākṣasas.
Then the Goddess said to them, "So shall it be in the world."
Then that Lord, the Supreme Ishvara, accompanied by the Goddess, by Nandi,
and by all his attendants, entered his own abode.
Falling upon the eyes of Bhaga, the remover of the pride of the Daityas, a mass of frost for the lotus-city, the fire that consumes the fuel of the sacrifice of Kama,
traveling upon the bull of the clouds, the ender of all suffering, he whose banner is the bull in battle— the Moon-crested Lord— proceeded.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
"O Blessed One, by what means did Piṅgala attain the status of a Gaṇa?"
And that one of great splendor attained the status of a consumer of food in Vārāṇasī.
O son of Brahmā, I wish to hear from you how Kṣetrapāla was born and how he attained the state of being beloved. SkP_30.2 //
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O Vyāsa, how that Piṅgala obtained the status of Gaṇeśa,
the role of provider of food to the worlds, and the city of Vārāṇasī as his abode.
The glorious and powerful Yakṣa, the son of Pūrṇabhadra, was renowned as Harikeśa; he was devoted to Brahman and righteous.
From his very birth, he possessed unsurpassed devotion to Śarva;
he was intent upon his blessing, intent upon his salutation, devoted to him, and having him as his supreme goal.
Whether sitting or lying down, walking or standing,
moving along or even while eating or drinking, he should contemplate Rudra alone.
To him whose mind was thus disciplined, his father Pūrṇabhadra said:
"I do not consider you my son, for you have been born ill-fated, acting otherwise than you should."
"Indeed, this conduct does not belong to those born of the Yakṣa lineage. Alas, you Guhyakas are by nature cruel-minded;
you are meat-eaters, eaters of all things, and violent by habit, my son."
"Do not do this; such is not the livelihood seen for the high-souled ones.
That very way of life which was created by the Self-existent One is what is praised."
Harikeśa said:

"This mode of life, created by the Self-born One, is indeed wicked, unpraiseworthy, and always censured by the virtuous; it should be abandoned, were it not for the fact that we have no other recourse."
Therefore, householders should not perform the duties belonging to other stages of life (āśrama).
Having abandoned their human state through various karmas,
let them not seek divinity nor even a human birth again.
If their action is ordained as being dependent upon the attainment of that [state], then behold, this same action is ordained for me as well; there is no doubt in this matter.
Sanatkumāra said: Thus addressed by his son, the powerful Pūrṇabhadra spoke:
"Depart quickly; go wherever you please."
Then, having departed and abandoned his household, kinsmen, and relatives,
he reached Vārāṇasī and performed a most difficult penance.
Becoming like a pillar, with unblinking eyes, resembling dry wood or a stone,
he remained motionless, having completely restrained the collection of his senses.
Then, as he remained thus incessantly devoted to that and seeking its blessing,
a thousand divine years passed by.
O Vyāsa, he was overrun by an anthill, being devoured by ants with mouths like diamond needles,
and likewise pierced by them.
Devoid of flesh, blood, and skin, and possessing the luster of a kunda flower, a conch, or the moon, he became entirely reduced to bone; and the god considered him thus.
In the meantime, the Goddess addressed Śaṅkara:
"I wish to see this very garden once again at all times."
Indeed, I have a great curiosity to hear about the majesty of this sacred field,
since this is dear to you and because of its supreme fruit.
Thus addressed by Pārvatī, the Lord of the World, the God,
began to relate everything that had been asked in due order.
And Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, went forth together with Pārvatī;
the divine wielder of the Pināka bow showed the garden to the Goddess.
It was beautified by various kinds of blossoming shrubs, lovely with its bowing clusters of creeping vines,
and surrounded on all sides by *priyaṅgu* trees laden with sprouted flowers, as well as by thorny *ketaka* trees in full bloom.
It was densely covered everywhere with fragrant tamāla thickets and bakula trees in full bloom,
as well as forests of aśoka and puṃnāga trees in splendid flower, their clusters of blossoms swarming with swarms of bees.
In some places it resounded with birds smeared with the pollen of full-blown lotuses, uttering sweet and melodious cries;
with the calls of cranes and swans, and with the charming songs of intoxicated gallinules.
In some places it resounded with the cries of ruddy geese, in others it was filled with flocks of water-fowl;
in some places it echoed with the calls of ducks, and in others it was made tumultuous by swarms of intoxicated bees.
It was frequented by female bees intoxicated with honey and adorned with lovely, fragrant flowers;
in some places it was hidden by well-flowered mango trees and by *tilaka* trees entwined with creepers.

It was frequented by Vidyādharas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas who sang aloud; it was attended by throngs of Apsarases who danced incessantly; it was served by various kinds of joyful birds and resounded with the cries of intoxicated Hārīta flocks.

In some places it was graced by lakes and ponds filled with various kinds of blossoming, beautiful lotuses, where herds of deer had gathered here and there, their minds agitated and bowed by the roar of the king of beasts.
It was dark blue with dense *nicula* trees, delightful with peacocks, and charming with the songs of flocks of birds intoxicated with passion;
bees were clinging to the branches of flowering trees, and its peripheral boughs were adorned with the beauty of fresh sprouts.
In some places it had beautiful creepers bitten by elephants, in others beautiful trees embraced by vines;
and in some places it was frequented by the wives of the kimpuruṣas, moving with the languid grace of amorous play.
It was illuminated by numerous celestial temples of the gods, which were adorned with peaks as beautiful as the cooing of pigeons, reaching to the clouds, white and enchanting in their lovely form,
and possessing smiles in the form of clusters of scattered flowers.
The royal road was graced by reservoirs provided with canopies of thousands of blooming blue lotuses and aloe-wood incense;
it was filled with birds perched upon thickets and branches, which were variegated with the patterns of flowers fallen from the intervening paths.

Its interior was illuminated by lovely Aśoka trees, whose high-topped branches were bent at their ends by the weight of clusters of blue flowers, producing pleasure to the ear with the songs of swarms of intoxicated bees;

at night, through the light of the moon, they attained a unity with the blooming Tilaka trees, while the tips of the Darbha grass shoots were nibbled by herds of deer that had slept, awakened, and remained in the shade.
Its vast waters are clear from the lotuses stirred by the wind from the wings of swans; on its banks, peacocks dance within groves of blossoming plantain trees;
in some places, patches of earth are colored by fallen moon-like peacock feathers; and here and there, flocks of intoxicated hārīta birds are seen hidden away, sporting with joy.
In some places its regions were frequented by deer, in others it was covered with various heaps of flowers;
and in yet other places there were groves of trees where joyful and intoxicated *kiṃnara* maidens sang most sweetly.
In some places it was surrounded by the dwellings of sages, where flowers were strewn and scattered upon the ground;
in other places it was filled with vast and towering jackfruit trees, laden with fruit from their very roots.
There, perfected beings dwell within bowers of flowering atimuktaka creepers, delightful with the tinkling of the golden anklets of the wives of the siddhas;
there, bees cling to the clusters of blossoms on lovely priyaṅgu trees, while the copper-hued kadamba flowers are variegated by swarms of bees.
With the tips of its trees shaken by the wind carrying heaps of flowers, with thickets of bamboos cast down at its front by the gods,
and with herds of terrified does emerging from within its thickets, it grants liberation to embodied beings who approach it.
It was filled with beautiful tilaka trees white as a mass of moonbeams, with aśoka trees resembling vermilion, saffron,
and safflower, and with karṇikāra trees like refined gold, all possessing vast branches and clusters of blossoms.
In some places the ground was strewn with flowers resembling powdered collyrium, in some places like coral, and in others like gold.

With hundreds of birds warbling among the *puṃnāga* trees, bent low under the weight of clusters of red *aśoka* blossoms, its borders delightful with winds that dispel fatigue, and bees sporting over the blooming lotuses; (such is the place).
Then the Lord of the World, the sustainer of all the worlds, together with the daughter of the snowy-peaked mountain and his beloved lords of the Gaṇas,
showed the goddess a most delightful grove, vast with various trees and filled with intoxicated cuckoos.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, the garden has been shown to me, endowed with supreme splendor;
you ought to speak here once more of all the qualities of this sacred field."
Even having heard the greatness of this sacred field, Avimukta, at that time, I am not yet satiated; therefore, tell me more about it.
The God said:
This most secret field, Vārāṇasī, is always mine;
it is at all times the cause of liberation for all living beings.
O Goddess, in this place the perfected ones (siddhas) always abide, having taken refuge in my vow;
constantly assuming various emblems, they desire my world and,
with disciplined minds and conquered senses, practice the supreme yoga.
It was crowded with various trees, frequented by various birds,
and adorned with lakes rich in lotuses, water-lilies, and other flowers.
"In this auspicious place, which is always frequented by hosts of Apsarases and Gandharvas, a permanent residence pleases me; hear now for what purpose this is so."
With his mind fixed on me, devoted to me, and having surrendered all his actions to me,
he attains liberation here in this world in a way that it cannot be attained anywhere else.
This is my divine city, great and more secret than the secret;
Brahmā and others, as well as the Siddhas who seek liberation, know it.
Therefore, this sacred field is dear to me, and here my delight lies.
Because it has not been liberated by me, nor will it ever be liberated,
this field of mine is therefore known as "Avimukta" (the Unliberated).
Since liberation is not attained merely by bathing or by frequenting Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, Gaṅgādvāra, or Puṣkara,
this [place] is superior because it is here that liberation is obtained.
Liberation may occur either at Prayāga or here, through my acceptance;
for this very [acceptance] is remembered as greater even than Prayāga, the foremost of sacred fords.
Jaigīṣavya, that man of great austerity who attained supreme perfection,
did so through the majesty of this sacred field and through his sincere devotion to me.
The cave of Jaigīṣavya is the most excellent, desired as the abode of yogins;
for one who meditates upon me there constantly, the fire of yoga blazes intensely,
and he attains the supreme state of absolute liberation, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Liberation, which is difficult to attain anywhere else at any time, is achieved here by sages whose outward signs are unmanifest and who know all philosophical systems.
And to them I grant unsurpassed mastery in yoga,
as well as union with my own self and the desired station.
O Goddess, that great yakṣa Kubera, having dedicated all his actions in this manner,
attained the status of Gaṇeśa through the service of the sacred field.
And he who shall become Saṃvarta— he too, through devotion to me alone,
O Goddess, shall worship me right here and attain unsurpassed perfection.
The son of Parāśara, the yogi, the seer Vyāsa of great austerity,
the speaker of dharma and the future establisher of the Vedic order—
he too, O lotus-eyed one, that bull among sages, shall take delight in this sacred field.
Brahmā together with the celestial sages, Viṣṇu, Vāyu, Divākara,
Śakra the king of the gods, and whatever other inhabitants of heaven there may be— all these high-souled ones worship me here, O lady of excellent vows.
And other yogins and perfected ones, disguised in form under the great vow,
always worship me here, having become single-minded.
And by my grace, Alarka shall regain this city;
and he, having restored it as before, shall fill it with the four social orders.
Having enjoyed this prosperous land filled with people for a very long time, the king,
having surrendered all his life-breaths to me, shall attain me alone.
From that time forward, O lady of beautiful limbs, even those who dwell in this sacred field—
whether householders or ascetics— who are my devotees and intent upon me,
shall attain liberation, so difficult to reach, by my grace.
Even a man whose mind is attached to sense objects and who has abandoned delight in the Dharma,
if he dies in this field, shall not enter saṃsāra again.
Furthermore, those wise ones who are free from possessiveness, established in the welfare of beings, have conquered their senses,
observe vows, and are devoid of worldly undertakings— they are all cultivated within me.
O lady of excellent vows, having attained the dissolution of the body, the wise, freed from all attachments,
have indeed gone to the supreme liberation through my grace.
The yogi who practices for thousands of other births may attain that which he reaches here and now,
the supreme liberation, immediately upon death.
O Goddess, this great fruit of this sacred field, Avimukta, has been described by me to you in brief as the supreme secret.
"Therefore, O Goddess, there is no sacred field more secret than this;
those who know yoga and the lords of yogins on earth understand this."
This alone is the supreme knowledge; this alone is the supreme auspiciousness;
this alone is the supreme Brahman; this alone is the supreme state.
O daughter of the mountain king, Vārāṇasī is a delightful city that is the very essence of the three worlds; it is always mine.
Even mortals who have arrived here, though they have committed various misdeeds, appear free from passion through the destruction of their sins.
O Goddess, this sacred field, filled with various trees and shrubs and blossoming with flowers at will, is always remembered by me as most beloved.
Those embodied beings who die here attain the state known as liberation; even those devoted to sin, there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
In the meantime, the Lord spoke to the Goddess, the daughter of the King of Mountains.
O noble lady, I am prepared to grant a boon to this devoted Yakṣa.
"O lady of excellent hips, this devotee of mine has had his sins destroyed by austerity;
O Sovereign of the World, he is worthy to receive a boon from me."
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the World, together with the Goddess,
then went to where the Yakṣa remained— emaciated and covered with veins.
Seeing Harikesha prostrating with devotion,
the bull-bannered Lord granted him divine vision, by which he beheld Shankara.
Sanatkumāra said: Then, O Vyāsa, the Yakṣa slowly opened his eyes and beheld the God together with his attendants, seated upon his bull.
The god said:
"I shall first grant you strength, as well as the vision of the three periods of time; and with your body restored to its natural color, behold me, free from all distress."
Sanatkumāra said: Then, having obtained that boon and with his body uninjured,
he stood bowing at [his] feet, placing his joined palms upon his head.
Then that Yakṣa, being thus addressed, said, "I am a granter of boons;
O Blessed One, grant me supreme and undivided devotion unto you."

O Lord of Gods, I desire this unsurpassed boon to be granted: that I may always behold the state of being the provider of food for the worlds, as well as the imperishable leadership of the Gaṇas, within your abode at Avimukta.
The God said:
"You shall become a leader of the Gaṇas, free from old age and death, devoid of all sorrow, a bestower of boons, and honored by all."
Invincible by all, endowed with the sovereign power of yoga,
and a giver of food to the worlds, you shall become a protector of the field (kṣetrapāla).
He is of great strength, a great being, devoted to sacred knowledge, and dear to me;
he is three-eyed, holds a staff in his hand, and is likewise a great yogin.
Udbhrama and Sambhrama are your two attendants;
by your command, they shall cause confusion and agitation among the world.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, having thus made the Yakṣa the lord of the Gaṇas, the Blessed One,
the Lord of Gods and Sovereign of the Suras, went to his own abode together with him.
